title: Flower Girl in Holland
creditLine: Potter Palmer Collection
description: After studying in London, Paris, and at the Hague, Hitchcock settled in 1884 in the Netherlands, living and working for twenty years in Egmond. Attracted to the region’s landscape and peasant communities, the artist specialized in scenes featuring women in traditional dress set among voluptuous, blooming flowers. Here, Hitchcock revised the environment behind the Dutch flower seller, editing out other houses nearby in favor of a bucolic vista.
altText: Painting of a young woman outdoors in a light purple dress and head covering with a wooden yoke around her neck suspending large bundles of brightly colored flowers. She stands on a path adjacent to a river, facing the wall of a red-brick house at right.

title: Column-Krater (Mixing Bowl)
artistDisplay: Attributed to a Member of the Earlier Mannerist Group Greek; Athens
creditLine: Gift of Philip D. Armour and Charles L. Hutchinson
description: The Greeks diluted their wine with water, and it was the master of ceremonies at the symposium, or drinking party, who determined the ratio of wine to water. Both were poured into a large mixing bowl like this one decorated with a mythological scene. Salmoneus, king of Elis, pretended to be Zeus by imitating the sound of thunder and the appearance of lightning. Angered by this, Zeus here strikes Salmoneus dead with a lightning bolt.
altText: A work made of terracotta, red-figure.

title: Amphora (Storage Jar)
artistDisplay: Attributed to the Achilles Painter Greek; Athens
creditLine: Gift of Philip D. Armour and Charles L. Hutchinson
description: This vase type, called Nolan amphora after Nola, Italy, where the first examples were discovered, has a distinctive shape: an elongated body on a thick disk foot, an offset flaring neck, an inverted lip with grooves for a lid, and handles that rise from the shoulder and curve below the height of the mouth to join the neck. It probably was used to hold wine, olives, or oil. Nolan amphorae are small, usually less than 15 inches high.
altText: Terracotta vessel glazed in black, decorated with an orange figure of a woman holding a shield and a spear.

title: Stamnos (Mixing Jar)
artistDisplay: Attributed to the Chicago Painter Greek; Athens
creditLine: Gift of Philip D. Armour and Charles L. Hutchinson
description: Among the first objects purchased for the museum's collection, this ancient Greek jar was originally used to mix water and wine. Painted in the red-figure style (so called because the figures remain the natural red of the clay), this vessel portrays the women followers of Dionysos, the Greek god of wine. Remarkably this millennia-old vase retains its original lid.
altText: A work made of terracotta, red-figure.

title: Kantharos (Wine Cup)
creditLine: Gift of Philip D. Armour and Charles L. Hutchinson
description: This cup is an example of Gnathia ware, named after the ancient town (modern Egnazia) where the first examples were found. Gnathia ware is characterized by polychrome motifs and patterns created by applying purple-red, yellow, and white directly on top of black gloss before the vessels were fired.
altText: Terracotta cup with handles that appear tied in knots, a simple design around the middle, and a fluted section at the foot.

title: Kantharos (Wine Cup)
artistDisplay: Greek; Apulia, Italy probably made in Canosa, said to have been found in Tarento, Italy
creditLine: Gift of Philip D. Armour and Charles L. Hutchinson
description: This is an example of one of the most popular types of wine cup in ancient Greece, the kantharos. Rising from a round foot and a thin stem, the cup flares out to a wide bowl with two handles on opposite sides. While most examples are glazed, this elegant exception bears evidence it was once gilded. Before firing it was also inscribed with the word "Aphrodites" near the lip of the cup.
altText: Cream-colored cup with a small round foot and a thin stem. Two thin arms flare up and out from mid-cup in a "V" shape and bend inward without reconnecting to the cup. The cup's opening tapers in before flaring out again at the lip. Greek letters are inscribed on the cup between the arms and lip.

title: Fish Plate
creditLine: Gift of Philip D. Armour and Charles L. Hutchinson
description: This skillfully decorated Athenian plate was made to serve the sea life it depicts. A scallop sits between a gilt-head bream and a red mullet. Opposite them, a lettered perch confronts a spiny scorpion fish. Shells, a small fish, and a mollusk or crustacean ring the outside. The central cavity, decorated with wave patterns, would have collected the delicious juices from the cooked fish.
altText: A work made of terracotta, red-figure.

title: Lekythos (Oil Jar)
creditLine: Museum Purchase Fund
description: During the 5th and 4th centuries BCE, black vessels (commonly called black-glaze vessels) were made with increasing frequency in both Greece and southern Italy. Many of them replicate the shape of metal vessels; others have detailing that is molded or incised. While the quality of these vessels varies greatly, all would have been less expensive than vessels decorated in contemporary techniques such as red-figure.
altText: A work made of terracotta, black-glaze.

title: Ushabti (Funerary Figurine) of Horudja
creditLine: Gift of Miss Amelia B. Edwards
description: Egyptians stocked their tombs with at least one figurine called an ushabti, who acted as a servant in the afterlife. The message carved on each of the figurines explained that if the deceased is called on to do any work in the afterlife, the ushabti would respond and do the job. Some tombs had as many as one ushabti for every day of the year and another 36 overseers to keep order.
altText: A full-body figure of a human carved in what looks to be light-colored stone. The figure wears an ancient Egyptian style headdress, its arms are crossed holding symbolic instruments, and the body is covered with carved symbols.

title: The Family Concert
creditLine: Gift of Timothy B. Blackstone
description: This well-appointed interior sets the scene for the courtship ritual of music-making, through which men and women became acquainted by singing and playing instruments together. The boy in the foreground, mimicking the adults, strums a cello with a pipe and breaks a string, a subtle allusion to the perils of unbridled passion. Steen crafted his scenes upon the contemporary notion that comedy mirrors everyday life
altText: Painting of several light-skinned people gathered around a table in front of a gilded mirror, playing instruments. At left, seated next to a woman in an off-the-shoulder gown, a man in a plumed hat plays a lute. At center right, another man plays a cello, while a dog and cat eat from a dish underfoot.

title: Amphoriskos (Container for Oil)
creditLine: Gift of Charles L. Hutchinson
description: Located on the narrow isthmus that joins the Greek mainland and the Peloponnese, with natural harbors facing east and west, Corinth was the major port of trade in Greece for most of the Archaic period (700–480 BCE). Producers exported scented oil around the Mediterranean in terracotta containers like this one known as an amphoriskos, literally a "little amphora." Today they survive in the thousands.
altText: A work made of terracotta, black-figure.

title: Statuette of Osiris
dateDisplay: Late Period, Dynasty 26 or later, 664–332 BCE
creditLine: Gift of Henry H. Getty, Charles L. Hutchinson, and Norman W. Harris
description: Ancient Egyptians purchased statuettes like this one from temple workshops and deposited them in temples or shrines. They made such offerings in thanks for answered prayers or to request good health, long life, and other favors from the gods. This finely cast statuette depicts the mummified Osiris, ruler of the underworld. The god holds a shepherd’s crook and a flail, symbols of royal authority that signify his role as Egypt’s first king.
altText: A work made of copper alloy.

title: Oinochoe (Pitcher)
creditLine: Museum Purchase Fund
description: This jug was probably used to serve wine. In Corinth, vase painters embellished their pottery with real and imaginary creatures and occasionally humans and gods. These artisans explored new methods of decoration, often painting their subjects in silhouette with black gloss and with details added by incising the black to reveal the lighter clay below. Sometimes a reddish-purple or creamy white gloss was also added, as is the case here.
altText: A work made of terracotta, black-figure.

title: Necklace with Pendant
dimensions: L. 35.6 cm (14 in.) (with clasp); pendant: h. 3.1 cm (1 1/4 in.)
creditLine: Gift of Henry H. Getty and Charles L. Hutchinson
description: The Romans frequently incorporated colorful gemstones into their jewelry. This delicately woven gold chain features a single emerald pendant. At the back, a gold wire rosette fastening is decorated with a central garnet stud. Ornamental fastenings such as this were a Roman innovation, and they required a fashionable, upswept hairstyle—a clear sign of the wearer’s social standing—in order to be fully appreciated.
altText: A work made of gold, garnet, and emerald.

title: Earring with Dolphin Head Finial
creditLine: Gift of Henry H. Getty, Charles L. Hutchinson, and Robert H. Fleming
description: Originally one of a pair, this earring is formed from gold wire that is strung with one gold, one glass, and one sardonyx (stone) bead, and then terminates in the form of a dolphin head.
altText: A work made of gold, glass, and sardonyx.

title: Bracelet
creditLine: Gift of Henry H. Getty and Charles L. Hutchinson
altText: A work made of glass.

title: Hand Mirror
creditLine: Gift of Henry H. Getty and Charles L. Hutchinson
description: The round area of this object was once polished to a mirrored sheen. The handle shape references papyrus plants that grew in Egypt’s marshy regions. Together, the handle and disk evoke an image of the sun rising from a papyrus umbel (flower cluster), a symbol of the sun’s daily regeneration. The ancient Egyptian words for mirror and life are homonyms, so this object’s shape also playfully refers to the ankh hieroglyph used to write both words.
altText: A work made of copper alloy.

title: Earring
dateDisplay: New Kingdom, mid- to late Dynasty 18, about 1400–1295 BCE
creditLine: Gift of Henry H. Getty and Charles L. Hutchinson
description: This earring style was popular during the New Kingdom (about 1550–1069 BCE), when Egyptian men, women, and children of all social classes wore earrings made from glass, precious metals, or stone. This glass earring, half of a pair, was made by heating blue glass, bending it around a rod, and fusing it with a twisted cane of white-and-black glass. A wire (now broken off) through the top would have have slipped through the wearer's pierced ear.
altText: A work made of glass.

title: Earring
dateDisplay: New Kingdom, mid- to late Dynasty 18, about 1400–1295 BCE
creditLine: Gift of Henry H. Getty and Charles L. Hutchinson
description: This earring style was popular during the New Kingdom (about 1550–1069 BCE), when Egyptian men, women, and children of all social classes wore earrings made from glass, precious metals, or stone. This glass earring, half of a pair, was made by heating blue glass, bending it around a rod, and fusing it with a twisted cane of white-and-black glass. A wire (now broken off) through the top would have have slipped through the wearer's pierced ear.
altText: A work made of glass.

title: The Wedding at Cana
creditLine: Wirt D. Walker Fund
description: This depiction of the feast where Jesus performed his first miracle is filled with luxurious details and quiet, personal interactions. On the left, Jesus talks with his mother; on the right, the wedding’s astonished host and his servant taste the water Jesus has miraculously turned into wine. The piece brings together Venetian color and grandeur with the close character study popular in Crespi's native Bologna.
altText: Painting of a lively wedding reception with a man in red kneeling in front of a table. The wedding party is dressed in pale pink clothes and seated.

title: Hydria (Water Jar)
medium: terracotta, black-glaze with gilded raised clay and ribbing
creditLine: Gift of Mrs. Charles L. Hutchinson
description: The ribbed body of this vase was formed in a mold, After the feet, handles, neck, and mouth were attached, it was coated with black gloss and fired. Certain parts were left in the natural color which, along with the egg-and-dart pattern on the lower edge of the rim, provides decorative contrast. The pattern and the necklace represented on the vase's neck were made from tiny pieces of clay which were gilded.
altText: A work made of terracotta, black-glaze with gilded raised clay and ribbing.

title: Study for "Arrangement in Grey and Black, No. 2: Portrait of Thomas Carlyle"
creditLine: Gift of Emily Crane Chadbourne
description: In 1872, James McNeill Whistler began a large portrait of historian and philosopher Thomas Carlyle. He made several studies, including this one, which strongly resembles the finished painting. Concerned with harmonious arrangements of color and form, the artist focused on his sitter's black coat. The composition is strikingly similar to Whistler’s Arrangement in Grey and Black: Portrait of the Artist’s Mother, also known as Whistler’s Mother.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Skyphos (Drinking Cup)
artistDisplay: Attributed to the CHC Group Greek; Athens
creditLine: Gift of John Astley-Cock
description: This cup was shaped to fit easily in the drinker's hand and was likely used as part of ancient symposia. Much like modern academic symposia, the ancient version featured Athenian men discussing a common topic in private homes and then continuing the conversation or engaging in other acttivities well into the night. Wine played a major role in fueling these evenings; with small vessels like this one used to serve and drink it.
altText: A work made of terracotta, black-figure.

title: Mère Grégoire
creditLine: Wilson L. Mead Fund
description: Gustave Courbet played a crucial role in the development of modern French Realism. Critics and the public, however, did not easily accept his large, naturalistic, and unsentimental depictions of commonplace, often rural subjects. They called him the “apostle of ugliness.” This painting's subject, Mère Grégoire, was inspired by the heroine of a popular song, the proprietor of a brothel, written in the 1820s.
altText: Dark portrait of older woman in black dress with lace collar, flowers.

title: Bodhisattva
creditLine: Lucy Maud Buckingham Collection
description: In eighth-century China, Buddhist sculptors adopted new standards of secular beauty for spiritual figures. Whereas images of the Buddha appear sternly formal, bodhisattvas, the merciful deities that guide people toward salvation, often display more sympathetic and relatable features. This bodhisattva's graceful proportions, upswept hair, sinuous drapery, and delicate jewelry convey an appealing physical elegance.
altText: A work made of limestone with traces of polychromy.

title: Judith
artistDisplay: Jan Sanders van Hemessen (Netherlandish, active c. 1519–1556)
creditLine: Wirt D. Walker Fund
description: According to the biblical story, the widow Judith saved her people from being slaughtered by the Assyrian army by infiltrating the tent of the enemy general, Holofernes. She then seduced and beheaded him. Jan van Hemessen's life-size interpretation reflects men's ambivalence toward female agency in 16th-century Netherlands. It celebrates Judith's physical and moral strength but also foregrounds the sexuality that enabled her triumph.
altText: Painting of Judith, naked, holding sword, with head of Holophernes.

title: Mrs. George Swinton (Elizabeth Ebsworth)
creditLine: Wirt D. Walker Collection
description: John Singer Sargent was one of the most fashionable portraitists in late 19th-century Europe and America. Extravagant color and brushwork were central to Sargent’s success, as was his ability to present a refined image of his sitter. Here, Sargent accentuated Mrs. George Swinton's regal bearing and feminine dress, harmonizing the realism of her face with bursts of impressionistic brushstrokes describing her gown's shimmering fabric.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Stoke-by-Nayland
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. W. W. Kimball Collection
description: John Constable produced this full-size oil sketch for an unrealized painting near the end of his life. Its subject—the countryside of Constable's youth in Suffolk, England—was one of the artist's favorites. To achieve the effect of sparkling wetness and fresh earth and air, Constable painted with a palette knife, flecking the surface with white highlights as he sketched and scraped the picture into existence.
altText: Large English country landscape painting, farmers with horses, green trees.

title: Isabella Wolff
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. W. W. Kimball Collection
description: This portrait depicts Isabella Wolff, one of Sir Thomas Lawrence’s closest friends. Shown contemplating a printed image of the Delphic Sibyl from Michelangelo's Sistine Chapel ceiling, Wolff assumes a pose that cleverly echoes another Sibyl from that same work. Sibyls, priestesses of Classical legend who made enigmatic judgments and prophecies, were often pictured according to Western fantasies of the Near East, hence Wolff’s elaborate turban.
altText: A light-skinned woman in a long, shiny white dress sits at a desk reading a book. The book is propped on a large red pillow. Her head is propped in her hand.

title: Poppy Field (Giverny)
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. W. W. Kimball Collection
description: In July 1890, Claude Monet began four almost identically scaled canvases showing poppy fields near his home in Giverny. Although he did not consider these to be a series, like the 25 paintings of stacks of wheat that he began that same summer, the works certainly show his growing interest in developing several canvases simultaneously. They also demonstrate more uniform brushwork than his earlier landscapes.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Lady Sarah Bunbury Sacrificing to the Graces
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. W. W. Kimball Collection
description: As a portrait painter, Sir Joshua Reynolds liked to give his sitters Classical attributes and poses. Dressed in robes, Lady Sarah Bunbury pours a libation of oil as an offering to the Three Graces, positioned behind her. Her fiancé, Charles Bunbury, commissioned this marriage portrait, making her association with the Graces—symbols of fertility and attendants to the Roman goddess of love, Venus—all the more appropriate.
altText: Large painting, woman in pink dress in front of classical sculpture, shrine.

title: Irises
creditLine: Art Institute Purchase Fund
description: Irises is one of a series of paintings Monet undertook during World War I experimenting with familiar motifs on an ever-expanding scale. Lacking a discernible horizon or clear sense of depth, the viewer is both on top of and submerged its encrusted and disorienting surface. This work remained in Monet's studio long after his death in 1926 and was only rediscovered in the 1950s, having suffered damage by shrapnel from shells during World War II.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Aryballos (Cointainer for Oil)
creditLine: Gift of Mrs. Edwin Brand
description: Located on the narrow isthmus that joins the Greek mainland and the Peloponnese, with natural harbors facing east and west, Corinth was the major port of trade in Greece for most of the Archaic period (700–480 BCE). Producers exported scented oil around the Mediterranean in terra-cotta containers, such as this aryballos, that survive today in the thousands.
altText: A work made of terracotta, black-figure.

title: New England Headlands
creditLine: Walter H. Schulze Memorial Collection
description: This panoramic landscape depicts Gloucester, Massachusetts, one of Childe Hassam’s favorite destinations. During the summer months Gloucester was home to many artists, who, like Hassam, chose to emphasize its picturesque aspects such as quaint architecture and sailing vessels rather than its fish-processing plants. The composition exhibits Hassam’s broken brushwork and his use of bare canvas.
altText: A seascape painted in pastel tones, light-colored houses with red chimneys and light-green shutters in the foreground. The scene is set on a rocky, green hillside overlooking a blue sea with small sailboats.

title: Portrait of a Man Wearing an Ivy Wreath
dateDisplay: Roman Period, early to mid–2nd century
medium: Lime (linden) wood, beeswax, pigments, gold, textile, and natural resin
creditLine: Gift of Emily Crane Chadbourne
description: Painted works from antiquity rarely survive due to their delicate materials. The exception is funerary portraits painted in encaustic, or pigmented wax, like this example produced in Roman-ruled Egypt. Here, the subject’s large, heavy lidded eyes, narrow chin, and full lips express his individuality, while his thick, curly hair and neatly trimmed beard indicate the adoption of contemporary Roman fashions.
altText: A portrait of a young man with dark hair and beard painted on an irregular piece of wood. The background is gold as a wreath of ivy and necklace he wears. There are many areas where the paint has come off the surface.

title: Cat Coffin
creditLine: Gift of Emily Crane Chadbourne
description: Ancient Egyptians dedicated animal coffins, like this wooden example, to gods in temples. The enclosed mummified animal would be chosen for its specific connection to the deity whose favor was sought. The animal’s soul acted as a messenger between the human and divine realms, seeking resolution to issues such as illness or crimes committed against its dedicator.
altText: A work made of wood and plaster.

title: Denarius (Coin) Portraying Julius Caesar
dateDisplay: 42 BCE, issued by L. Mussidius Longus
creditLine: Gift of Martin A. Ryerson
description: Ancient Rome began producing coinage in the late 4th century BCE. Early coins depicted gods and goddesses. It was not until 44 BCE that a portrait of a living person—Julius Caesar—appeared on coins. Thereafter coins showed a sovereign’s portrait on the front, and the ruler’s accomplishments on the back. This coin portrays Caesar wearing a laurel crown on one side and on the other a rudder, globe, cornucopia, caduceus, and apex (priest’s cap)
altText: A work made of silver.

title: Aureus (Coin) Portraying Emperor Otho
creditLine: Gift of Martin A. Ryerson
description: After the death of Emperor Nero, a chaotic power struggle saw four generals, one after another, rule and die in quick succession. The harsh character of these emperors, including Otho (reigned January–April 69), were emphasized by the features of their coin portraits, like Otho's double chin and vain curls in his portrait on the front of this coin. The back shows Securitas standing, with a wreath in his right hand, a scepter in his left.
altText: A work made of gold.

title: Aureus (Coin) Portraying Emperor Caracalla
creditLine: Gift of Martin A. Ryerson
description: The front of this coin portrays a bust of Emperor Caracalla, wreathed and wearing a breastplate and military cloak. The back depicts the Greco-Egyptian sun god Serapis standing with his right hand raised and holding a scepter. Emperor Caracalla began as co-emperor with his brother Geta. Within a year of the death of their father, Caracalla killed Geta in order to rule alone.
altText: A work made of gold.

title: Aureus (Coin) Portraying Emperor Aurelian
creditLine: Gift of Martin A. Ryerson
description: On the front of this coin is a portrait of Roman Emperor Aurelian. He wears armor and is crowned with a wreath of laurel. On the back is a rearing lion carrying a thunderbolt in his mouth. Inscriptions on coins help identify the ruler. While the front side depicted the sovereign’s portrait, the back was often used to communicate the ruler’s accomplishments or aspirations.
altText: A work made of gold.

title: Stater (Coin) Depicting a Shield
creditLine: Gift of Martin A. Ryerson
description: Though ancient Greece's population was largely illiterate, it could identify the place of origin of a coin by its imagery. Many of these images referred to myths that were associated with the history of the city. The distinctive shield shown on the front of this coin was particular to the Theban army. It remained a symbol of the city for centuries. The back of this coin depicts a volute krater (mixing bowl) with wreath above.
altText: A work made of silver.

title: Drachm (Coin) Depicting the Goddess Hera
creditLine: Gift of Martin A. Ryerson
description: The front of this coin depicts the goddess Hera, while the back shows a square labyrinth of the Minotaur myth. The Minotaur, born to the queen of Crete, was hidden away in a labyrinth, where he yearly he devoured sacrificial youth. He was killed after his sister, Ariadne, helped the hero Theseus navigate the labyrinth using a ball of string. This story was so famous that anyone seeing the labyrinth on this coin knew that Knossos was its source.
altText: A work made of silver.

title: Stater (Coin) Depicting a Horseman
artistDisplay: Greek; minted in Taras (now Taranto), Italy
creditLine: Gift of Martin A. Ryerson
description: The front of this coin depicts a nude man galloping on a horse and holding a shield. The back depicts Taras, also nude, riding on a dolphin. According to the founding myth of the city of Taras (Tarentum), when Taras was lost at sea, a dolphin rescued him and deposited him on the shore of Calabria in Italy; it was there that the city of Taras grew and prospered. This coin was made 400 years after the city’s founding.
altText: A work made of silver.

title: Stater (Coin) Depicting the Siren Parthenope
artistDisplay: Greek, minted in Neapolis (now Naples), Italy
creditLine: Gift of Martin A. Ryerson
description: Coins like this were issued during the festivals and games dedicated to Parthenope, the siren of The Odyssey, who after failing to lure Odysseus with her song, drowned herself and washed to shore where she was honored as a local goddess. The front of this coin depicts the head of Parthenope, a symbol beside it. The back depicts a man-headed bull to right, crowned by Nike.
altText: A work made of silver.

title: Drachm (Coin) Depicting the Gorgon Medusa
creditLine: Gift of Martin A. Ryerson
description: The ancient city of Neapolis (near modern Kavala, Greece) was famous for horse-breeding, so they chose to honor the snake-haired Medusa, mother of the miraculous winged horse Pegasus, on the front (obverse) of their coins. On the back (reverse), they depicted the maiden Parthenos, a local moon goddess and patron of the city. These images helped link Neapolis to a set of Greek deities and myths shared by city-states across the Mediterranean.
altText: A work made of silver.

title: Hecta (Coin) Depicting the Goddess Demeter
artistDisplay: Greek, minted in Lesbos, probably Mytilene
creditLine: Gift of Martin A. Ryerson
description: This coin was produced by a mint shared by two rival cities on the island of Lesbos, Mytilene and Phocaea. The front (obverse) depicts the head of Demeter, the island's patron goddess. Veiled and crowned with grain, she wears her hair rolled at the brow and sports a circular earring. The back (reverse) depicts a tripod lebes, a cauldron in a three-legged stand used for religious ritual.
altText: A work made of electrum.

title: The Banks of the Marne in Winter
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Lewis Larned Coburn Memorial Collection
description: Exhibited at the Salon of 1866, Pissarro made this work in deliberate opposition to the pastoral scenes of his mentor and unofficial teacher Camille Corot. Instead of using various brushes to create a beautifully crafted and refined surface, he loaded his paint on heavily in emulation of Gustave Courbet. The empty landscape, is resolutely unpicturesque and purposefully devoid of the great oaks and ancient ruins of traditional Salon landscapes.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: The Beggar Boy (The Young Pilgrim)
creditLine: Charles H. and Mary F. S. Worcester Collection
description: Art historians long identified the subject of this painting as a beggar boy; however, it is now believed to portray the artist’s oldest child, Giacomo, in the costume of a pilgrim bound for Santiago de Compostela, Spain, where the apostle James reputedly settled. Carrying a loaf of bread and a rosary, Giacomo sports the hat and staff of a Santiago pilgrim.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Portrait of Balzac
creditLine: Gift of Silvain and Arma Wyler
description: In 1891 Auguste Rodin was commissioned by a literary society to produce a posthumous monument to the French writer Honoré de Balzac. Over the course of seven years, the sculptor created numerous studies, including this deliberately ungainly nude portrait. A departure from the idealized classical bodies typical of public statuary, this study stresses Balzac’s vitality and candor through its bold modeling, imposing torso, and confident stance.
altText: A work made of bronze.

title: Serving Dish (Tabaq) with Vegetal and Fish-Scale Patterns
medium: Iznik ware, fritware with underglaze painting in blue, turquoise, red, and black on white slip
creditLine: Gift of Martin A. Ryerson
description: When Iznik pottery production began in the late 15th century, its style and colors were influenced by Chinese porcelain. By the late 16th century, when this dish was made, Iznik potters had developed their own distinctive style of colorful floral and abstract motifs. Here, atop a fish-scale motif, we see two opposing leaves in the saz (reed) style, referring to the reed pen used by Persian and Turkish artists to create black-ink drawings.
altText: A work made of iznik ware, fritware with underglaze painting in blue, turquoise, red, and black on white slip.

title: Shukongojin
creditLine: Kate S. Buckingham Endowment
description: This statue of Shukongojin, the Buddhist Thunderbolt Diety, would have originally stood guard at a temple and was intended to frighten away any thoughts or entities that might distract devotees in the sacred temple space. A fierce protector of the Law of Buddhism, he brandishes a vajra, a ritualistic weapon symbolizing the power of wisdom to penetrate ignorance and destroy evil.
altText: A wooden sculpture of a muscular red figure with flaming hair and a third eye, stares fiercely down at us. Left head raised over head holds a vajra, a ritual object.

title: The Annunciation
creditLine: Potter Palmer Collection
description: In George Hitchcock’s unusual presentation of the Annunciation, the virgin is depicted as a Dutch peasant girl standing in a field of lilies. The lily is a symbol of the angel Gabriel, and Mary’s downcast eyes imply that she has received his divine message. Hitchcock spent much of his life in Holland, and his choice of a religious subject, unusual composition, and interest in light effects synthesizes elements of several European art movements.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Fudo Myo-o
medium: Wood with polychromy and gilt-bronze accessories
creditLine: Gift of the Joseph and Helen Regenstein Foundation
description: One of five myo-o, or lords of light, whose threatening appearance guards the Law of Buddhism, Fudo Myo-o is equipped to guide the spiritual traveler past temptation on the path to enlightenment. This finely modeled figure of Fudo Myo-o, which means “the immovable or unshakable one,” reflects the highly detailed, realistic direction taken by Japanese sculptors in the Kamakura period (1185–1333).
altText: A wooden sculpture of an angry looking diety, holding a sword in his right hand and ope in his left, sitting cross-legged on an stylized rock formation

title: Te burao (The Hibiscus Tree)
creditLine: Joseph Winterbotham Collection
description: Completed early in Paul Gauguin’s first Tahitian sojourn, this landscape shows the artist grappling with representing an unfamiliar environment. Rather than documenting botanical species scientifically, Gauguin focused on the artistic potential of their variegated colors, textures, and forms. The human figure in the distance and the dog roaming through fallen branches activate the landscape and establish a sense of scale.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: The Capture of Samson
creditLine: Robert A. Waller Memorial Fund
description: This subject of this panel comes from a story in the Hebrew Bible in which the mighty Samson awakes to find that his lover, Delilah, has cut off his hair, the source of his strength. Rubens drew from ancient Roman sculpture for Samson’s contorted pose, while the strong contrast of light and dark recalls the work of Italian painter Tintoretto.
altText: A work made of oil on panel.

title: Beggar with Oysters (Philosopher)
creditLine: Arthur Jerome Eddy Memorial Collection
description: This work and Beggar with a Duffle Coat (Philosopher) were probably conceived as companion pieces. Manet exhibited them together in 1872, along with paintings of an absinthe drinker and a ragpicker, under the collective title Philosophers. Parisian beggars held a particular fascination for Realist artists and writers. By setting his large-scale figures against empty, dark backgrounds, Manet added to their portraitlike, indeed heroic, presence.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Coast of Maine
creditLine: Arthur Jerome Eddy Memorial Collection
description: Winslow Homer observed the shoreline in various weather conditions and seasons after moving to live in near isolation in Prouts Neck, Maine, in 1883. Amid the remote and dramatic landscape, he depicted seascapes void of human life, focusing instead on an emotional response to nature. His marine scenes, larger than his earlier works, emphasize the vastness and power of the sea.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Painting with Troika
artistDisplay: Vasily Kandinsky Born Moscow (formerly Russian Empire, now Russia), 1866; died Neuilly-sur-Seine, France, 1944
medium: Oil on cardboard; in artist's painted frame
creditLine: Arthur Jerome Eddy Memorial Collection
description: Vasily Kandinsky was a founding member of Blaue Reiter (Blue Rider), a loose alliance of artists based in Munich. Often working in a common palette and using expressive brushwork, they shared a belief in the symbolic and spiritual importance of forms and colors, including their effect on emotions and memories. Blaue Reiter also promoted a intuitive approach to painting, looking to non-Western, European medieval, and folk art for inspiration.
altText: Vibrant colored painting of beachscape with figures, structure, and ox pulled cart.

title: Improvisation No. 30 (Cannons)
artistDisplay: Vasily Kandinsky Born Moscow (formerly Russian Empire, now Russia), 1866; died Neuilly-sur-Seine, France, 1944
creditLine: Arthur Jerome Eddy Memorial Collection
description: In his 1912 book Concerning the Spiritual in Art, Vasily Kandinsky advocated for an art that could move beyond imitation of the physical world, inspiring, as he put it, “vibrations in the soul.” Between 1910 and 1914 he produced a series of “improvisations," which he described as unconscious, spontaneous expressions. This painting—one of his first improvisations—is a standout work within the museum's modern art collection.
altText: Abstract painting in various bright colors—yellow, blue, red, green, orange, pink—with lines indicating building-like structures as well as canons in the lower right corner.

title: The Bewitched Mill
creditLine: Arthur Jerome Eddy Memorial Collection
description: Among the German Expressionists, who used strong color and exaggerated form to express emotional content, Franz Marc was unique in his empathic interest in animal life. He painted this work following a sojourn to the Italian town of Merano. Its title refers to the "magical" harmony he sensed there between human life, represented by the houses and mill on the left, and nature, embodied by the lyrical region of trees and animals on the right.
altText: Vibrantly colored geometric painting of a central white and blue waterfall with birds visible through it. A stylized red jungle cat and black wild boar drink at bottom right. Red water wheel at left, angular blue and white cityscape top at left, tree top at right.

title: Seated Guanyin
medium: Paulownia wood with polychromy and gilding
creditLine: Lucy Maud Buckingham Collection
description: Guanyin is the Bodhisattva of Compassion, one of the most beloved Chinese Buddhist deities. He can be identified by the small figure of Amituo (Amitabha), Buddha of the Western Paradise, in his headdress. His pose—seated with one leg hanging and his right arm resting on the other knee—further distinguishes him as Guanyin of the Southern Sea, a reference to the deity’s island home.
altText: A work made of paulownia wood with polychromy and gilding.

title: Oribe-Type Ewer
creditLine: Gift of Robert Allerton
description: The military general Furuta Oribe (1544–1615) was a tea connoisseur whose style of presentation at tea gatherings catered to the samurai class and rulers of 17th-century Japan. In contrast to his predecessors, Oribe preferred tea wares that were bold and eccentric rather than subtle and rustic. He was the first to recognize the beauty of artfully misshapen ceramics for use in tea gatherings.
altText: Greenish brown ceramic kettle with floral and geometric designs.

title: Head of Guanyin
dateDisplay: late Northern Qi/Sui dynasty, late 6th century
medium: Marble with traces of metal fittings at crown
creditLine: Samuel M. Nickerson Collection
description: Serene benevolence emanates from this beautifully sculpted marble head of the bodhisattva Guanyin, made in far northern China in the late sixth century. The figure has many classic Buddhist features, including the concave forehead circle (urna)—an auspicious mark from which wisdom radiates—and elongated earlobes, an allusion to the aristocratic Indian custom of wearing heavy earrings and thus to the Buddha's early life as an Indian prince.
altText: A large marble head with eyes closed and a serene expression, a large incised crown of figures upon her head.

title: Stater (Coin) Depicting a Land Tortoise
creditLine: Gift of Mrs. William Nelson Pelouze
description: Coins of Aegina depicted images of sea turtles when the island of Aegina was the supreme sea power among the Greek city-states. After its defeat by Athens in 458 BCE, Aegina stopped using the sea turtle and substituted the land tortoise to symbolize its lost sea power, as on the front of this coin. On the back is a geometric design of a square divided into five triangles.
altText: A work made of silver.

title: Drachm (Coin) Depicting the Goddess Nike
creditLine: Gift of Mrs. William Nelson Pelouze
description: One of the last coins issued by the Bruttii after being conquered by the Romans, this coin depicts the goddess Nike on the front and the god Pan, crowning himself, on the back. The image of the winged goddess Nike was a favorite of the Bruttii, but a profile face of Nike is rare because of the difficulty in rendering the goddess’s trademark wings. Here, the artist daintily tucked them on either side of her throat.
altText: A work made of silver.

title: Stater (Coin) Depicting Pegasus
creditLine: Gift of Mrs. William Nelson Pelouze
description: The front of this coin depicts the winged horse Pegasus, facing toward the left in flight. On the back is the head of Athena Chalinitis ("the bridler"), an epithet of the goddess that refers to her role in inventing the bridle and bit, initially to tame Pegasus. She is shown facing left; behind her head is a dove surrounded by a wreath.
altText: A work made of silver.

title: Diobol (Coin) Depicting an Ear of Grain
creditLine: Gift of Mrs. William Nelson Pelouze
description: The front of this coin depicts an ear of barley. The back features a bull with its head and horns facing downwards. The city-state Metapontum that made this coin became wealthy through farming rather than trade, so the depiction of grain on its coins reminded its trading partners of its agricultural abundance.
altText: A work made of silver.

title: Tetradrachm (Coin) Depicting the Goddess Tyche
creditLine: Gift of Mrs. William Nelson Pelouze
description: In antiquity, the goddess Tyche symbolized cities. Her identifying feature is a crown shaped like the walls of a city. The front of this coin depicts the goddess Tyche wearing a turreted crown. On the back, the goddess Nike stands facing left while holding a palm branch. Some cities chose Tyche as their emblem, but often they also selected another divinity as their particular patron and protector.
altText: A work made of silver.

title: Aureus (Coin) Portraying Emperor Antoninus Pius
creditLine: Gift of Mrs. William Nelson Pelouze
description: Starting in 96 CE with the reign of Emperor Nerva, Rome was ruled by five wise leaders known as the “Good Emperors.” Nerva (reigned 96–98) was an honest and respected senator who ushered in a period of peace and prosperity, which is suggested by the sheer abundance of coins produced during this era as well as by the skill of the images created. Antoninus Pius (reigned 138–161), continued Nerva's example, ruling over a strong and prosperous Rome.
altText: A work made of gold.

title: Mirror with "TLV" Pattern
dateDisplay: Eastern Han dynasty (25–220 CE), about 1st century
dimensions: Diam.: 21 cm (8 1/4 in.); Thickness: D.: 0.5 cm (3/16 in.)
creditLine: Samuel M. Nickerson Endowment
description: The design of this mirror reflects principles of ancient Chinese cosmology that envisioned a circular universe enclosing a square earth. Within the border of the square are characters denoting the 12 animals of the Chinese zodiac. This mirror was designed to place its owner at the center of the cosmos, a favorable position symbolically protected by the Animals of the Four Directions.
altText: A work made of bronze.

title: Tibor chocolatero (Chocolate jar)
artistDisplay: Workshop unknown (Viceroyalty of New Spain, present-day Mexico) Puebla, Mexico
medium: Earthenware and tin glaze, with iron
creditLine: Gift of Eva Lewis in memory of her husband, Herbert Pickering Lewis
description: Talavera poblana, a tin-glazed earthenware, has been made in the Mexican town of Puebla since the 16th century. Though its colors and motifs were influenced by fashionable imported ceramics, Spanish and Mexican artisans adapted designs to reflect local cultural symbols. The owners of this jar likely added the locking metal lid to protect valuables such as cocoa beans, which were expensive at this time.
altText: A work made of earthenware and tin glaze, with iron.

title: Knight, Death, and the Devil
medium: Engraving in black on ivory laid paper
creditLine: Robert Alexander Waller Memorial Fund
description: Albrecht Dürer’s masterful engraving is meant to prompt reflection on the inevitability of mortality. Lurking behind the knight on his muscular warhorse, the skeletal figure of Death sits astride his aging steed and demonstrates the running hourglass of Time. The juxtaposition of the knight and Death suggests the knight’s impending demise, though he shows no outward signs of fear or of temptation by the devil, who follows closely behind.
altText: A work made of engraving in black on ivory laid paper.

title: Adam
creditLine: Gift of Robert Allerton
description: Auguste Rodin's figure of Adam was originally intended to be paired with a sculpture of Eve to flank his monumental bronze portal, The Gates of Hell, for the Musée de Arts Décoratifs, Paris. Rodin created over 200 of its figures and groupings, exploring the expressive potential of the human body. However, the museum building was never constructed and the portal never completed as originally conceived.
altText: Dark colored sculpture of muscular man standing in a contorted pose.

title: Salome with the Head of Saint John the Baptist
creditLine: Louise B. and Frank H. Woods Purchase Fund
description: Guido Reni was the most famous and successful Italian painter of his day. This painting depicts Salome receiving the head of John the Baptist on a platter, the gruesome reward she chose for having pleased her stepfather, Herod, by performing a seductive dance. This episode from the New Testament had long been popular in Italian art thanks to its combination of religiosity, violence, and eroticism.
altText: Large painting of woman, in gold and pink dress, placing severed head on platter.

title: Portrait Head of a Young Woman
creditLine: Edward E. Ayer Endowment in memory of Charles L. Hutchinson
description: This portrait is the likeness of a young woman in her early 20s who had a delicate brow, high cheekbones, wide-set eyes, a bow-shaped mouth, and a prominent chin. Her long hair is arranged in an elaborate fashionable hairstyle, in which the hair was parted in the center, combed in waves over the forehead, and plaited into braids that were wrapped around the head like a turban. Broken off at the neck, it was once part of a larger statue.
altText: A work made of marble.

title: Maitreya Buddha
creditLine: Gift of Alice Getty
description: Seated depictions of the Buddha originated in Indian art, perhaps in portraits of Indian royalty. The Chinese reserved this imagery for Maitreya (Chinese: Mi-le), the Buddha of the Future, who waits in a cosmic heaven before descending to earth. This figure of Maitreya is about to step off his throne into this world, fulfilling the hopes and prayers of the faithful.
altText: A work made of limestone.

title: Woman at Her Toilette
creditLine: Stickney Fund
description: Rendered with feathery brushstrokes in shades of lavender, pink, blue, white, and gray, this Impressionist painting captures a subject often explored by male artists of the day but seldom broached by the period's few women artists. Morisot presents a decidely female perspective, intimate yet not eroticized. She signed her name along the bottom of the mirror, as if to suggest that the image in her painting is as ephemeral as a silvery reflection.
altText: Painted portrait dominated by loose, large brushstrokes of a woman, seen from the back, wearing a gauzy white off-the-shoulder dress and black choker, blond hair swept up, examining herself in a mirror at left. The background is a feathered swirl suggesting floral pattern in cool pale tones of gray, purple, pink, and blue.

title: Bell (nao)
creditLine: Lucy Maud Buckingham Collection
description: Bells are among China's earliest percussion instruments. This example was designed to be mounted on its hollow stem with its curved mouth facing up and struck from the outside with a mallet. Unlike other types of bronze bells that were assembled as chime sets, this one was intended to be played as an individual instrument. It may have been sounded during ceremonies or military campaigns.
altText: A bell with two convex sides of nearly rectangular shape and an opening at top rests on a slim cylindrical base. It boasts a green patina and is decorated with a geometric pattern and spikes. A small portion is missing at upper right.

title: Dragon-Handled Amphora 三彩双龙耳瓶
dateDisplay: Tang dynasty, (A.D. 618–907), 1st half of 8th century 唐 (公元 618-907),八世纪前半段
medium: Earthenware with three-color (sancai) lead glazes 三彩铅釉陶器
creditLine: Lucy Maud Buckingham Collection
description: Many scholars suggest that this distinctive Tang form may have been inspired by earlier Hellenistic ceramic and glass vessels, such as the Greek amphora. If so, Chinese artisans thoroughly transformed that ancient shape. They created a high-shouldered silhouette with a slender neck gracefully framed by curved handles, whose dragon heads bite the cupped mouth-rim in their open jaws.
altText: A work made of earthenware with three-color (sancai) lead glazes 三彩铅釉陶器.

title: Sōgyō Hachiman
medium: Wood with traces of white pigment
creditLine: Gift of the Joseph and Helen Regenstein Foundation
description: This sculpture depicts the Shinto deity Hachiman, specifically Sōgyō Hachiman, or “Hachiman in the guise of a monk.” The cult devoted to Hachiman originated at Usa in northeast Kyushu, a site near the Korean peninsula and also a prominent early Buddhist center. Buddhism had been introduced into Japan in the sixth century, and monks became one of the most recognizable symbols of its practice.
altText: A work made of wood with traces of white pigment.

title: Ritual Impersonator of the Deity Xipe Totec
creditLine: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Samuel A. Marx
description: The god of the late dry season and early rainy season (May–June), Xipe Totec (“The Flayed One”) signifies regeneration. By the time of Spanish contact in 1519, the worship of this deity was widespread throughout Mesoamerica. During agricultural fertility ceremonies dedicated to Xipe Totec, young men would wear the skin of a sacrificed victim, as depicted in this figure—an embodiment of the relationship between death and the renewal of life.
altText: A work made of ceramic and pigment.

title: Theodosius Repulsed from the Church by Saint Ambrose
creditLine: Clyde M. Carr Fund
description: This painting depicts an event from the year 390 when Ambrose, the archbishop of Milan, refused to give communion to Emperor Theodosius I until he made public penance for the massacre of thousands. The brushwork and arrangement of figures showcase Alessandro Magnasco’s fluid, energetic style. However, for the background, he most likely employed an unidentified specialist in architectural painting.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Fragment of a Stela of Neferhotep
artistDisplay: Egyptian; probably Theban Tomb 216, Deir el-Medina, Egypt
creditLine: Lois H. Culver Fund
description: Stelae, or commemorative stones, like this example allowed nonroyal Egyptians to demonstrate their devotion to the gods. The hieroglyphs at the top of this fragment identify the man depicted as Neferhotep, a foreman of the workers who built the royal tombs in Thebes. Finely dressed, Neferhotep raises his hands before him in a gesture of adoration toward the deity, who would have been depicted in the upper portion of the stone.
altText: A fragment of scarved stone shows a figure in profile, with its arms raised in front of him. He wears a wig and a garment with pleated sleeves. Above him are hieroglyphics.

title: Statue of Shebenhor
creditLine: Gift of Mrs. George L. Otis
description: While we might think of portraits as capturing an individual’s likeness, for the nonroyal Egyptians, it was the addition of a name in hieroglyphs that identified them; their facial features and clothing were determined not by physical likeness but by contemporary styles. The inscriptions on the front and back of this statue distinguish it as a representation of a man named Shebenhor.
altText: A work made of basalt.

title: Young Spartan Girls Challenging Boys
creditLine: Charles H. and Mary F. S. Worcester Collection
description: This picture takes its subject from the life of Lycurgus. The legendary ninth-century BCE Spartan lawgiver made many social reforms including physical training in which adolescent girls competed on an equal footing with boys, exercising nude in public. Degas would have worked up this monochromatic sketch with layers of color had he completed it, but he left it unfinished when he began a second version of the subject.
altText: A brown-toned image of a group of scantily clad young women at left, one holding out her arm toward a group of naked young men standing at right.

title: Herself
creditLine: Walter H. Schulze Memorial Collection
description: Robert Henri painted Himself and Herself (Irish terms of endearment for a husband and wife) during a summer trip to Ireland; the canvases depict the fisherman Johnnie Cummings and his wife, Biddy. The rich hues and thick, lush paint add depth to the works, while the figures’ elusive expressions and informal poses give them a brusque, forthright quality.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Himself
creditLine: Walter H. Schulze Memorial Collection
description: Robert Henri painted Himself and Herself (Irish terms of endearment for a husband and wife) during a summer trip to Ireland; the canvases depict the fisherman Johnnie Cummings and his wife, Biddy. The rich hues and thick, lush paint add depth to the works, while the figures’ elusive expressions and informal poses give them a brusque, forthright quality.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Portrait Head of Antinous
creditLine: Gift of Mrs. Charles L. Hutchinson
description: This portrait depicts Antinous (about 111–130), the young lover of Emperor Hadrian (reigned 117–38). His characteristic features include an oval face, smooth complexion, almond-shaped eyes, full lips, and thick, wavy locks. This sculpture is a fragment, and for many years it was unclear what form the original, intact work had taken. Recent scholarship indicates that it once belonged to a bust of Antinous currently in the Palazzo Altemps in Rome.
altText: A work made of marble.

title: Karttikeya, Commander of the Divine Army, Seated on a Peacock
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by Mr. and Mrs. Sylvain S. Wyler
description: This basalt sculpture, carved in the round, depicts Karttikeya, the Hindu god of war, with six heads (shanmukha) and 12 arms, 10 of which hold weapons. According to legend, Karttikeya was born from the spilled seed of the Hindu divinity Shiva. He developed his six heads in order to nurse from his six mothers, the Pleiades (or Krittikas—hence his name, Karttikeya), a constellation of stars.
altText: Gray statue with multiple heads and arms seated on Peacock.

title: Coast Scene, Bathers
creditLine: Walter S. Brewster Collection
description: James McNeill Whistler dedicated much of his artistic practice to capturing the mood and color harmonies of marine scenes. In this intimately scaled seascape, he employed the sparest of compositional elements to evoke a coastal atmosphere. Broad horizontal bands of blues and gray suggest sky, ocean, and sand, with dabs of thin pigment giving economical yet expressive form to around a dozen figures on the windswept beach.
altText: A work made of oil on panel.

title: Study of a Girl's Head and Shoulders
creditLine: Walter S. Brewster Collection
description: In addition to large-scale portraits, James McNeill Whistler created small-scale likenesses, often on wood panel, as in this painting of a young sitter. A well-known beauty, Olga Caracciolo lived in Dieppe, France, likely where this work was executed, and later married the photographer Adolf de Meyer. Rather than a swift, abbreviated study for a larger composition, Whistler considered a work such as this to be a satisfying aesthetic whole.
altText: A work made of oil on panel.

title: Auvers, Panoramic View
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Lewis Larned Coburn Memorial Collection
description: Paul Cezanne made this work while being mentored by Impressionist Camille Pissarro. He rendered the unusual perspective—looking down onto the rooftops of Auvers and out to the distant countryside—with blocky, energetic patches of color and areas of ragged brushwork that might seem unfinished. These choices mark Cezanne's attempt to communicate not merely the landscape’s appearance but also the feeling of seeing it and painting it.
altText: View of a village surrounded by hills, fields, and trees, shown from a vantage point above the scene. Subtly rolling hills recede into a bluish gray-ish sky punctuated by white clouds. Thick brushstrokes built up atop each other are visible throughout.

title: The Vase of Tulips
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Lewis Larned Coburn Memorial Collection
description: Typical of Cezanne’s work, this painting is carefully considered and the composition hard-won: the traces of at least three other pieces of fruit at lower left attest to Cezanne's struggles to make the arrangement work. Even in the final version, there remains a tense spatial relationship between the objects, which seem to float in the picture plane rather than being anchored to the tabletop.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: The Millinery Shop
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Lewis Larned Coburn Memorial Collection
description: When this work was painted, millinery work (hat making) was considered a prestigious trade, elevating the women who succeeded in the business. Degas addressed this subtle shift in the class hierarchy: He gave his milliner a dress nice enough to be worn by an affluent woman, and though she does not wear the expected hat of a high-class lady, Degas playfully positioned the hat with green trimmings so it seems to sit atop the woman’s head.
altText: Impressionist painting of woman wearing green dress trying on hats.

title: Henri Degas and His Niece Lucie Degas (The Artist's Uncle and Cousin)
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Lewis Larned Coburn Memorial Collection
description: Perhaps the most subtle portrait painter in the Impressionist group, Edgar Degas painted this double portrait in the mid-1970s. It shows his orphaned first cousin, Lucie, and their uncle Henri, in whose care the girl had recently been placed—two people who are tentatively accepting the circumstances of their new relationship. Having recently lost his own father, Degas addressed his subjects with awareness and sensitivity.
altText: Impressionist painting of seated man, girl with brown, black hues.

title: Woman Reading
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Lewis Larned Coburn Memorial Collection
description: Édouard Manet was a pivotal figure in the development of Impressionism and modern art. Here, an elegantly dressed Parisian woman reads a magazine, a beer close at hand—a scene that would have struck contemporary viewers as fashionable and modern. While the woman appears to be outdoors, one of Manet’s paintings serves as a backdrop and other props suggest the scene was staged in Manet’s studio.
altText: A young woman in a dark hat and coat with light ruffled collar sits reading a large periodical held up in her gloved hands. Flowers and foliage are suggested behind her.

title: The Beach at Sainte-Adresse
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Lewis Larned Coburn Memorial Collection
description: In 1867 Monet stayed with his aunt in Sainte-Adresse, a suburb of the port city of Le Havre in Normandy, where the artist grew up. Monet began the painting outdoors but likely revised it in his studio. Technical analysis of the work revealed that it started as a beach scene of yachts and tourists but ultimately became a view of sailboats and local fishermen.
altText: Painting of a beach on a cloudy day with several sailboats on the water, a few rowboats on the shore, and two groupings of people on the sand.

title: Cliff Walk at Pourville
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Lewis Larned Coburn Memorial Collection
description: In the 1880s, Monet went to paint in Normandy and became increasingly enamored of his surroundings. He wrote to his second wife and her children: "How beautiful the countryside is becoming, and what joy it would be for me to show you all its delightful nooks and crannies!" Eventually they joined him in Pourville. The two young women strolling here are probably the eldest daughters.
altText: Painting of a cliff overlooking the sea. Two figures in long dresses, one with a parasol, stand on the cliff beneath blue sky.

title: Stacks of Wheat (End of Day, Autumn)
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Lewis Larned Coburn Memorial Collection
description: Through 1890 and 1891, Monet created a series of paintings depicting the stacks of wheat that stood outside his farmhouse in Giverny. He worked both in the field, painting simultaneously at several easels, and in the studio, refining pictorial harmonies. In this view, and in nearly all of the autumn views, the conical tops of the stacks break the horizon and push into the sky.
altText: Painting mostly in soft yellow, green, purple, blue, and pink of two wheatstacks, the right nearer than the left, in a country landscape at sunset.

title: Vétheuil
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Lewis Larned Coburn Memorial Collection
description: In summer 1901 Monet rented a house in Lavacourt across the Seine from Vétheuil. He began 15 paintings of Vétheuil from the balcony of the same restricted view, documenting the changes in light throughout the day. Rather than replicating the area’s topography, he emphasized the decorative over the descriptive qualities of this riverscape. His loose brushwork and subtle color transitions dissolve the borders between the water, land, and sky.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Young Woman Sewing
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Lewis Larned Coburn Memorial Collection
description: This painting's model may be the woman Renoir went on to marry, Aline Charigot. He depicted her here with vibrant color, a light-filled atmosphere, and freely handled paint. While blue dominates the composition, there are striking contrasts of red and touches of yellow. These primary colors in close proximity optically mix, enlivening the composition with a sense of spontaneity.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Two Sisters (On the Terrace)
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Lewis Larned Coburn Memorial Collection
description: Despite the title, the young women in this painting were not actually sisters. The older girl in the center gazes absently beyond her younger companion, whose red cheeks suggest that she just dashed into the picture. These casual expressions make this “sisterly” moment feel genuine. Renoir juxtaposed the girls’ figures against a dreamy landscape, the basket of yarn evoking an artist’s palette.
altText: Impressionist painting of two girls on balcony, bright flower hat, knitting basket.

title: Moulin de la Galette
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Lewis Larned Coburn Memorial Collection
description: With this painting of the dance hall known as the Moulin de la Galette, Toulouse-Lautrec established his reputation as the chronicler of the Montmartre district’s famed nightlife. A wooden barrier bisects the composition, dividing the frenzied action of the dance floor in the background from the stillness of the women waiting in the foreground.
altText: A scene in brown and green tones of people dancing indoors. In the foreground, three women stand near boothed tables while a man sits.

title: Mural Fragment Depicting a Maguey Bloodletting Ritual
artistDisplay: Teotihuacan Tlacuilapaxco apartment compound, Teotihuacán, Mexico
creditLine: Ada Turnbull Hertle Endowment Fund
description: The ancient Mexican city of Teotihuacan was once the largest city in the Americas. Its pyramid facades and palace interiors were frequently decorated with splendid frescoes. This fragment was part of a cycle painted on the interior walls of an aristocratic palace. It shows a rain priest with a speech-scroll adorned with seashells and plants, indicating a prayer for water and agricultural prosperity.
altText: Fragment of a mural from the city of Teotihuacan mural painted in red and white tones that depicts a ritual figure with speach scroll and scatting sacred bjects.

title: At Mouquin's
creditLine: Friends of American Art Collection
description: William Glackens here portrayed members of his circle at a New York restaurant. The proprietor’s wife shares a drink with a wealthy playboy and restaurateur, while the artist’s wife and an art critic are reflected in the mirror. By combining portraiture and everyday scenes, Glackens helped usher in a mode of painting suited to the uncertainties and new social activities of modern urban life.
altText: Opulently dressed light-skinned man and woman drink at a small table. A mirror behind them reflects a crowd. Her blue dress and dark hat dominate.

title: Saint George and the Dragon
creditLine: Gift of Mrs. Richard E. Danielson and Mrs. Chauncey McCormick
description: Bernat Martorell was one of the greatest painters in Catalonia, Spain, during the first half of the 15th century. Here, he rendered a frequently depicted episode from the popular legend of Saint George, in which the model Christian knight saves a town and rescues a beautiful princess. George’s halo and armor and the scaly dragon are richly modeled with raised stucco decoration.
altText: St. George on white horse, piercing green, gold dragon

title: Resting
creditLine: Gift of Charles Deering McCormick, Brooks McCormick, and Roger McCormick
description: In Resting, 19th-century Italian painter Antonio Mancini uses an impasto technique—the brushwork clearly visible from the thickly applied paint—to evoke the haziness between wakefulness and sleep. Mancini combines his interest in the French avant-garde with the rich palettes and dark tonal contrasts of Italian Baroque painting, applying his oils with ecstatic and reckless abandon.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Equestrienne (At the Cirque Fernando)
creditLine: Joseph Winterbotham Collection
description: This work, set at a circus, captures the tense moment in which a female trick rider prepares to stand up on her horse and leap through a paper hoop held by a clown. Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec may have based the rider, dressed in a tutu of gauze and sequins, on Suzanne Valadon, a former circus performer, model, and artist with whom he had a relationship.
altText: Painting of a performance inside a circus ring. A man wearing a suit holds a whip in his hand and looks towards a woman with red hair riding a gray horse and wearing a green dress. Audience members wearing suits and top hats watch from red and white benches on the side.

title: The Beheading of Saint John the Baptist
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection
description: These six paintings illustrate scenes from the life of Saint John the Baptist. We see John enter the wilderness to live as a hermit, foretell Christ’s role as redeemer, be imprisoned, and finally be martyred at the request of Salomé, the step-daughter of King Herod. The artist, Giovanni di Paolo, represented figures multiple times to indicate their movement through highly imaginative and stylized settings.
altText: A headless figure leans out of the first-floor window of a light-colored stone building from which two iron bars have been detatched, his blood spurting to the ground. A figure bends to collect the head while another looks away to sheath a long sword. From right, a robed man beholds the guesome scene.

title: Processional Cross with Saint Mary Magdalene and a Blessed Hermit
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection
description: Representative of the early work of Lorenzo Monaco, a monk and leading Florentine painter, this Crucifixion boasts delicate colors and simplified forms that are exceptionally well preserved. The panel has a hole drilled at the base, allowing it to be mounted on a pole and used as a processional cross, likely in the monastic Camaldolese community where Lorenzo had lived and worked.
altText: Framed gold panel of the Crucifixion, kneeling figures, flying angels.

title: Portrait of Jean Gros (recto); Coat of Arms of Jean Gros (verso)
artistDisplay: Rogier van der Weyden (Netherlandish, c. 1399–1464) Workshop of Rogier van der Weyden (Netherlandish, c. 1399–1464)
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection
description: This portrait was once part of a diptych. The sitter—identifiable through his coat of arms, personal motto, and initials on the panel's back—is Jean Gros, an administrator to the future duke of Burgundy. His prayerful gaze was originally directed at the other panel depicting Mary and the infant Jesus. Rogier van der Weyden created similar diptychs for the Burgundian court's highest level of patrons.
altText: Painted dark colored portrait of man, hands in prayer.

title: The Annunciation
artistDisplay: Jean Hey (Master of Moulins; Netherlandish, c. 1480-c.1504)
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection
description: Jean Hey, known as the Master of Moulins, was a leading painter in 15th-century France. Here, he captured the moment the archangel Gabriel announced to Mary that she would give birth to a son. The painting once formed the right side of an altarpiece, with the left side depicting Mary’s own Immaculate Conception and a central section, now lost, featuring the enthroned Virgin and Child.
altText: Painting of the Annunciation, dove flying above Mary with angel.

title: An Elegant Company
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection
description: A master of scenes of finely dressed revelers known as “merry companies,” Pieter Codde here demonstrated his sharp sense of composition. He animated a gathering of guests and attendants through a complex network of gestures, glances, and poses, with a young woman dressed in luxurious silver satin at center. Such images of joyful gatherings would have functioned as models of polite behavior to cosmopolitan art collectors.
altText: A work made of oil on panel.

title: Friar Pedro Offers Shoes to El Maragato and Prepares to Push Aside His Gun
artistDisplay: Francisco José de Goya y Lucientes (Spanish, 1746–1828)
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection
description: In small, lively paintings made for his own pleasure or a few patrons, Francisco de Goya explored satirical and popular aspects of Spanish life. This series was inspired by the capture of notorious criminal El Maragato in 1806. After escaping from prison and committing theft, El Maragato tried to take Friar Pedro de Saldivia and other innocent people hostage. The friar outsmarted the bandit, however, shooting him in the thigh and tying him up.
altText: A work made of oil on panel.

title: Friar Pedro Wrests the Gun from El Maragato
artistDisplay: Francisco José de Goya y Lucientes (Spanish, 1746–1828)
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection
description: In small, lively paintings made for his own pleasure or a few patrons, Francisco de Goya explored satirical and popular aspects of Spanish life. This series was inspired by the capture of notorious criminal El Maragato in 1806. After escaping from prison and committing theft, El Maragato tried to take Friar Pedro de Saldivia and other innocent people hostage. The friar outsmarted the bandit, however, shooting him in the thigh and tying him up.
altText: A work made of oil on panel.

title: Friar Pedro Clubs El Maragato with the Butt of the Gun
artistDisplay: Francisco José de Goya y Lucientes (Spanish, 1746–1828)
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection
description: In small, lively paintings made for his own pleasure or a few patrons, Francisco de Goya explored satirical and popular aspects of Spanish life. This series was inspired by the capture of notorious criminal El Maragato in 1806. After escaping from prison and committing theft, El Maragato tried to take Friar Pedro de Saldivia and other innocent people hostage. The friar outsmarted the bandit, however, shooting him in the thigh and tying him up.
altText: A work made of oil on panel.

title: Friar Pedro Shoots El Maragato as His Horse Runs Off
artistDisplay: Francisco José de Goya y Lucientes (Spanish, 1746–1828)
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection
description: Francisco de Goya explored satirical and popular aspects of Spanish life. This work, from a series about the notorious criminal El Maragato, features his capture. After escaping prison, El Maragato spent two months stealing food, guns, and money before trying to take Friar Pedro de Saldivia and other people hostage. The friar outsmarted the bandit, however, seizing his gun and shooting him in the thigh.
altText: Small painting, friar shoots man with yellow pants as horse runs off.

title: Friar Pedro Binds El Maragato with a Rope
artistDisplay: Francisco José de Goya y Lucientes (Spanish, 1746–1828)
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection
description: In paintings made for his own pleasure, Goya explored popular aspects of Spanish life. This series was inspired by the capture of notorious criminal El Maragato by Friar Pedro de Saldivia. After escaping from prison, El Maragato spent two months stealing food, guns, and money before trying to take Friar Pedro and other people hostage. The friar outsmarted the bandit, however, seizing his gun, shooting him in the thigh and finally tying him up.
altText: A work made of oil on panel.

title: The Music Lesson
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection
description: One of Ochtervelt’s finest works, The Music Lesson was probably painted in Rotterdam, where the artist spent most of his career. The delicate light, which illuminates the girl and leaves the youth partly in shadow, is indebted to Johannes Vermeer, who worked in the nearby city of Delft. Characteristic of Ochtervelt, however, are the angled poses and the playful interchange between the figures.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Innocence Prefers Love to Riches
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection
description: In this allegorical work, a personification of Innocence at center signals her preference for Love, represented as a cupid, over Riches, taking the form of a woman in Grecian robes and offering a chest of golden baubles. Prud’hon complicated this straightforward parable by manipulating the figures’ postures: while Innocence embraces Love, she gazes longingly over her shoulder at Riches, inviting us to wonder about the finality of her decision.
altText: A work made of oil on panel.

title: Virgin and Child with Saints Dominic and Hyacinth
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection
description: In this altarpiece, Giovanni Battista Tiepolo conceived the traditional subject of the Virgin and Child with saints as if the two figures have miraculously appeared on an altar. The infant hands a rosary to Saint Dominic, who founded a preaching order closely associated with the rosary's use. The altar cloth shows key events in the lives of Mary and Jesus, which believers would have meditated on while repeating the prayers marked by rosary beads.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Rinaldo and Armida in Her Garden
creditLine: Bequest of James Deering
description: This is the second of four large paintings in a sequence by Giovanni Battista Tiepolo depicting the crusader Rinaldo and the sorceress Armida. Here Armida has abducted Rinaldo and carried him away to her magical garden. She looks into a magic mirror while the knight sits enthralled, gazing into her eyes. Meanwhile, Rinaldo’s two companions, Carlo and Ubaldo, arrive to persuade him to return to their quest to seize control of Jerusalem.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Armida Encounters the Sleeping Rinaldo
creditLine: Bequest of James Deering
description: Giovanni Battista Tiepolo’s work epitomizes the brilliant exuberance of the Late Baroque style. Internationally renowned, Tiepolo was often commissioned to transform palaces and monasteries in Venice and elsewhere in Italy, as well as in Germany and Spain. This painting and three others at the Art Institute once graced the cabinet of mirrors, a richly decorated room in the Venetian palace of the powerful Cornaro family.
altText: Large painting of soldier asleep outdoors surrounded by two women and a cupid.

title: Armida Abandoned by Rinaldo
creditLine: Bequest of James Deering
description: This is the third of four scenes from Giovanni Battista Tiepolo’s decorative Rinaldo and Armida suite. At the emotional climax of the story, the knight Rinaldo has been persuaded by his companions, Carlo and Ubaldo, to renounce his love for the sorceress Armida. Bareheaded and pensive, Rinaldo has taken up his shield again and appears to hesitate as the older knights gesture toward the boat that will carry them back to the crusader army.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Rinaldo and the Magus of Ascalon
creditLine: Bequest of James Deering
description: The fourth and final large narrative canvas from Giovanni Battista Tiepolo’s decorative Rinaldo and Armida suite takes place as Rinaldo rejoins the crusader army. The magician of Ascalon uses Rinaldo’s shield to conjure the heroic deeds of his ancestors and urge him to live up to their legacy. In his choice to return to battle, Rinaldo would have served as a positive example of civic duty for the family who commissioned these decorations.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: No te aha oe riri (Why Are You Angry?)
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection
description: In this canvas, women of varying ages appear to go about daily life within a colorful, stylized outdoor environment. Like much of Gauguin's work, the composition combines observed detail with artistic fantasy to create a dreamlike scene that resists simple interpretation. Its deliberately provocative title enhances this effect, leaving us to wonder if the “you” refers to someone in the painting or to the viewer.
altText: A work made of oil on jute canvas.

title: The Flight into Egypt
creditLine: Gift of Mrs. Michael W. Straus in memory of Michael Straus
description: The flight into Egypt—a common subject in European art—refers to an episode in the life of Christ when his family fled King Herod, who sought to kill the infant Jesus. Abraham van Diepenbeeck made the theme his own by including an angel and the inquisitive cow at bottom right. This panel was not intended to be a finished painting; it is instead a grisaille (monochrome grey) oil sketch, which could then translated into an engraving.
altText: A work made of oil on panel.

title: Charing Cross Bridge, London
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection
description: Beginning in September 1899, Claude Monet made almost 100 paintings of the river Thames. These works show only three different views—Charing Cross Bridge and Waterloo Bridge, both painted from the Savoy Hotel, and the Houses of Parliament, painted from Saint Thomas’s Hospital. In the smoggy, industrial city, Monet challenged himself to capture effects of light seen through a dense atmospheric screen.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Brooklyn Bridge
creditLine: Gift of Charles L. Hutchinson
description: Although best known for his rural views, Ranger primarliy lived in New York City and was inspired by the urban environment. Here, he recorded a true icon of modernity. Completed in 1883, the Brooklyn Bridge was still the world's longest suspension bridge when he painted it 16 years later. Yet instead of emphasizing its massive scale or modern construction, Ranger produced a fairly traditional view, integrating the bridge into the landscape.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Apples and Grapes
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection
description: Monet probably painted this and other still lifes knowing that they would be more marketable than his landscapes. Here, however, he used the complexity of color, light, and texture found in his most Impressionist landscapes. Particularly evident in the cloth's surface—the light on the horizontal brushstrokes recalls earlier works in which he used similar horizontals of variegated colors to suggest water rippling in the sunlight.
altText: Apples and grapes rest in a shallow wicker basket on a table covered with a light-colored cloth. Additional fruit is scattered on the table.

title: Beata Beatrix
creditLine: Charles L. Hutchinson Collection
