description: Dante Gabriel Rossetti was a founder of the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood, a circle of Victorian artists united in their regard for medieval aesthetics. Inspired by his namesake, Dante, Rossetti drew parallels in this work between the Italian poet's love for Beatrice and his own affection for his deceased wife and muse, Elizabeth Siddal, a talented artist and writer who died at age 32.
altText: Serene red-haired woman, framed with allegorical symbols of red bird, sundial.

title: The Artist's House at Argenteuil
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection
description: Claude Monet and his family lived in Argenteuil, outside Paris, from 1871 to 1878. In this painting, he depicted his five- or six-year-old son, Jean, playing with a hoop, and his wife, Camille, standing in the doorway of their vine-covered house. The pleasant weather and neatly kept garden, a forerunner of the artist’s celebrated garden at Giverny, give a sense of tranquility and well-being.
altText: Among potted flowers and lush foliage, a tiny child in a white dress plays with a hoop. A woman peers at the child from an ivy-covered building at right.

title: Stack of Wheat (Snow Effect, Overcast Day)
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection
description: Through 1890 and 1891, Monet created a series of paintings depicting the stacks of wheat that stood outside his farmhouse in Giverny. He painted at several easels simultaneously in the field and then refined pictorial harmonies in the studio. In most of the winter views, like this one, the stacks seem wrapped by bands of hill and field, as if bedded down for the season.
altText: A lone wheat stack, in shadow, rests on a snow-covered field that is rendered in shades of white, blue, yellow, and purple. A house can be seen in the distance on the right against the blue hills beyond.

title: Branch of the Seine near Giverny (Mist)
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection
description: Claude Monet painted the 18 works in his Mornings on the Seine series from a flat-bottomed boat anchored to the riverbank where the Epte River flows into the Seine. There, as the light changed from dawn to day, he worked on one canvas after another. To keep them in order, he numbered them, placed them in grooves built into the boat, and had the gardener whom he enlisted as his assistant hand them to him.
altText: Painting of softly rendered shapes in pale blue, green, and white. A textured green mass at left resembles foliage. Blue and white cloud-like forms fill the rest of the frame.

title: Arrival of the Normandy Train, Gare Saint-Lazare
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection
description: The Impressionists frequently paid tribute to the modern aspects of Paris, depicting scenes of grand boulevards and modern constructions. Monet made 12 paintings of the Gare Saint-Lazare. Here, he focused on the glass-and-iron train shed, where he found an appealing combination of artificial and natural effects: the rising steam of locomotives trapped within the structure and daylight penetrating the large, glazed sections of the roof.
altText: Loosely painted image of an open-air train station. On the right, a parked train gives off an enormous plumb of white smoke, making the scene look as though it were full of clouds. A huddled mass of barely discernible people crowd around the train on both sides of the tracks. Blue, green, and gray tones dominate.

title: Vétheuil
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection
description: In the summer of 1901, Claude Monet rented a home across the Seine from Vétheuil and not far from his property at Giverny. From the balcony of his rental he began 15 paintings of Vétheuil, all of which feature the same view of the riverbank and town—punctuated by the church—and document the changes in light throughout the day. The Art Institute holds two paintings from this series, one from midday and another from sunset.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Houses of Parliament, London
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection
description: Monet painted the Houses of Parliament in the afternoon and at sunset from a terrace at Saint Thomas’s Hospital. This viewpoint was close to that of the English artist J. M. W. Turner in his visionary paintings of the fire that had destroyed much of the old Parliament complex in 1834. In his response to the poetry of dusk and mist, however, Monet was actually inspired by the work of a more recent painter of the Thames, James McNeill Whistler.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: The Seine at Port-Marly, Piles of Sand
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection
description: Of all the landscapes Alfred Sisley painted in and around France's Marly-le-Roi, where he lived from 1875 to 1878, this scene of workers dredging sand to facilitate barge traffic is perhaps the most original. Unlike other Impressionists who showed the Seine River as a place of weekend leisure for Parisians, Sisley depicted the river during the workweek, along with some of the men who depended on it for their livelihood.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Old Tower at Avignon
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection
description: Depicting a 14th-century fortress in southern France, Samuel Colman's Old Tower at Avignon captures the romance of the age-old structure amid sunlight, storm clouds, and reflections on the Rhône River. An accomplished landscapist, Colman began his career depicting New England scenery, as did his contemporaries among the Hudson River School, the dominant style of landscape painting in mid-19th-century America.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Virgin and Child with the Young Saint John the Baptist
creditLine: Charles H. and Mary F. S. Worcester Collection
description: This painting provides a revealing glimpse into the workshop practice of Agnolo Bronzino. Three examples of the composition are known: an original version and two copies, including this one. All are unfinished. This version and the other copy follow a cartoon, or pattern drawing, based on the original work, and may be from a later date. It is unclear why these replicas were begun and then abandoned.
altText: A work made of oil on panel.

title: Eve after the Fall
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection
description: Eve owes its genesis to The Gates of Hell, Rodin's commission from the French government in 1880, whose sculptural doors led Rodin back to the art of Lorenzo Ghiberti and Michelangelo. Eve recalls Michelangelo’s panels from the Sistine Chapel Ceiling and Masaccio’s Expulsion from the Garden of Eden. Its naturalism shocked critics when it was first exhibited, since Eve seemed to them more like a flesh-and-blood woman than an idealized creation.
altText: A work made of marble.

title: Virgil Reading the "Aeneid" to Augustus, Octavia, and Livia
creditLine: Wirt D. Walker Fund
description: In the late 18th centurly, the French Academy and artist Jacques-Louis David promoted Classical subjects in history paintings as moral exemplars for contemporary audiences. Here, Wicar, one of David's students, depicted the Roman emperor Augustus and his family listening to Virgil’s reading of his epic poem The Aeneid. The emotionally charged gestures of the family suggest that they identify with the heroic events of the poem.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Ceremonial Knife (Tumi)
artistDisplay: Chimú Lambayeque Valley, north coast, Peru
creditLine: Ada Turnbull Hertle Endowment
description: Naymlap, the heroic founder-colonizer of the Lambayque Valley on the north coast of Peru, is thought to be the legendary figure represented on the top of this striking gold tumi (ceremonial knife). It would have been carried by a dynastic ruler during state ceremonies to represent, in a more precious form, the copper knives used for animal sacrifices.
altText: Gold knife with figure on handle, round turquoise inlays on crown.

title: Yellow Dancers (In the Wings)
creditLine: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Gordon Palmer, Mrs. Bertha P. Thorne, Mr. and Mrs. Arthur M. Wood, and Mrs. Rose M. Palmer
description: Edgar Degas first painted dancers as an independent subject in 1871. He would go on to devote almost half his output as an artist to this subject, observing countless performances and rehearsals at the Paris Opéra. Here, he placed the viewer in the wings, as if among the elite opera subscribers who paid for the privilege to roam and socialize backstage.
altText: Three light-skinned, dark-haired ballerinas, painted in muted tones, wear off-the-shoulder yellow leotards and tutus as they huddle near each other. One adjusts her costume, while one holds her hands clasped above her head. At left is a painted screen with four pairs of feet visible underneath.

title: Arlésiennes (Mistral)
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Lewis Larned Coburn Memorial Collection
description: One of 17 canvases that Paul Gauguin completed during a brief and tumultuous visit with Vincent van Gogh in Arles, this powerful and enigmatic painting depicts the public garden directly across from Van Gogh’s house. The painting's large, flat areas of color, arbitrary handling of space, and enigmatic silhouettes exemplify the deliberateness with which Gauguin sought visual harmony and symbolism in his work.
altText: Painting of four women with blue shawls walking near red fence.

title: Final Study for "Bathers at Asnières"
creditLine: Gift of the Adele R. Levy Fund, Inc.
description: Georges Seurat made this painting as a preparatory work for his monumental Bathers at Asnières, now in the National Gallery, London. It shows men and boys on the bank of the Seine River in the working-class Parisian suburb of Asnières. The view presented here is just across the river from the leisure park Seurat immortalized in his best-known work, A Sunday on La Grande Jatte—1884.
altText: A work made of oil on panel.

title: Tea Bowl
medium: Jian ware; dark-gray stoneware with dark-brown glaze and overglaze “hare’s fur” markings in iron oxide
creditLine: Lucy Maud Buckingham Collection
description: This type of Song dynasty blackware—iron-rich, chocolate-brown stoneware with lustrous dark glazes—is popularly referred to as temmoku, the Japanese name of a mountain in south China and the site of a Buddhist monastery where Japanese monks treasured bowls like this example for tea-drinking rituals. The conical shape fit perfectly in cupped hands, and the color visually intensified the milky froth of white tea.
altText: A work made of jian ware; dark-gray stoneware with dark-brown glaze and overglaze “hare’s fur” markings in iron oxide.

title: Rabbit Warren at Pontoise, Snow
creditLine: Gift of Marshall Field
description: Along with Impressionist painters Claude Monet and Alfred Sisley, Pissarro pursued the theme of snow throughout his career, producing nearly 100 “snow” paintings. In 1879 France experienced an extraordinarily severe winter, which Pissarro explored in this and other works painted at his home in Pontoise, 30 miles west of Paris. Here snow covers the ground, houses, and vegetation in a frothy coat that resulted from the artist’s vigorous brushwork.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Étretat: The Beach and the Falaise d'Amont
creditLine: Gift of Mrs. John H. (Anne R.) Winterbotham in memory of John H. Winterbotham; Joseph Winterbotham Collection
description: Monet arrived in Étretat, on the Normandy coast, with his family for a vacation in September 1885. By the time he left in December he had initiated 51 canvases, many of which he reworked back at his studio in Giverny. The majority feature the rock formations that flank the bay of Étretat. These subjects proved to be among Monet’s most precipitous and enchanting: the location was as physically dangerous to navigate as it was sublime to behold.
altText: At seascape rendered in pastel tones. At right, boats line a pink shore underneath a tall cliff. At left, a single red sailboat floats in blue water.

title: Rocks at Port-Goulphar, Belle-Île
creditLine: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Chauncey B. Borland
description: Belle-Île, a small island off the southern shore of Brittany, was known for its dramatic cliffs, rock formations, and grottoes. As he often did, Monet misjudged the time he would need to explore and capture the beauty of the place, which he variously called “lugubrious,” “terrifying,” and “very beautiful.” He came for two weeks and stayed for more than two months.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Paris Street; Rainy Day
creditLine: Charles H. and Mary F. S. Worcester Collection
description: Considered Caillebotte’s masterpiece, this view of a busy intersection captures both an everyday moment and all that was new in a rapidly changing Paris. The clothes are the latest fashion. The retractable umbrella was just invented. And a decades-long renovation had transformed the medieval streets of Paris into grand boulevards, like the ones seen here. It's a painting you want to walk into.
altText: Life-size painting of an urban scene in Paris. A man in a top hat holding an umbrella and a woman in a long fashionable dark dress walk arm in arm toward the viewer as other city dwellers with umbrellas walk in various directions across cobblestone roads and sidewalks.

title: El Maragato Threatens Friar Pedro de Zaldivia with His Gun
artistDisplay: Francisco José de Goya y Lucientes (Spanish, 1746–1828)
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection
description: In paintings made for his own pleasure, Goya explored popular aspects of Spanish life. This series was inspired by the capture of notorious criminal El Maragato by Friar Pedro de Saldivia. After escaping from prison, El Maragato spent two months stealing food, guns, and money before trying to take Friar Pedro and other people hostage. The friar outsmarted the bandit, however, seizing his gun, shooting him in the thigh and finally tying him up.
altText: A work made of oil on panel.

title: Waterloo Bridge, Sunlight Effect
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection
description: If not for the fog, Monet remarked, “London wouldn't be a beautiful city. It’s the fog that gives it its magnificent breadth.” While working on his London Series, Monet painted Waterloo Bridge early in the morning and moved on to Charing Cross Bridge at midday. He finished his London works in his Giverny studio, working until he was satisfied with them as an ensemble.
altText: Horizontal oil painting in shades of pale purple, pink, and light blue of a bridge composed of multiple linked archways over water, engulfed in hazy fog. Various indistinct, colorful forms cross the bridge, and factory smokestacks rise in the distance.

title: Buddha Shakyamuni Seated in Meditation (Dhyanamudra)
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by Mr. and Mrs. Robert Andrew Brown
description: Seated in a posture called the lotus, this serene 12th-century Buddha rests his hands and feet atop one another as he gazes downward, his eyelids lowered, the touch of a smile on his lips. The symbols that distinguish him as a great being—such as the urna on his forehead and ushnisha on top of his head—are delicately carved in the hard granite.
altText: Dark stone sculpture of Buddha sitting cross-legged, hands in lap, eyes closed.

title: Saint Francis Kneeling in Meditation
artistDisplay: El Greco (Doménikos Theotokópoulos; Greek, active in Spain, 1541–1614)
creditLine: Robert A. Waller Memorial Fund
description: Saint Francis appears here surrounded by symbols associated with his sainthood. The book, for example, speaks to his devotional studies, and the skull is a reminder of the inevitability of death. The painting prompts the viewer to meditate upon the saint in the same way that he prays before the sculpture of the crucified Jesus.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Kitchen Scene
creditLine: Robert A. Waller Memorial Fund
description: In this kitchen scene, a type known as a bodegón (Spanish for pantry), Diego Velázquez depicted a young African woman at work, surrounded by exquisitely rendered pots and jugs and a crumpled paper wrapper for spices. Slavery was widespread in the young artist’s hometown of Seville—Velázquez, his father, and his teacher were all enslavers. Velázquez may have used an enslaved woman from one of these households as a model for this painting.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Carpet
medium: Wool, plain weave with supplementary wefts forming cut pile through a technique known as "Spanish knots"
creditLine: Gift of Mrs. Richard Ely Danielson
description: Since this carpet was made for the Royal Monastery of Santa Clara in Spain, wear and likely two extensive restorations have changed it significantly. Over a century ago skilled restorers replaced designs in the carpet’s well-worn areas, but they used dyes that have changed in color—most notably a pink hue has replaced the original brown. Today, research into the carpet's original workshop, the restoration workshop, and the dyestuffs is ongoing.
altText: A work made of wool, plain weave with supplementary wefts forming cut pile through a technique known as "spanish knots".

title: Duck-Shaped Ewer with Daoist Priest
medium: Stoneware with celadon glaze and underglaze incised decoration
creditLine: Bequest of Russell Tyson
description: One of the notable artistic accomplishments of Korea's Goryeo period was the production of sculptural celadons like this duck-shaped vessel. The duck’s tail forms a handle, which supports a human figure who holds a bowl to receive wine, and its beak is the spout. The figure's clothing indicates he is a Daoist immortal and suggests this ewer was used for ritual or ceremonial purposes.
altText: A work made of stoneware with celadon glaze and underglaze incised decoration.

title: Pastoral Scene
creditLine: Charles H. and Mary F. S. Worcester Collection
description: This painting of a half-naked boy holding a basket of grapes has been interpreted as the infant Bacchus, the god of wine, although Piazzetta, one of Vencie's leading painters, made no reference in his description. The artist was probably responding to his patron’s taste for pastoral scenes, a genre that appealed to middle- and upper-class city dwellers for its idealized views of rural life.
altText: A light-skinned woman, the bodice of her mauve dress pulled down, lounges against a rock, her arm extended on it. A child, mostly nude, stands in front of her looking downward while two men in her party, largely in shadow, lean toward each other as if in conversation.

title: Statuette of an Enthroned Figure
creditLine: Wirt D. Walker Endowment
description: Most ancient Roman homes had domestic shrines called lararia that included bronze statuettes of household gods (the Lares) and other deities. This statuette likely belonged to such a shrine and is thought to depict Concordia, the Roman personification of harmony, a principal virtue of the Roman Empire. She likely held a libation dish in her right hand and a cornucopia in her missing left hand.
altText: A work made of bronze and silver inlay.

title: Virgin and Child with the Young Saint John the Baptist
creditLine: Clyde M. Carr Fund
description: This intimate devotional panel, an early work by Antonio da Correggio, reveals the young artist's evolving style. The distant landscape demonstrates his awareness of Northern European precedents, and the figural composition references the manner of Raphael, while its soft outlines recall Da Vinci. The gentle sensuousness of the figures and the tenderness they show one another, however, are unique to Correggio.
altText: Vividly colored painting of Virgin Mary with baby Jesus and baby John the Baptist.

title: Shiva as Lord of the Dance (Nataraja)
creditLine: Kate S. Buckingham Fund
description: In this sculpture, the Hindu divinity Shiva, depicted as the Lord of the Dance (Nataraja), performs a cosmic dance that sets in motion the rhythm of life and death. Considered one of the most sublime images in Indian art, the dancing Shiva destroys everything, allowing creation to start all over again. His right leg, planted on the demon of darkness, stamps out ignorance.
altText: A bronze sculpture of the Hindu divinity Shiva. Shiva, who has two pairs of arms, is depicted dancing inside of a circular ring. Balancing on one leg, Shiva gestures his arms to the side and front, as his loose locks of hair flow behind him.

title: Triptych with Scenes from the Life of Christ
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection
description: Ivory was used to make highly prized devotional objects in the Gothic era. This triptych, featuring scenes from the life of Jesus Christ, might have been kept on a stand or cabinet in a bedroom and used as a focus for prayer along with an illuminated Psalter or Book of Hours. The intimate scale and movable wings made the triptych easy to store or carry.
altText: Three connected ivory panels carved with scenes from the life of Jesus.

title: Crucifixion Relief from a Rosary Bead
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection
description: Private prayer and contemplation were fundamental to Catholic practice. The intimate scale and detailed workmanship of this wooden bead was intended to inspire both visual and spiritual wonder. The sequence and number of beads in a rosary also gave structure to prayers; rosaries could also be personalized with detailed ornaments, like a prayer nut carved to depict Jesus's crucifixion.
altText: A work made of wood.

title: The Adoration of the Eucharist
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection
description: Rubens designed this elaborate oil sketch as part of a tapestry series intended for a convent in Madrid. He created two tiers of celebrants—the heavenly on the upper level and the earthly on the lower level. The series’ patron, Spanish archduchess Isabella Clara Eugenia, is represented in a nun’s habit at the lower left to signify her piety and reinforce her status as an important patron of the arts in the ruling family.
altText: A work made of oil on panel.

title: Bullfight
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection
description: Manet’s trip to Spain in the fall of 1865 lasted about 10 days, though it had a profound impact on him. In a letter to his friend the poet Charles Baudelaire, he described a bullfight he attended in Madrid as “one of the finest, most curious and most terrifying sights to be seen.” He made quick sketches there that informed several later canvases, including this one.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Wine Cistern
creditLine: Mary Waller Langhorne Endowment
description: Elaborately fashioned platters, vessels, and containers, often decorated with embellishments that indicated their owner’s status, were displayed on the banquet tables of Renaissance Italy. Cisterns such as this were filled with cold water and used to cool wine bottles at feasts. Decorated by the Italian ceramic painter Francesco Durantino, this work typifies the Renaissance interest in both Christian imagery and scenes from pagan antiquity.
altText: Large bowl completely covered in scenes of battles on land and sea.

title: The Herring Net
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection
description: One of the most influential American painters of the 19th century, Winslow Homer is known for his dynamic depictions of both upper-class leisure pursuits and nature's power and beauty. The paintings he created after 1882 focus almost exclusively on humankind’s contest with nature. Here, Homer depicted the heroic efforts of fishermen hauling in an abundant catch of herring while steadying their boat amid turbulent swells.
altText: Painting of two fishermen in small wooden boat on rocky seas.

title: The White Bridge
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection
description: The White Bridge depicts a brook that traversed John Henry Twachtman's Connecticut property. The artist painted at least six versions of the bridge over six years, changing its shape slightly in each work. Twachtman may have altered the actual bridge or simply changed its appearance in each painting. Loosely rendered with feathery brushstrokes, and incorporating expanses of unprimed canvas, this scene captures the verdant blossoming of spring.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: New Year’s Eve Fox Fires at the Changing Tree (Ōji shozoku enoki omisoka no kitsunebi), from the series One Hundred Famous Views of Edo (Meisho Edo hyakkei)
artistDisplay: Utagawa Hiroshige 歌川 広重 Japanese, 1797-1858
creditLine: Clarence Buckingham Collection
description: Unlike most prints by Utagawa Hiroshige, this work is based on folklore. Japanese tradition holds that on New Year’s Eve, foxes gather at a specific tree near the Oji Inari Shrine in preparation for a visit there. On the way to the shrine, the foxes produce distinctive flames from their mouths that the local farmers can use to predict the coming year's crops.
altText: A work made of color woodblock print; ōban.

title: On a Balcony
creditLine: Gift of Mrs. Albert J. Beveridge in memory of her aunt, Delia Spencer Field
description: Shown at the 1880 Impressionist exhibition, 'On a Balcony' depicts a woman in a private garden surrounded by flowers rendered in energetic brushstrokes of red, blue, yellow, and pink. Cassatt signaled the modernity of her subject through the woman’s choice of reading material: she peruses a newspaper rather than a novel, demonstrating that even at home, Cassatt’s subjects are connected to the contemporary world.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Madame de Pastoret and Her Son
creditLine: Clyde M. Carr Fund and Major Acquisitions Endowment
description: The French Revolution probably accounts for this portrait's unfinished state. While David completed the stippled underpainting, he did not create the smooth surface characteristic of his finished paintings. He did not even place a needle and thread in the subject's hand. Objecting to David’s revolutionary ideals, Madame de Pastoret refused the painting but had her adult son purchase the portrait after the artist's death.
altText: Large painting of young woman in white dress sitting next to crib.

title: The Holy Family with Saints Elizabeth and John the Baptist
creditLine: Major Acquisitions Fund
description: Here, Rubens presented a distinctly human take on the figures of Jesus, Mary, and Joseph. They lack the halos that often identify them, and the adult characters wear contemporary Flemish attire. Mary’s exposed breast brings to mind Jesus’s need for physical nourishment as the human son of God. Her central placement underscores the growing veneration of Mary in the Catholic community of the Spanish Netherlands.
altText: Large painting of Holy Family: Mary in red, holding baby Jesus.

title: Tetradrachm (Coin) Depicting the Nymph Arethusa
creditLine: Gift of Mrs. Tiffany Blake
description: The front of this coin depicts Arethusa, a water nymph who is often accompanied by dolphins, as she is here. On the back a four-horse chariot called a quadriga is shown advancing to the left.
altText: A work made of silver.

title: Approaching Storm
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Lewis Larned Coburn Memorial Collection
description: This painting of a beach for middle-class vacationers is by Eugène Boudin, a Norman painter and Claude Monet’s teacher, and exemplifies the artist’s style and subject matter. Monet later followed Boudin’s practice of painting in the open air, the technique that gave this image its vivid spontaneity and atmospheric light. This practice would be particularly important for Monet and his contemporaries, who became known as the Impressionists.
altText: A work made of oil on cradled panel.

title: Mahana no atua (Day of the God)
creditLine: Helen Birch Bartlett Memorial Collection
description: Drawn from fantasy and memory, this composition is one of the most abstract and avant-garde works of Gauguin's career. In a tropical paradise, a deity presides over figures by an embankment. Arranged in groups, the figures appear more as symbolic forms than as individuals. Pools of water in interlocking zones of acidic color surround the feet of a bather, who is flanked by two prone figures—or perhaps the same person seen from two angles.
altText: Brightly colored painting of a medium-skinned nude woman sitting on pink sand with her feet in a multicolored body of water, flanked by two nude figures resting in the fetal position. Behind them is a deity sculpture and individuals carrying objects, dancing, and swimming.

title: Madame Roulin Rocking the Cradle (La berceuse)
creditLine: Helen Birch Bartlett Memorial Collection
description: Van Gogh saw in Augustine Roulin—along with her husband, Joseph, and their children—a model of love and family life. He completed this work in 1889, soon after returning from his stay in the hospital following Paul Gauguin’s fraught departure. Madame Roulin sits in Gauguin’s chair, an attempt by Van Gogh to fill the space left by the older artist. In May 1889, Van Gogh gave this canvas to Gauguin as a gesture of reconciliation and friendship.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Terrace and Observation Deck at the Moulin de Blute-Fin, Montmartre
medium: Oil on canvas, mounted on pressboard
creditLine: Helen Birch Bartlett Memorial Collection
description: This painting dates to 1887, roughly a year after Van Gogh arrived in Paris to join his brother, the art dealer Theo van Gogh. It is one of a group of landscapes featuring the Butte Montmartre, a short climb from the apartment on the rue Lepic where Vincent and Theo lived. Montmartre was dotted with reminders of its quickly receding rural past—abandoned quarries, kitchen gardens, and three surviving windmills, including the Moulin de Blute-Fin.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas, mounted on pressboard.

title: Jacques and Berthe Lipchitz
creditLine: Helen Birch Bartlett Memorial Collection
description: Amedeo Modigliani created his finest paintings between 1914 and his premature death in 1920. Focusing on a limited range of subjects, mainly portraits and nudes, he developed a highly distinctive style of sensitively elongated forms. Sculptor Jacques Lipchitz commissioned Modigliani to paint this portrait on the occasion of his marriage to the poet Berthe Kitrosser as a way of helping his troubled friend financially.
altText: Large painting, standing man blue turtleneck, sitting woman with white collar.

title: A Sunday on La Grande Jatte — 1884
creditLine: Helen Birch Bartlett Memorial Collection
description: For his largest and best-known painting, Georges Seurat depicted Parisians enjoying all sorts of leisurely activities—strolling, lounging, sailing, and fishing—in the park called La Grande Jatte on the River Seine. He used an innovative technique called Pointillism that was inspired by optical and color theory, applying tiny dabs of different colored paint that viewers would see as a single, and Seurat believed, more brilliant hue.
altText: Large painting of people in a crowded park, brushstrokes are dots.

title: The Bedroom
creditLine: Helen Birch Bartlett Memorial Collection
description: In 1888, Van Gogh moved into his own home in Arles, France. He dubbed it the “Studio of the South,” hoping that fellow artists would join him there to work. This is one of three versions he painted of his beloved Arles bedroom. While its vivid palette and dramatic perspective seem to burst with nervous vitality, Van Gogh intended the painting "to express utter repose."
altText: Painting of bedroom, blue walls, green window, tan bed, red bedding.

title: A City Park
creditLine: Bequest of Dr. John J. Ireland
description: William Merritt Chase was one of the most influential painters at the turn of the 20th century. In this painting, which probably depicts Brooklyn’s Tompkins Park, half the canvas is filled by the wide, empty walkway. Its strong diagonal borders carry the eye into the scene. This informal piece, capturing the sparkle of a summer day, affirms the fresh perspective Chase brought to painting scenes like this one.
altText: Small painting of woman in pink and black sitting on park bench.

title: A Peasant Woman Digging in Front of Her Cottage
creditLine: Bequest of Dr. John J. Ireland
description: Driven by the loneliness and poverty he had experienced in the Hague, Vincent van Gogh returned to his parents’ home in the Netherlands in 1883. There he created a series of paintings of cottages based on his walks through the village. He wrote to his brother, "I feel for the brood and the nests—particularly those human nests, those cottages on the heath and their inhabitants.”
altText: Painting in tones of gray and brown, with some green and blue, of a woman digging with a garden tool before a structure with a thatched roof that descends almost to the ground. Above her the sky is gray and blue, a haze of clouds.

title: St. Albert of Louvain
creditLine: Bequest of Dr. John J. Ireland
description: Rubens executed this study and 38 more as he prepared to decorate the ceiling of the Jesuit church in Antwerp. It shows a foreshortened saint gliding majestically on a cloud. The bold perspective would have furthered the illusion that the painting was a window in the church's ceiling, offering a view to the sky. The man depicted is the 12th-century martyr Albert of Louvain, patron saint of Archduke Albert, governor of the Spanish Netherlands.
altText: A work made of oil on panel.

title: Bishamon
creditLine: Robert Allerton Endowment
description: This wooden figure, the most significant Japanese Buddhist sculpture in the museum's collection, depicts the chief of the guardian devas who protect the four cardinal directions in a Buddhist sanctuary. The skillful carving of the wood hints at the deity’s strong body beneath his armor, which still has traces of elaborate painted decoration, including patterns of dragons and flowers in gold and bright colors.
altText: A work made of wood with traces of polychromy.

title: Buddhist Votive Stele
creditLine: Gift of The Orientals
description: Buddhist stone tablets known as votive steles were commissioned by pious individuals and families and erected in temple courtyards and other public spaces. Inscribed around the lower portion are the names of donors who paid for this stele to commemorate their ancestors. By commissioning such tablets, devotees hoped to gain spiritual benefits for themselves and their families.
altText: A large stone steele with multiple registers of images from Buddhas life and sacred texts carved on all four sides

title: Boy with Pitcher (La Régalade)
creditLine: Bequest of Katharine Dexter McCormick
description: X-radiographs have revealed that this painting is a fragment of Les Gitanes, a large portrait of a gypsy family exhibited by Manet in 1863 and 1867. Apparently dissatisfied with his complex imitation of Spanish Baroque art, he cut the original painting into three sections and reconceived this portion as an individual work of art. Manet renamed it La Régalade, which means to pour liquid from a bottle down the throat without touching the lips.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Hercules and Lichas
artistDisplay: Attributed to Pietro Tacca (Italian, 1577–1640) After Giambologna (Flemish, active Italy, 1529–1608)
creditLine: Robert Allerton Endowment
description: Both this bronze and its companion represent legendary struggles related to Hecules’s labors, a frequent source of inspiration for Renaissance and later artists. The figures' virtuoso displays of movement, which seem to transform violent struggle into ballet, reflect the sculptor’s intense preoccupation with the human form.
altText: A work made of bronze.

title: Entrance to the Port of Honfleur
creditLine: Louise B. and Frank H. Woods Purchase Fund in honor of The Art Institute of Chicago Diamond Jubilee
description: Johan Barthold Jongkind brought a new spirit to the painting of coastal scenes. Claude Monet claimed that it was Jongkind who “educated his eye,” and his content, palette, and technique played an important part in the development of Impressionism. Though Jongkind painted his final compositions in the studio, the artist strove to retain the freshness of his plein-air (outdoor) sketches.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Bar-room Scene
creditLine: The William Owen Goodman and Erna Sawyer Goodman Collection
description: William Sidney Mount was one of the first American artists to specialize in scenes of everyday life. Here, Mount portrayed a boisterous group of patrons in a country tavern. Standing in the back corner is an African American figure who, as a free black man in 1830s New York, may have been able to frequent the tavern but did not participate fully in this community.
altText: In a beige room, a group of light-skinned men of various ages and a young boy clap as a figure in tattered clothing at center, his back to the viewer, dances and holds a tin cup in the air. At dark figure in shadows looks on from the far-right corner.

title: Portrait of Mary Adeline Williams
creditLine: Friends of American Art Collection
description: Thomas Eakins first met Mary Adeline Williams when she was a childhood playmate of his sister. Later, the unmarried Williams lived with Eakins and his wife, Susan. Although Eakins’s portrait presents Addie as straight-laced and severe, this is in marked contrast with the active woman Susan Eakins described in her diary, who rode bicycles, went to art exhibitions, and socialized between sittings for the painting.
altText: Dark portrait of an older light-skinned women with dark hair in a black dress and white collar, her hair pinned up. Her face is in partial shadow.

title: After the Bullfight
creditLine: Bequest of Mrs. Sterling Morton
description: Mary Cassatt chose a quintessentially Spanish subject, executing this composition of a bullfighter, or torero, in full regalia during an extended stay in Seville. Having trained in Philadelphia and Paris, Cassatt ventured to Spain to study the country’s Renaissance and Baroque works and to follow the path of French avant-garde artists like Édouard Manet.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Goblet (jia)
creditLine: Lucy Maud Buckingham Collection
description: The monumental scale and precise casting of animal imagery distinguish this vessel as a commission of late Shang royalty. Two tiers of monster masks encircle the flared bowl, while elongated versions of these masks, which may also be interpreted as paired serpents, descend the sharply tapered legs. A bovine head with sculpted horns crowns the strap handle.
altText: A fluted vessel with a green patina and three spear-like legs, a round handle at the side shaped like a cow's head, and two vertical protrusions at top.

title: Filagree Pendant in the Form of a Frog or Toad
artistDisplay: Coclé Venado Beach, Coclé province, Panama
creditLine: Wirt D. Walker Fund
description: Throughout the ancient Americas, the animal world was closely linked to social hierarchies and obligations. In this worldview, and in connection with the onset of the rainy season, frogs like the one depicted here were seen as summoners of water. This in turn was connected to the idea of a ruler’s ultimate responsibility to the community being to ensure the continuity of the agricultural cycle.
altText: A work made of cast gold.

title: Mountain-Shaped Incense Burner
dateDisplay: Han dynasty (206 BCE–220 CE), 100 BCE–100 CE
creditLine: Lucy Maud Buckingham Collection
description: The conical lid of this incense burner, shaped like towering peaks, is associated with the mountainous Isles of the Blessed. These islands were described as the realm of immortal beings (xian) in the Han dynasty religion. Fragrant smoke wafting through holes in the lid of this incense burner would evoke just such a mist-shrouded utopia.
altText: A work made of bronze.

title: Cabinet
artistDisplay: Cabinet: Augsburg (now Germany); internal panels: Eger, Bohemia (now Cheb, Czech Republic)
medium: Ebony, ivory, pine, oak, fruitwood, walnut, iron, steel, silver, brass, gilded brass, tinned brass, glass, paper, silk textile, and bone
creditLine: Anonymous Purchase Fund
description: Cabinets made in the German town of Augsburg during the 16th and 17th centuries are famous for their ornate decoration, typically executed in ebony veneer and ivory inlay. This example also includes carved figures, bronze mounts, and panels made from stained wood and ivory. The exquisite craftsmanship is matched by the inventiveness of the interior, which includes a display case, tool chest, and safe-deposit box.
altText: Large ebony cabinet with white designs, ivory figures, clock.

title: Polynesian Woman with Children
creditLine: Helen Birch Bartlett Memorial Collection
description: The figures in this work have never been identified. Their pose and other details, such as the woman’s gold ring and the red mark on the girl’s hand, invite speculation as to their relationship to each other and to Gauguin. Technical analysis has revealed that he reworked the position of the woman’s hands to align diagonally with those of the young girl. Together, they form an upward axis reinforced by the cat, also a later addition.
altText: A work made of oil on linen canvas.

title: Equestrienne
creditLine: Gift of Mrs. Potter Palmer
description: Chinese ceramic figures made for burial often evoke the fashions and recreational activities of their aristocratic owners. This figure sensitively captures a woman gently guiding her horse. Her weight, costume, and hairstyle reflect early-to-mid-eighth-century ideals of feminine beauty. Stylistically, the woman closely resembles figures recently unearthed from the tombs of high-status individuals that are datable to about 740.
altText: A female figure with a round face in a full orange robe is bent almost wearily as she rides a horse. White pigment has worn away on the horse, and orange has worn from her robe, revealing a terracotta tone.

title: Women's Bathhouse and Laundry
creditLine: Margaret Gentles Endowment
description: In Japan during the Edo period (1615–1868), bathing was considered a communal activity, and bathhouses were popular places to socialize. The women in this painting—most likely courtesans—are performing a variety of tasks in addition to bathing, such as doing laundry and combing one another’s hair. Two women near the back of the scene are reading a book; one of them seems to express shock and whispers to the other about the content.
altText: A work made of ink and colors on paper.

title: Tetradrachm (Coin) Depicting the God Dionysos
creditLine: Gift of Emily Crane Chadbourne
description: This coin depicts the god Dionysos crowned with ivy leaves on the front and holding grapes on its back. Dionysos is believed to have come from Thrace, where this coin was minted, though several Thrace cities claimed to be his birthplace. One was Maroneia, on the coast of Thrace, which was said to be named after Dionysos’s son Maron. Dionysos was the city’s protective deity and appeared on its coinage.
altText: A work made of silver.

title: Girl with Cherries
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Lewis Larned Coburn Memorial Collection
description: The daughter of an affluent and cultured family, Eva Gonzalès was Édouard Manet’s first and only official pupil. Girl with Cherries, which features a freely painted figure lit dramatically against a dark background, shows a clear debt to Manet’s contemporary Spanish-style works. The model wears the frilled linen cap and loose, striped gown of an 18th-century servant girl—an occupation further suggested by her rolled-up sleeve.
altText: Painting of a young woman in a black and white striped gown, seated at a table with cherries, staring directly at the viewer.

title: Watering Place at Marly
creditLine: Gift of Mrs. Clive Runnells
description: In 1875 Alfred Sisley moved to the French village of Marly-le-Roi. His home flanked the pool, or “watering place,” featured on the left of this canvas, which had once been the water gardens of King Louis XIV's country retreat. Sisley faithfully depicted landscapes throughout his career, spending most of his life painting in the villages along the Seine River, in the region referred to as the cradle of Impressionism.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Fragment of a Statue of Venus
creditLine: Museum Purchase Fund
description: This type of female torso—which depicts Venus (Aphrodite to the Greeks) wearing a sheer, revealing garment—was frequently used in the Roman world to represent the goddess in her role as mother (or genetrix in Latin). The statue type, which was likely based on an earlier Greek bronze statue of Aphrodite, was also used in portraits of Roman empresses, who, in producing future emperors, likened themselves to Venus as mothers of the imperial line.
altText: A fragment of a marble sculpture beginning at the hips and ending below the knee. The female figure wears a thin, draping fabric showing the outline of the body.

title: The Valley of Arconville
creditLine: Friends of American Art Collection
description: One of the first American artists to paint in Giverny, France, Theodore Robinson drew upon the teachings of its most famous resident, Claude Monet. Using layered, broken brushwork, Robinson captures the effects of light on the landscape like Monet and other progressive French painters. Robinson's forms, however, have a measure of solidity that was more typical of American artists who worked in an Impressionist style.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Statue of Meleager
creditLine: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Eugene A. Davidson
description: This statue depicts the legendary Greek hunter Meleager, who earned his fame by killing a ferocious boar that terrorized the people of Calydon. About 40 Roman sculptural representations of Meleager survive today, leading scholars to conclude that they were based on an earlier Greek statue, possibly by the architect and sculptor Skopas of Paros, who incorporated a marble relief depicting the Calydonian boar hunt on one of his buildings.
altText: A work made of marble.

title: Inscribed Mina'i Bowl with an Enthroned Figure and Narrative Scenes in Three Registers
medium: Mina'i ware, fritware with polychrome painting over an opaque white glaze
creditLine: Gift of Mrs. Andrew Dole
description: Iranian 12th- and 13th-century overglaze-painted ceramics, or mina'i (meaning enameled), are particularly opulent and luxurious objects due to their broad color palette. Prior to the late 12th century, only one or two colors could be applied to a ceramic, while this mina'i features a whole range of colors. This expanded palette allowed for the depiction of increasingly complex scenes on ceramic vessels.
altText: A work made of mina'i ware, fritware with polychrome painting over an opaque white glaze.

title: Stemless Kylix (Drinking Cup)
creditLine: Museum Purchase Fund
description: During the course of the 5th and 4th centuries BCE, black vessels (commonly called black-glaze vessels) were made with increasing frequency in both Greece and southern Italy. Many of them replicate the shape of metal vessels; others have detailing that is molded or incised. While the quality of these vessels varies greatly, all would have been less expensive than vessels decorated in contemporary techniques such as red-figure.
altText: A work made of terracotta, calenian relief ware.

title: Pyxis (Container for Personal Objects)
artistDisplay: Attributed to the Ampersand Painter Greek; Corinth
creditLine: Museum Purchase Fund
description: In the Archaic period (700–480 BCE) scented oils were exported around the Mediterranean in terra-cotta containers. Around the time that this jar was made, Egypt’s king gave the Greeks the Egyptian port city of Naucratis.The sphinx on this jar commemorates this cultural encounter. The artist who decorated this container is called the Ampersand Painter because here and elsewhere the looping tail of the sphinx takes the shape of an ampersand.
altText: A work made of terracotta, black-figure.

title: Rhyton (Drinking Vessel) in the Shape of a Donkey Head
artistDisplay: Attributed to the Painter of London E 55 (Manner of Douris) Greek; Athens
creditLine: Museum Purchase Fund
description: This drinking cup could not have been set down without spilling its contents. It is fashioned after the head of a bridled donkey with a white muzzle, teeth, and ears. Like the naked satyr chasing a fleeing maenad on the vessel’s neck, the donkey belongs to the entourage of the wine god Dionysos.
altText: A work made of terracotta, red-figure.

title: Guttus (Pouring Vessel)
creditLine: Museum Purchase Fund
description: During the course of the 5th and 4th centuries BCE, black vessels (commonly called black-glaze vessels) were made with increasing frequency in both Greece and southern Italy. Many of them replicate the shape of metal vessels; others have detailing that is molded or incised. While the quality of these vessels varies greatly, all would have been less expensive than vessels decorated in contemporary techniques such as red-figure.
altText: A work made of terracotta, black-glaze.

Many of them replicate the shape of metal vessels; others have detailing that is molded or incised. While the quality of these vessels varies greatly, all would have been less expensive than vessels decorated in contemporary techniques such as red-figure.
altText: A work made of terracotta, black-glaze.

title: Oinochoe (Pitcher) in the Shape of a Female Head
artistDisplay: Attributed to the Canessa Class Greek; Athens
creditLine: Museum Purchase Fund
description: Three techniques were used to create this vessel. The lower portion, in the shape of a woman’s face, was made in a mold; the shoulder, neck, and mouth of the pitcher were formed on a potter’s wheel; and the handle was made by hand. The woman's flesh and thick, parted hair are the natural color of the clay, but her brows and the contours of her eyes and irises are drawn in black.
altText: A work made of terracotta, red-figure.

title: Kantharos (Wine Cup) in the Shape of a Female Head
artistDisplay: Attributed to the London Class (Class G) Greek; Athens
creditLine: Museum Purchase Fund
description: This kantharos, a popular type of wine cup in ancient Greece, takes the form of a woman's head, with faces on both the front and back. The woman's neck rises from a rounded foot forming a wide stem. Above the cup flares out to a wide bowl of her head with two handles on opposite sides.
altText: A work made of terracotta, white-ground and black-figure technique.

title: Pair of Cups
dateDisplay: Qing dynasty (1644–1911), Yongzheng reign mark and period (1723–1735)
medium: Porcelain painted in underglaze blue and overglaze enamels (doucai)
creditLine: Bequest of Henry C. Schwab
description: Among the Qing emperors, the Yongzheng emperor particularly valued decorative objects and personally oversaw the imperial kilns, setting exacting standards. These thin cups are a testament to his precise tastes. Delicate cobalt blue floral medallions filled with translucent enamels showcase the doucai technique. Different from typical Qing porcelains, these were perhaps influenced by Japanese lacquers imported in the 16th and 17th centuries.
altText: Small white porcelain cups with circular patterns and no handles.

title: Portrait of Jeanne Wenz
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Lewis Larned Coburn Memorial Collection
description: Toulouse-Lautrec painted this portrait when he was only 22 years old and still an art student. He used subtle coloring with accents of pink and green and showed his subject, Jeanne Wenz, in full profile, a compositional device often found in Renaissance portraiture. Wenz was the mistress of Frederic Wenz, Toulouse-Lautrec’s fellow student at the painter Fernand Cormon’s studio.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: View of Delphi with a Procession
creditLine: Robert A. Waller Memorial Fund
description: Like other foreign artists drawn to the ruins of antiquity, Claude Lorrain was fascinated with the Roman Empire. This painting of the ancient city of Delphi (in what is now Greece) presents a glowing Mediterranean atmosphere. Here, he evokes a serene, bucolic world akin to the poetic vision of the Roman writer Virgil, depicting the ruins restored to what Lorrain imagined was their original glory.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Aryballos (Container for Oil)
creditLine: Gift of Theodore W. and Frances S. Robinson
description: Containers like this one were used to store precious oils. The flaring rim functioned as an applicator to spread the thick, scented oil over the skin, while the vessel itself was designed to fit comfortably in the user's hand.
altText: A work made of glass, core-formed technique.

title: Kohl Container in the Shape of a Palm Column
dateDisplay: New Kingdom, mid–Dynasty 18 or early Dynasty 19, about 1352–1213 BCE
creditLine: Gift of Theodore W. and Frances S. Robinson
description: This small container was designed to hold kohl, a cosmetic eye paint made of ground galena or malachite. Ancient Egyptian men and women wore kohl for its aesthetic appeal but also to dampen the harsh sunlight of North Africa and possibly even for medicinal purposes. Columns shaped like palm trees were common in ancient Egyptian architecture and inspired the elegant form of this glass vessel.
altText: A work made of glass.

title: E1: English Great Room of the Late Tudor Period, 1550–1603
artistDisplay: Designed by Narcissa Niblack Thorne American, 1882–1966
creditLine: Gift of Mrs. James Ward Thorne
description: Mottled light passing through a floor-to-ceiling window of handmade glass illuminates the many intriguing details Narcissa Niblack Thorne included in this miniature room. Above the ornately carved paneling at the back is a door, the entrance for troupes of musicians who might have provided entertainment during a banquet. The portraits and armor that flank the fireplace convey Thorne’s romantic vision of a noble household.
altText: To-scale great room with a double-height ceiling. The bottom half of each wall is clad in elaborately carved wooden panels. The right wall features a tall bay window, the left a fireplace flanked by suits of armor. A long, rustic table with bench is centered in the room.

title: E3: English Reception Room of the Jacobean Period, 1625–55
artistDisplay: Designed by Narcissa Niblack Thorne American, 1882–1966
creditLine: Gift of Mrs. James Ward Thorne
description: In this English reception room of the Jacobean Period (1625–55), one of the 68 miniature rooms conceived by Narcissa Niblack Thorne, the major influences are Italian Renaissance architecture and Baroque ornamentation. Here, Mrs. Thorne drew from two lavish rooms at Wilton, the magnificent house designed for Philip Herbert, fourth Earl of Pembroke.
altText: Miniature of an ornate room with red walls and white and gold trim, a large fireplace at center, and black and white checkered flooring. Two armchairs flank a window on the left side. Three large painted portraits in golden frames hang on the back wall. There is a small table directly in front of the fireplace.

title: E12: English Drawing Room of the Georgian Period, c. 1800
artistDisplay: Designed by Narcissa Niblack Thorne American, 1882–1966
creditLine: Gift of Mrs. James Ward Thorne
description: This English Drawing Room is one of 68 miniature rooms conceived of by Narcissa Niblack Thorne and constructed by master craftsmen according to her specifications. It was intended to illustrate the late 18th-century Neoclassical style of designer Thomas Sheraton, distinguished by elegant, light shapes and colors. The furniture replicas, made in England, include a harpsichord that is strung with wires attached to moveable ivory keys.
altText: A work made of miniature room, mixed media.

title: E14: English Drawing Room of the Victorian Period, 1840–70
artistDisplay: Designed by Narcissa Niblack Thorne American, 1882–1966
creditLine: Gift of Mrs. James Ward Thorne
description: Narcissa Niblack Thorne must have imagined the occupants of this miniature Victorian drawing room to be loyal English subjects, as it abounds with images of Queen Victoria and her husband, Albert. The room's many ornate objects were constructed using a mix of faux and genuine materials: the candelabras are painted to look like gold, whereas the lamps flanking the doorway are made from real ivory.
altText: A work made of miniature room, mixed media.

title: E22: French Provincial Bedroom of the Louis XV Period, 18th Century
artistDisplay: Designed by Narcissa Niblack Thorne American, 1882–1966
creditLine: Gift of Mrs. James Ward Thorne
description: This is one of the 68 miniature rooms conceived by Narcissa Niblack Thorne and constructed by master craftsmen according to her specifications. Thorne intended this bedroom of a Normandy country home to show the how a growing middle class outside of Paris adapted some of the innovations in comfort and style characteristic of Louis XV's reign for their relatively modest homes.
altText: A work made of miniature room, mixed media.

title: E24: French Salon of the Louis XVI Period, c. 1780
artistDisplay: Designed by Narcissa Niblack Thorne American, 1882–1966
creditLine: Gift of Mrs. James Ward Thorne
description: Narcissa Niblack Thorne designed this miniature interior “entirely in the spirit of Marie Antoinette—dainty in coloring and full of her symbols of design.” The queen was fond of roses, which were often incorporated into the molded decorations of swags, garlands, and baskets. The garden tools and musical instruments in the carvings of the panel heads represent her love of nature and music.
altText: A work made of miniature room, mixed media.

title: Croquet Scene
creditLine: Friends of American Art Collection; Goodman Fund
description: One of America’s foremost painters, Winslow Homer began his career as an illustrator. In the late 1860s, he turned to oil painting, depicting figures bathed in sunlight. These early paintings feature scenes of upper-class leisure pursuits—in this case, women and men playing the popular sport of croquet, a game that had recently been introduced to the United States from the British Isles.
altText: Painting of four figures in blue, red, brown dresses playing croquet.

title: Milton Dictating to His Daughter
creditLine: Preston O. Morton Memorial Purchase Fund for Older Paintings
description: This painting by Swiss artist Henry Fuseli depicts 17th-century English poet John Milton, who became blind in his 40s, dictating his epic poem Paradise Lost to his daughter, while another woman listens intently and sews. A forerunner of the Romantic Movement, Fuseli created drama through chromatic contrast. A cool light illuminates the rosy-cheeked women and casts deep shadows around Milton’s ghostly figure and face.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: The Annunciation
creditLine: Edward E. Ayer Endowment in memory of Charles L. Hutchinson
description: Venetian artist Alessandro Vittoria translated into bronze the flickering light of Renaissance paintings. Here, the highly animated figures, drapery, clouds, and sky seem to move with excitement, heightening the drama between the Virgin Mary and the archangel Gabriel, who has descended from heaven to announce that Mary will bear the son of God.
altText: Relief sculpture of angel confronting Virgin Mary. Cherubs and dove in sky.

title: Are They Thinking about the Grape? (Pensent-ils au raisin?)
creditLine: Martha E. Leverone Endowment
description: This painting is based on a 1745 pantomime about a young shepherd’s awakening love for a shepherdess. The couple feed each other grapes—a fruit associated with Bacchus, god of pleasure—suggesting that their encounter is not entirely chaste. François Boucher’s compositions on pastoral themes are his most influential contribution to 18th-century French art.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Venus and Cupid
creditLine: A. A. Munger Collection
description: The most important and inventive painter in 16th-century Genoa, Luca Cambiaso developed a highly personal style characterized by a geometric simplification of anatomy and dramatic, often silvery light. Here, the canopied bed and profile view lend an unusual intimacy to the representation of the goddess of love and her son.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Fish (Still Life)
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Lewis Larned Coburn Memorial Collection
description: This painting, like many of Manet’s still lifes, recalls 17th-century Dutch models. The directness of execution, bold brushwork, and immediacy of vision, however, suggest why the public found Manet’s work so unorthodox and confrontational. While this painting depicts “dead nature” (nature morte is French for still life), there is nothing still about the work: the produce seems fresh and the handling of the paint vigorous.
altText: Still-life painting, fish, open oysters, eel, lemon on tablecloth.

title: The Bathers
creditLine: Amy McCormick Memorial Collection
description: Paul Cezanne set this idyllic view of bathers in a frame of foliage. He rendered the ground, water, trees, and sky with patches of hatching, conveying the energy he felt when painting. His primary concern, however, seems to have been striking a balance between the vigor of the bodies and the restfulness of the setting through individual poses and figure groupings.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: A17: Pennsylvania Kitchen, 1752
artistDisplay: Designed by Narcissa Niblack Thorne American, 1882–1966
creditLine: Gift of Mrs. James Ward Thorne
description: Narcissa Thorne aimed to design convincingly lived-in miniature interiors, so to contend with the absent fourth wall, she employed techniques of stage design. Here, for instance, the chairs around the kitchen table face outward, and the pieces of furniture are arranged so as not to obstruct one another. This careful placement allows viewers to see each element while also encouraging them to imagine scenes playing out within the space.
altText: Scale miniature of a rustic but refined kitchen with a varnished wooden table at center and one chair. A dark wooden chest sits beneath the window at left, a spinning wheel in the left back corner. In the right corner is an ornately carved door adjacent to a staircase. Metal plates line a wide hearth.

title: A20: Virginia Dining Room, 1758
artistDisplay: Designed by Narcissa Niblack Thorne American, 1882–1966
creditLine: Gift of Mrs. James Ward Thorne
description: The wallpaper in this room is perhaps its most elaborate element. In her study of interior decoration sources from the 18th century, Narcissa Thorne learned of the taste among Americans and Europeans for imported Chinese wallpaper. The walls in this space are covered with a hand-painted pattern of birds, trees, and flowers produced in the same manner as the full-scale wallpapers from China 150 years earlier.
altText: Miniature dining room with dark wood floors, dark wooden furniture, walls decorated with floral paintings.

title: A33: “Middletown” Parlor, 1875–90
artistDisplay: Designed by Narcissa Niblack Thorne American, 1882–1966
creditLine: Gift of Mrs. James Ward Thorne
description: “Middletown” is a fictionalized town in Indiana, Narcissa Thorne’s home state, and the eclectic decorative accessories in this miniature room impart a personal, lived-in quality. Objects like porcelain vases, crystal paperweights, books, newspapers, and even tiny photographs suggest that this room is based on Thorne’s memories of her childhood.
altText: Miniature parlor room with green walls, carpeted floor, gothic-like window, and wooden furniture.

title: A36: California Living Room, 1850–75
artistDisplay: Designed by Narcissa Niblack Thorne American, 1882–1966
creditLine: Gift of Mrs. James Ward Thorne
description: This miniature living room is based on the Casa Soberanes, an adobe house built in 1842 in Califiofrnia and opened to the public as a historic home in the early 20th century. Narcissa Thorne was an avid visitor to such historic houses, and she sought to evoke the same history and nostalgia in her designs. The furniture here recalls the weighty mahogany items families transported across the country as they moved out West in the mid-19th century.
altText: Bright miniature living room with white walls and ceiling, wooden floors, large windows, double doors, and minimal furniture.

title: Reliquary Casket of Saints Adrian and Natalia
creditLine: Kate S. Buckingham Endowment
description: This rare casket, fashioned like a miniature tomb complete with Romanesque columns, was made to contain the relics of Saint Adrian, patron saint of soldiers and protector against the plague. A Roman officer charged with persecuting Christians, Adrian so admired the virtues of those he oppressed that he converted. After declaring himself a Christian, Adrian was arrested and brutally martyred in the early fourth century.
altText: Silver-toned reliquary in the shape of a long rectangle with an upper resembling a pitched roof. In relief on its side, armed figures surround a falling figure in distress as a single figure attacks him.

title: Kohada Koheiji, from the series "One Hundred Ghost Tales (Hyaku monogatari)"
artistDisplay: Katsushika Hokusai 葛飾 北斎 (Japanese, 1760-1849)
creditLine: Clarence Buckingham Collection
description: This frightening print illustrates the story of Kohada Koheiji, a Kabuki actor who was drowned by his wife’s lover but later came back to haunt the couple. The tale was popular in the 18th century, eventually inspiring a novel and several Kabuki plays. Here, the skeletal ghost of Kohada Koheiji pulls down the mosquito net and eerily peers at the sleeping couple in their bed.
altText: A color woodblock print of a ghostly skeletal figure, pulling down a shear blue cloth, sticks its head out from the darkness. From the left, wisps of orange and black, escape.

title: Oiwa (Oiwa-san), from the series "One Hundred Ghost Tales (Hyaku monogatari)"
artistDisplay: Katsushika Hokusai 葛飾 北斎 (Japanese, 1760-1849)
creditLine: Clarence Buckingham Collection
description: Here, Oiwa, a character from the Japanese ghost play Yotsuya Kaidan, emerges from a paper lantern. In the story Oume wants to steal Oiwa’s husband and sends her poisoned face cream. The poison immediately scars Oiwa. When she realizes the deception, Oiwa becomes hysterical and accidentally kills herself. After her death, she seeks revenge on Oume, her husband, and others. The inscription on the lantern begs us to pray for Oiwa's soul.
altText: A work made of color woodblock print; chuban.

title: The Mansion of the Plates (Sara yashiki), from the series "One Hundred Ghost Tales (Hyaku monogatari)"
artistDisplay: Katsushika Hokusai 葛飾 北斎 (Japanese, 1760-1849)
creditLine: Clarence Buckingham Collection
description: This print illustrates the legend of a woman murdered by her husband because she accidentally broke plates. Her corpse and the pieces of the dishes were thrown into a well, but her ghost returned every night to haunt him in the eerie form seen here. This small-format work features a bright blue color that may seem cheery to us, but Hokusai’s original audience would have associated it with death and the occult.
altText: A color wood block print of a human ghost head with long black hair and blue/white plates for a spine, emerging out of a broken barrel shape

title: The Laughing Demoness (Warai Hannya), from the series "One Hundred Ghost Tales (Hyaku monogatari)"
artistDisplay: Katsushika Hokusai 葛飾 北斎 (Japanese, 1760-1849)
creditLine: Clarence Buckingham Collection
description: This image of a demon holding the decapitated head of a child refers to the legend of Kishimojin (Hariti in Sanskrit), a Buddhist goddess. Originally, she was a terrifying ogress who wanted to eat all of the babies in the town of Rajgir. The Buddha heard the pleas of the townspeople and hid one of the ogress's children. Understanding the grief she was causing, she converted to Buddhism and was accepted as a goddess and a protector of children.
altText: A work made of color woodblock print; chuban.

title: Votive (Gift) in the Shape of a Woman's Head
creditLine: Katherine K. Adler Memorial Fund
description: Supplicants placed votive heads in temples to accompany requests and offerings of thanks to the gods. Such heads, depicting men and women, were made by artisans using molds. On finer examples, such as this head, a pointed tool was used to refine elements of the face and hair before the object was fired in the kiln. Earrings once hung from holes in the ears, and traces of pigment suggest that the hair was originally painted bright red.
altText: A work made of terracotta, pigment.

title: Armored Guardian
dateDisplay: Tang dynasty (618–907), late 7th or early 8th century
medium: Buff earthenware with polychrome and gilding
creditLine: Gift of Russell Tyson
description: Ceramic figures made for burial in the tombs of princes and officials vividly evoke aspects of the elite life of China's expansive and multicultural Tang dynasty (618–907). This haughty armored guardian stands on a rocky plinth and was probably stationed close to the burial chamber to repel potential evil. Unlike most Tang figures that were formed in molds, this guardian appears to have been primarily hand-modeled, probably from coils of clay.
altText: A work made of buff earthenware with polychrome and gilding.

title: Richard Bill
creditLine: Friends of American Art Collection
description: The Scottish-born painter John Smibert studied in London and Italy before settling in Boston in 1728. His skills as a trained formal portraitist were in great demand among Boston's wealthy and powerful colonists. Here, he depicted Richard Bill, a prosperous merchant and politically involved citizen. The large ship, visible through the window in the background, combined with Bill's elegant clothing, suggests his success and prestige.
altText: Portrait of a light-skinned man in a long white wig and red-orange coat, holding a folded piece of paper and standing next to a desk, a large sailing ship off his left shoulder.

title: Head of an Apostle
creditLine: Kate S. Buckingham Endowment
description: This head probably comes from a full-length sculpture of one of the apostles flanking the portals of Notre-Dame Cathedral in Paris. With its references to ancient and Byzantine models, it bears all the stylistic hallmarks of the beginning of the Gothic style. Medieval sculpture like this was purposely damaged in the 1790s during the French Revolution because of its presumed royal associations.
altText: Sculpture in light stone of the head of a bearded man with wavy hair and wide eyes, missing a nose.

title: Storage Jar with Horizontal Bands of Interlocking Scrolls
artistDisplay: Ceramist unknown (Ancestral Puebloan), Black Mesa Black-on-white Kayenta area, northeastern Arizona, United States
creditLine: Tillie C. Cohn Fund
description: Ancestors of the modern Pueblo Indians, the Anasazi people flourished in the southwestern United States beginning about 2,000 years ago. Skilled farmers, the Anasazi were also creative artisans, as seen in this striking olla, a storage vessel, decorated in the black-on-white ground of the Black Mesa style. In Anasazi tradition, as among the Pueblos today, ceramic vessels were primarily made by women.
altText: Round ceramic jar with large black S-shaped geometric designs on cream ground.

title: Statuette of a Female Figure
artistDisplay: Cycladic; probably from the island of Keros
creditLine: Katherine K. Adler Memorial Fund
description: Cycladic sculpture is characterized by the abstract treatment of the human form. The vast majority of Cycladic white marble statuettes depict pregnant females, suggesting an association with fertility or regenerative forces. Although they are admired today for their stark simplicity, these statuettes once had hair, eyes, jewelry, or other ornaments added in red, blue, and black pigment, which has since faded.
altText: A light-colored, highly polished stone figure, faceless but with a prominent nose, crossed arms, and a slim, rectangular built. A portion of its legs at bottom have broken off and are missing.

title: Corpus of Christ, from the Altarpiece of the Crucifixion
artistDisplay: Jacques de Baerze (Netherlandish, active before 1384–1399) Melchior Broederlam (Netherlandish, about 1355–about 1411)
medium: Wood with gilding and traces of polychromy
creditLine: Gift of Honoré Palmer
description: This work was originally part of a large triptych commissioned for the Charterhouse of Champol, a monastery outside Dijon. Even separated from its context within the altarpiece, however, the painting remains a powerfully expressive work. Christ’s tensed hands and feet and earthy features are realistically observed, while the curving contour of his torso and the folds of his loincloth reflect a more courtly ideal.
altText: Brown and gold sculpture of crucified Jesus without the cross.

title: Ritual Cache
artistDisplay: Salado branch of the Mogollon New Mexico, United States
medium: Wood, stone, plant fibers, cotton, feathers, hide, and pigment
dimensions: Male figure: H.: 64 cm (25 1/4 in.); Female figure: H.: 36 cm (14 3/16 in.)
creditLine: Major Acquisitions Centennial Endowment
description: Discovered hidden in a remote cave, this cache of ritual figures comes from the Salado culture, which flourished in the mountains of southwestern New Mexico and southeastern Arizona between the 14th and 15th centuries. Brilliantly colored and adorned with flicker feathers and dyed cotton string, these effigies once formed an altar as agents for communion with the life-giving spirits of the earth and sky.
altText: Carved ceremonial objects colored with orange and blue of a man, woman, snake, curved sticks, and cougar.

title: Peach Blossoms
creditLine: Gift of George B. Harrington
description: Early in his career, Homer often depicted scenes of leisure, such as this young woman looking at peach blossoms. The setting itself reflects nostalgia for a fading rural past. Homer's use of a lighter palette was inspired by Impressionism, and the linearity of the tree is reminiscent of Japanese calligraphy. While critics often noted the innate American quality of Homer's work, this painting indicates the global artistic exchange of the time.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Fragment of a Funerary Naiskos (Monument in the Shape of a Temple)
creditLine: Alexander White Collection
description: Travelers along ancient Greece and Roman roads regularly encountered large stone monuments like this, which marked the burial sites of elite families and often contained hints about the deceased person. Here, two male individuals are clasping hands—a parting gesture common in funerary scenes. The standing man is likely the person who died, shown sharing a final farewell with his loved ones, perhaps his mother and father.
altText: A work made of marble.

title: Relief of a Falling Warrior
creditLine: Gift of Alfred E. Hamill
description: Roman artists adapted Greek imagery for new functions and contexts. Originally, this image of a wounded Greek warrior decorated the shield of the monumental gold-and-ivory statue of the goddess Athena in the Parthenon. Roughly five to six centuries later, the same figure was adapted from its original religious setting for use on this Roman architectural relief, likely for a public building or a lavish home.
altText: A work made of marble.

title: Legends of the Yūzū Nembutsu Sect
medium: Handscroll; ink, colors, and gold on paper
creditLine: Kate S. Buckingham Endowment
description: Commissioned and executed in the mid-14th century, this lengthy horizontal scroll illustrates the founding of the Yūzū Nembutsu sect of Japanese Buddhism. Yūzū Nembutsu means “chanting [Amida’s] name in communion”—a reference to the belief that one person chanting the Amida Buddha’s name would affect all other beings, whether in attaining individual rebirth or allowing souls in hell to be saved.
altText: Long painted scroll, green, brown mountains, wooden house, Amida Buddha on cloud.

title: Nocturne: Blue and Gold—Southampton Water
creditLine: Stickney Fund
description: In the 1870s James McNeill Whistler took a radical step toward abstraction with his "Nocturnes" series. In keeping with his art-for-art’s-sake creed, these works capture the stillness of evening while evoking the artistry of music. The subject of this work—an inlet along the English Channel—is obscured by the approaching night, allowing Whistler to fully explore the tonal harmonies of darkness.
altText: A sparsely painted waterside scene in dark tones with minimal ghostly shapes suggesting ships, yellow glitches of paint for light reflections, and the orb of an orange moon overhead.

title: The Old Temple
creditLine: Gift of Adolphus C. Bartlett
description: The four large canvases by Hubert Robert in the Art Institute's collection were commissioned by wealthy financier Jean-Joseph, Marquis de Laborde, to decorate a salon in his château at Méréville, France. Robert was much sought after as a painter of architectural ruins, a genre that appealed to the late 18th-century taste for the antique. He cultivated his knowledge of antiquity over more than a decade of travel and study in Italy.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: The Fountains
creditLine: Gift of William G. Hibbard
description: In his paintings of ruins, Robert embodied French philosopher Denis Diderot's notion that "Everything vanishes, everything dies, only time endures." This work, one of four canvases commissioned for a wealthy financier’s château (all now in the Art Institute's collection), exploits Robert’s typical vocabulary of fictive niches, arches, coffered vaults, colonnades, majestic stairwells, and Roman statuary to create a fantasy of expansive space.
altText: Large painting of ancient arch ruins, statues, humans are small in comparison.

title: New England Scenery
creditLine: Nickerson Collection
description: Thomas Cole is best known for his scenes of American wilderness, but he also rendered pastoral views of cultivated landscapes, like this painting of New Hampshire’s White Mountains. The prominent church spire emphasizes the role of religion in agrarian society, and the sun's glow expresses optimism for rural America. Painted at a time of rapid industrialization, the work conveys an ideal that was increasingly far from reality.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Wall Clock
artistDisplay: Case by Jean-Pierre Latz (born Cologne [now Germany], active France, 1691–1754) Clockwork by Francis Bayley (active Austrian Netherlands [now Belgium], mid-1700s) Case: Paris; clock: Ghent, Flanders, Austrian Netherlands (now Belgium)
medium: Oak, tortoiseshell, kingwood, brass, gilded bronze, and glass
creditLine: Ada Turnbull Hertle Fund
description: An exuberant example of the French Rococo style, this sculptural wall clock epitomizes the extravagant era of Louis XV (r. 1715–74). Festooned with ormolu (gilt bronze) swirls and floral swags, the clock required the collaboration of numerous specialized artisans. Opulent clocks such as this did more than tell time; they dazzled the eye with dramatic scenes and delighted the ear with music.
altText: Golden-colored, ornate wall clock adorned with golden flourishes, a bent figure with an arrow at top.

title: Portrait Head of Emperor Hadrian
creditLine: Katherine K. Adler Memorial Fund
