description: Unlike previous emperors, who were clean shaven, Hadrian (reigned 117–38 CE) wore a beard, perhaps in emulation of the Greek philosophers he revered. Here, Hadrian’s closely cropped beard contrasts with the luxurious curls that frame his face. This sculpture also features an innovative trend in Roman portraiture: the artist carefully carved the irises and pupils of the eyes rather than conventionally rendering them in paint.
altText: The white head of a man with a blank expression, a missing nose that has broken off, low cheekbones, curly hair, and a close-cut wavy beard.

title: Bird-Shaped Container (zun)
creditLine: Lucy Maud Buckingham Collection
description: Animal-shaped vessels are the rarest of all Shang ritual bronzes. This creature is a fascinating blend of alert poise and solemn dignity. The scaled pattern on the neck and tail suggests the feathers of a bird, while other details reference more fantastical creatures. A dragon and a coiled serpent embellish each wing, and monster masks crown the head as well as the removable lid.
altText: A work made of bronze.

title: Woman (Elevation)
creditLine: Friends of American Art Collection
description: Lachaise modeled this work on Isabel Dutaud Nagle, whom he married in 1917. Although the sculpture evokes her individual appearance, its voluptuous torso recalls those of ancient fertility goddesses. Modernists like Lachaise were fascinated by preclassical art because they believed it possessed a primitive vitality. This sculpture represents Lachaise’s first full-scale expression of the idealized female form that would come to dominate his art.
altText: A work made of bronze.

title: Paperweight
artistDisplay: Baccarat Glassworks (Cristalleries de Baccarat) Lorraine, France, founded 1764
creditLine: Gift of Arthur Rubloff
description: Technological improvements to optical scientific instruments in the mid-19th century spurred a craze across Europe with identifying and classifying the natural world. Amateur botanists were eager to collect and preserve floral specimens, which they intently researched and catalogued. In response to this broad appeal, French glassmakers made paperweights that portrayed highly sought-after botanical subjects.
altText: A work made of glass.

title: Mrs. Daniel Hubbard (Mary Greene)
creditLine: Art Institute of Chicago Purchase Fund
description: John Singleton Copley garnered considerable success as a portrait painter before the Revolutionary War. The sitter here, Mary Greene Hubbard, was a member of Boston’s merchant class. Her pose, gown, and background were precisely copied from a British engraving of a noblewoman, yet Copley distinguished the work as his own by capturing Hubbard’s unique features and the luxurious fabrics she wears.
altText: Painted portrait of woman in green dress and cloud backdrop.

title: Winged Figure
creditLine: Simeon B. Williams Fund
description: Originally a painter of animals, Abbott Handerson Thayer created portraits and allegorical figures like Winged Figure after training in Paris. The artist wrote of his many seraphic subjects, “I have put on wings probably more to symbolize an exalted atmosphere . . . where one need not explain the action of his figures.” Thayer mixed this idealism with naturalism, individualizing the woman’s features and giving her a sense of mass and gravity.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Cupid Chastised
creditLine: Charles H. and Mary F. S. Worcester Collection
description: This dramatic scene by Bartolomeo Manfredi shows Mars, the god of war, beating Cupid for having caused his affair with Venus, the goddess of love. The sheer physicality of the figures as well as the bold illumination from the left further the work's dynamism. The composition is on one level a tale of domestic disturbance but also symbolizes the eternal conflict between love and war.
altText: Large painting of cupid being whipped, a woman tries to hold back the a man in red dress.

title: In the Café
creditLine: Charles H. and Mary F. S. Worcester Collection
description: Here, a fashionably dressed woman sits alone and alert in a Parisian café. Her presence is a sign of modern Paris’s changing social environment, in which café culture offered women new opportunities for leisure in public spaces. Although artist Fernand Lungren employed a dense, hard-edged style, his interest in modern life and the effects of light (here both gas and electric lighting) was nevertheless indebted to French Impressionism.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Boats on the Beach at Étretat
creditLine: Charles H. and Mary F. S. Worcester Collection
description: Forced indoors by inclement fall weather, Monet painted this work and The Departure of the Boats, Étretat while looking out the window of his room at the Hôtel Blanquet. The two form a pair that share a palette, subject, and vantage point. Monet centered each composition on the boats, combining pastel blues, pinks, purples, and greens to render wet surfaces.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Sketch for "Oath on the Rütli" (recto), Female Figure (verso)
creditLine: Anonymous gift
description: Although Fuseli spent most of his career in England, he was born Johann Heinrich Füssli in Zurich, Switzerland. This is a preliminary study for the artist’s first important commission, The Oath on the Rütli, in Zurich’s city hall. Both the study and the final painting depict the oath sworn on the Rütli meadow in 1291 by representatives of three Swiss cantons (territories) against the ambitions of their Habsburg overlords.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: The Essex Canal
medium: Oil on canvas mounted on board
creditLine: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Herbert Geist
description: Albert Pinkham Ryder was one of the most innovative artists of the late 19th century, creating reductive, yet expressive compositions out of thick, slowly worked paint along with glazes, varnishes, and unconventional materials. A younger generation of American artists celebrated Ryder as an important early modernist who pushed toward abstraction. Ryder’s reclusiveness added to his intrigue and mythic status as an artist ahead of his time.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas mounted on board.

title: The Pine of Success and Onmayagashi, Asakusa River (Asakusagawa shubi no matsu Oumayagashi), from the series One Hundred Views of Edo (Meisho Edo Hyakkei)
artistDisplay: Utagawa Hiroshige 歌川 広重 Japanese, 1797-1858
creditLine: Clarence Buckingham Collection
description: This print depicts a scene on the Sumida River, also known as the Asakusa River. The sun has set and the stars are already appearing in the clear sky of early evening. To the left is the famous Pine of Success, a tree that symbolized visitors’ desires to get their money’s worth in the nearby pleasure quarters of the Yoshiwara. In the lower left corner of the image, a roofed boat sits with its green blinds lowered, the figure of a woman silhouetted behind them. She must not be alone: two pairs of clogs are just visible in the prow.
altText: A work made of color woodblock print; ōban.

title: Landscape with the Ruins of the Castle of Egmond
creditLine: Potter Palmer Collection
description: The deteriorating Castle of Egmond was a visible reminder of the Dutch struggle for independence: it was sacrificially destroyed during the revolt against Spain more than 80 years before Jacob van Ruisdael produced this painting. Landscape specialists like Van Ruisdael invoked Dutch patriotism by selecting sites representative of the republic, including ruins, windmills, and city views.
altText: Dark moody painting of crumbling castle tower and walls amidst river and forest.

title: Merahi metua no Tehamana (Tehamana Has Many Parents or The Ancestors of Tehamana)
creditLine: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Charles Deering McCormick
description: In this portrait, Gauguin depicts the 13-year-old Tahitian girl Tehamana in a missionary dress holding a Samoan fan. A ripe mango alludes to fertility. In the background, Gauguin combined various non-European emblems—glyphs derived from an Easter Island tablet and a female deity inspired by Polynesian and Hindu sources—to build a generic sense of foreignness, transforming Tehamana into the embodiment of his own imagination.
altText: A young girl with medium skin wears a striking dress of black and white stripes with a short lace collar. Behind her is backdrop featuring symbols and native figures. Mangos sit beside her.

title: At the Moulin Rouge
creditLine: Helen Birch Bartlett Memorial Collection
description: Toulouse-Lautrec made a career depicting colorful personalities from Parisian cabarets and dance halls like the Moulin Rouge. He populated this painting with that nightclub's regulars, including himself—the diminutive figure in the center background. Dancer La Goulue arranges her hair behind the table where Jane Avril, another performer, socializes. Singer May Milton peers out from the painting's right edge, her face harshly lit and acid green.
altText: Painting, heavy in tones of blue-green and burnt orange, depicting a bar scene at night. The men wear top hats and many are bearded; the women are dressed in voluminous gowns and decorative hats. Five people converse in the center of the composition and a woman with a green face dominates the right foreground.

title: Nautilus Shell Cup
medium: Nautilus shell, ink, and gilded silver
creditLine: Kate S. Buckingham Endowment
description: During the Age of Discovery, European artists were inspired by the exotic materials suddenly available to them. Goldsmiths seized on the opportunity to include wondrous and seemingly magical materials—including coconuts, ivory, ostrich eggs, and, in this case, a nautilus shell from the Indian Ocean—into works of art that celebrated both nature and artifice.
altText: A work made of nautilus shell, ink, and gilded silver.

title: Statue of the Aphrodite of Knidos
creditLine: Katherine K. Adler Memorial Fund
description: This sculpture of Aphrodite, the Greek goddess of love and sexuality, is a Roman version of a renowned Greek statue known as the Aphrodite of Knidos. The original sculpture, carved in the mid-fourth century BCE, was acclaimed for its daring and innovative representation of the goddess: it was the first monumental nude depiction of a female deity in the classical Greek world.
altText: White and beige stone statue of a female nude standing in contrapposto position, with weight on the right leg. The head of the statue is missing. The left arm has been broken off just past the shoulder, and the left hand is also absent.

title: Saint Romanus of Antioch and Saint Barulas
creditLine: Gift of Mrs. Chauncey McCormick and Mrs. Richard E. Danielson
description: Francisco de Zurbarán created this painting for a church in Seville, Spain, dedicated to Saint Romanus of Antioch. Here, Romanus holds up his own tongue, torn out by his tormentors, and grasps a massive book inscribed with a prayer for the faithful. Painted to support the Counter-Reformation, the Catholic Church’s response to the Protestant movement, Zurbarán aimed to make the saints accessible to everyday people.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Still Life with Dead Game, Fruits, and Vegetables in a Market
creditLine: Charles H. and Mary F. S. Worcester Collection
description: This overflowing Flemish market stall is enlivened by dead animals splayed on the table, fighting roosters, and a pickpocket. An early example of Frans Snyders’s combination of ornamental still-life elements with secondary figures, this scene might have adorned the dining room of an aristocratic collector. Snyders was the leading Flemish painter of monumental still lifes. He regularly collaborated with his fellow Antwerp artist Peter Paul Rubens.
altText: An older man at left in red raises his hat toward a central table chaotically overflowing with dead game, fruits, and vegetables. The wings of dead birds and limbs of animals are splayed out at dramatic angles; a deer at center is suspended by his back legs. Live birds and a cat animate the scene.

title: Apples
creditLine: Gift of Florene May Schoenborn and Samuel A. Marx
description: When the 45-year-old Henri Matisse was rejected from military service at the outbreak of World War I, a friend encouraged him to contribute to the war effort the best way he could: by continuing to paint well. This led to a productive period of compositional and material experimentation—including this canvas—that Matisse hoped would sustain the tradition of French painting in the face of a cultural and national threat.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Nephthys, Horus the Child, and Isis Amulet
creditLine: W. Moses Willner Fund
description: Nephthys and her sister Isis appear in myths as mourners for Osiris. Here, identified by their headdresses, they flank the young Horus, the son of Osiris, symbolizing that from the death of Osiris comes renewed life. This amulet would assure rebirth in the afterlife.
altText: A work made of faience.

title: Funerary Mask
dateDisplay: Late Ptolemaic Period-early Roman Period, 1st century BCE
creditLine: W. Moses Willner Fund
description: Preserving the body and its individual parts through mummification or depiction, as with this funerary mask, was essential to life after death in ancient Egypt. Potent symbols, such as the amulets shaped like anatomical hearts strung around the neck of the mask, provided an extra layer of protection. For ancient Egyptians the heart—not the brain—was the center of thought and emotion.
altText: A wooden sculpture of the head and neck of a person, the skin painted gold, a geometrically decorated long wig, and many painted symbols.

title: Tomb Wall Fragment Depicting Donkeys
dateDisplay: Old Kingdom, late Dynasty 5, about 2375 BCE
creditLine: W. Moses Willner Fund
description: This fragment is part of a scene of donkeys being driven over grain to separate wheat from chaff—an image that was used in many Egyptian tombs. The tomb’s owner selected the decoration for his or her tomb chamber from a selection of established themes, much as one might select wallpaper today.
altText: A work made of limestone and pigment.

title: Early Morning, Tarpon Springs
creditLine: Edward B. Butler Collection
description: Over his career, Georges Inness became less interested in detailed paintings and more interested in "poetic truth," conveying mood and emotion through rich tone and broad handling. He made this painting in Tarpon Springs, Florida, after recently establishing his house and studio there. Through blurred outlines, subtle tonalities, and the solitary figure, Inness evoked the brightening day and peaceful mood of the moment.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Alabastron with Inscription
creditLine: Museum Purchase Fund
description: The style and material of this jar are nearly identical to those of Egyptian vessels made 3,000 years earlier. Although Egyptian in design, this vessel has an inscription in Greek—a dedication to the twin gods Castor and Pollux. It attests to the popularity of Greek gods in Egypt at the time of its creation, an interest that was reciprocated in Greece for Egyptian gods.
altText: A work made of travertine (egyptian alabaster).

title: The Serf
creditLine: Edward E. Ayer Endowment in memory of Charles L. Hutchinson
description: Between 1900 and 1909 Henri Matisse often turned to sculpture in an attempt "to put order into my feelings and find a style to suit me." The Serf, one of his earliest sculptures, consumed him: he was reported to have spent up to 500 sessions with his model, Bevilaqua, who also posed for Auguste Rodin.
altText: A work made of bronze.

title: Grapes, Lemons, Pears, and Apples
creditLine: Gift of Kate L. Brewster
description: This is one of a group of related canvases featuring fruit that Van Gogh painted in 1887. In these works, he employed more vibrant colors and used a thicker, broader paint application than he had earlier. Here, he used complementary colors whose contrasting effect is heightened by the pulsating pattern of brushstrokes that defines the tablecloth and creates a force field around the fruit.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Jupiter Rebuked by Venus
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by The Old Masters Society; the Alexander A. McKay Endowment
description: Abraham Janssens, Peter Paul Rubens's competitor in Antwerp in the 1610s, produced monumental paintings of mythological and secular subjects. Influenced by his five-year stay in Rome, he injected his paintings with recognizable quotations from ancient sculpture and Italian Renaissance painting. This scene of Venus reprimanding Jupiter on Mount Olympus is a direct reference to a composition by the Italian artist Raphael.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Statue of a Seated Woman
creditLine: Katherine K. Adler Memorial Fund
description: Roman sculptors often adapted the forms of earlier Greek artworks for use in entirely new contexts. This statue evokes the figures of seated, draped goddesses displayed at the Parthenon, the renowned temple on the Acropolis in Athens. Among the Romans, this statue type was used for sculptures of female deities such as Juno (Hera to the Greeks), the consort of Jupiter (Zeus to the Greeks), as well as for portraits of empresses and other women.
altText: A work made of marble.

title: Vessel with Dancing Maize Gods
artistDisplay: Aj Maxam (Maya) Vicinity of Naranjo, Petén region, Guatemala
creditLine: Ethel T. Scarborough Fund
description: This eighth-century Maya vessel was made by Ah Maxam, a royal member of the Naranjo kingdom of Guatemala. It depicts a Maya ruler dressed as the maize god, a deity connected with the cycle of death and resurrection. This scene shows the soul of the deceased accompanied into the domain of the dead. It would eventually be reborn, just as maize sprouts again in nature's cycle of renewal.
altText: Cup shaped ceramic vessel with red glyphs and dancing figures, orange on cream ground.

title: Masked Figurine with Boar Headdress, Possibly an Ocarina (Whistle)
artistDisplay: Tairona Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, Colombia
creditLine: Gift of Mrs. Everett McNear in memory of Everett McNear
description: To this day in Tairona communities, masked individuals dance, personifying the deified forces and phenomena of nature. This act associates the annual round of social and economic activities with the natural world’s cycle of death, fertility, and renewal.
altText: A work made of ceramic and pigment.

title: Head of Xilonen, the Goddess of Young Maize
creditLine: African and Amerindian Art Purchase Fund
description: This sculptural fragment represents Xilonen, the youthful Aztec (Mexica) goddess of new maize (corn), who embodies concepts of fertility and renewal. Two large ears of maize rise from her headband, with long tassels flowing down her back. The Aztecs held a July agricultural festival in Xilonen’s honor to celebrate the first fruits of summer. During this ceremony, a young girl impersonated the goddess, dancing to bring forth an abundant harvest.
altText: A work made of basalt.

title: The Feast in the House of Simon
artistDisplay: El Greco (Doménikos Theotokópoulos; Greek, active in Spain, 1541–1614) Workshop of El Greco (Doménikos Theotokópoulos; Greek, active in Spain, 1541–1614)
creditLine: Gift of Joseph Winterbotham Collection
description: Although this painting features the bold highlights, elongated figures, and vibrant colors characteristic of El Greco’s late career, the artist enlisted his workshop to execute some parts of the scene. The heads of the figures reflect the work of different artists, including likely the artist’s son, Jorge Manuel. The fantastical background, possibly conceived by an assistant, is unlike any other by El Greco.
altText: Painting depicting Christ anointed by a woman in yellow, seated centrally at a crowded table of guests with long thin grayish faces in colorful robes with strong white highlights. In the background, tall grey archways, a steepled building, and city architecture.

title: The Artist in His Studio
medium: Oil on paper mounted on panel
creditLine: Friends of American Art Collection
description: By the mid-1860s, American artist James McNeill Whistler was increasingly fascinated with the aesthetics of Asian art. Here, Whistler stares out at the viewer with palette and paintbrush in hand, surrounded by works from his collection: three Japanese scrolls on the wall and Chinese porcelain on the shelves at the left. The artist applied thin layers of paint in muted tones to evoke the flattened appearance of Japanese woodblock prints.
altText: A work made of oil on paper mounted on panel.

title: The Plate of Apples
creditLine: Gift of Kate L. Brewster
description: In this still life, Paul Cezanne disrupted expectations for painting in the late 1870s by tipping the tabletop and plate forward toward the viewer and constructing a table with edges that don’t quite align. These disorienting details are complemented by the heavy, sculptural forms he created by using a pointed tool to incise contours around the plate and some of the apples.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Composition (No. 1) Gray-Red
creditLine: Gift of Mrs. Gilbert W. Chapman
description: After World War I, many artists, including Piet Mondrian, believed that abstract art could contribute to a more harmonious society by communicating in a universal visual language. In 1917 Mondrian joined the De Stijl movement, which sought to develop a new aesthetic that corresponded to their utopian vision, and began developing his distictive style: compositions of off-white grounds divided by black lines that framed blocks of primary colors.
altText: Abstract line composition of black lines at right angles forming quadrants including a gray square at upper left and a gray rectangle and red rectangle at lower right, against a white background.

title: Movement
creditLine: Alfred Stieglitz Collection
description: Unlike many American artists, Marsden Hartley was more drawn to German Expressionism than to French modernism. This painting, made in Berlin, possesses an energy that evokes both the vibrancy of modern Berlin and movements of music. Like the painter Vasily Kandinsky, Hartley sought to make his work more like music, which he admired for its potential to be purely spiritual and separate from material reality.
altText: A multitude of vibrantly colored shapes interweave with one another.

title: The Last of New England—The Beginning of New Mexico
creditLine: Alfred Stieglitz Collection
description: In this painting, Marsden Hartley depicted an imagined scene in which the fallen trees of a New England forest in the foreground transition to the golden hills of New Mexico beyond. Weary of the East Coast, Hartley spent 18 months in the Southwest in 1918–19, believing that he could find rejuvenation in nature. Here, thick black lines define the Southwestern landscape, which he saw as alive with expressive potential.
altText: A work made of oil on paperboard.

title: Landscape No. 3, Cash Entry Mines, New Mexico
creditLine: Alfred Stieglitz Collection
description: In this painting, Marsden Hartley used short brushstrokes, patches of pigment, and abstracted cloud forms to portray soaring mountains under a vibrant sky, minimizing the industrial mines of the title. Hartley spent 18 months in New Mexico from 1918 until he returned to New York in 1919, but he continued to paint the Southwest from memory—the remembered landscape became a vehicle for modernist exploration of color and shape.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Trompe-l'Oeil Still Life with a Flower Garland and a Curtain
artistDisplay: Adriaen van der Spelt (Dutch, 1630–1673) Frans van Mieris (Dutch, 1635–1681)
creditLine: Wirt D. Walker Fund
description: Van der Spelt’s splendid garland displays about 20 floral varieties—including a tulip, a 16th-century import from Persia that is now an icon of Dutch culture. The deceptively realistic blue curtain, painted by Frans van Mieris, refers to the historical strategy for protecting paintings but also to the tale of Parhassius, a skilled Greek artist who fooled a rival into attempting to pull back a curtain painted onto one of his pictures.
altText: A work made of oil on panel.

title: Saint Martin and the Beggar
artistDisplay: El Greco (Doménikos Theotokópoulos; Greek, active in Spain, 1541–1614)
creditLine: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Chauncey McCormick
description: This painting by El Greco depicts Saint Martin, a popular saint in the 1600s when the Catholic Church was promoting acts of charity, like Martin giving his cloak to a beggar, as necessary for salvation. The composition includes other elements that would have resonated with El Greco's local audience: Saint Martin wears fashionable armor, and the walls of Toledo are visible in the distant background.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Catskill Mountains
creditLine: Edward B. Butler Collection
description: During the mid-19th century, the Catskill Mountains were America’s premiere tourist site. Inness’s painting of the area depicts a land tamed by human presence. The church, the carefully tended fields, and the hayrick are all finely delineated, reflecting Inness’s early style. The artist’s reverent handling of color and light has been linked to his interest in Swedenborgian spirituality, but it also relates to his love for this particular region.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Vase (Vase étrusque à rouleau)
artistDisplay: Sèvres Porcelain Manufactory (1756–present) Model designed by Charles Percier (born France, 1764–1838) Decoration designed by Alexandre-Theodore Brogniart (born France, 1739–1813) Flowers and ornament painted by Gilbert Drouet (active France, 1785–1825) Birds painted by Christophe-Ferdinand Caron (active France, 1792–1815) Sèvres, France
medium: Enameled and gilded hard-paste porcelain and gilded bronze
creditLine: Harold L. Stewart and Harry and Maribel G. Blum endowment funds
description: This vase epitomizes the achievements of the royal porcelain factory at Sèvres during the Napoleonic period. Commissioned by Napoleon in 1805 but produced only in 1813, this vase was still at the factory when Napoleon was exiled in 1814. It served as a diplomatic gift from his successor, King Louis XVIII, to Viscount Castlereagh, the British foreign secretary, and, later, the 2nd Marquess of Londonderry.
altText: Gold porcelain vase with flowers, birds, profile heads on handles.

title: A Marine
creditLine: Edward B. Butler Collection
description: George Inness’s rough, energetic brushstrokes evoke the raw beauty and destructive power of the ocean in this dramatic seascape created during a trip to Europe. Careful study of the surface of the central rock in the foreground illustrates the artist’s impressive manipulation of paint: by employing shifts in texture and shading, he was able to emphasize distinctions between sun and shadow, wet and dry, and clean and algae-covered.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Major-General Henry Dearborn
creditLine: Friends of American Art Collection
description: Gilbert Stuart’s idealized portrayal of Major-General Henry Dearborn presents an aging, yet robust military leader. Dearborn was a Revolutionary War hero who was secretary of war during Thomas Jefferson’s two presidential terms (1801–09) and served as senior major-general in the War of 1812. This work is one of several portraits Stuart made of American military and political men, among them his well-known depictions of George Washington.
altText: A work made of oil on mahogany panel.

title: Ewer with Incised Floral Decoration
medium: Gombroon ware, fritware with incised decoration under transparent glaze
creditLine: Mary Jane Gunsaulus Collection
description: This elegant ewer features lightly incised decoration under a transparent glaze. It is a type of ceramic commonly known as Gombroon ware, a name derived from the port from where these ceramics were exported in the 18th century, Bandar-e 'Abbas (known as Gombroon by the British). This ware was popular outside of the Islamic world because its delicate, glassy appearance was thought to closely resemble Chinese porcelain.
altText: A work made of gombroon ware, fritware with incised decoration under transparent glaze.

title: The Fountain, Villa Torlonia, Frascati, Italy
creditLine: Friends of American Art Collection
description: The year 1907 was a turning point for Sargent; the sought-after portraitist stepped away from his successful portraiture career to pursue plein-air landscape painting. This work, depicting his traveling companions and fellow artists Wilfrid and Jane Emmet de Glehn, captures that moment of transition. Combining landscape and portraiture, the composition speaks to friendship and painterly pursuits while also celebrating color, light, and movement.
altText: Portrait of a woman in white with a bonnet perched on an architectural feature painting something to her right, a spouting water fountain, greenery, and a an ornate, low white fence behind her. Beside her, a man leans back, eying the canvas.

title: The Walking Man
creditLine: Bequest of A. James Speyer
description: The Walking Man originated from one of Rodin’s early successes, his life-size Saint John the Baptist Preaching of 1878. Rodin made separate plaster studies of the sculpture’s components, and much later he returned to the legs of the Baptist, grafting onto them a torso from another composition. In 1900 he exhibited a half-life-size version of this work in plaster, and it made a deep impression on younger artists, notably Henri Matisse.
altText: A work made of bronze.

title: Cruet Stand
artistDisplay: Designed by Koloman Moser (Austrian, 1868-1918) Made by Alfred Mayer, silversmith for the Wiener Werkstätte (Austrian, 1903-1932) Austria, Vienna
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by Richard T. Crane, Mrs. Julian Armstrong, Jr., and Mrs. George B. Young
description: The geometric form of this cruet stand is characteristic of the Wiener Werkstätte—the Vienna Workshop—which was "dedicated to the artistic production of utilitarian items." They made baskets, trays, vases, and even furniture from sheets of metal perforated with latticework patterns. Abandoning references to historical design, Werkstätte artists created simple but elegant forms, hoping to bring “good design” to the masses.
altText: A work made of silver and glass.

title: Icebound
creditLine: Friends of American Art Collection
description: During the last decade of his life, John Henry Twachtman frequently painted views of the landscape surrounding his home in Greenwich, Connecticut. Almost square in format, this painting’s harmonious composition exemplifies Twachtman’s opinion that “never is nature more lovely than when it is snowing.” He enjoyed depicting the beauty of the frozen terrain, believing that it was conducive to contemplation and regeneration.
altText: Winter landscape painting with rocky stream lined by orange leafed trees.

title: Plum Vase (Maebyeong) with Clouds, Cranes, and Children Motifs
medium: Stoneware with red and white slip and celadon glaze
creditLine: Gift of Mr. Russell Tyson
description: This Goryeo dynasty (918–1392) vase showcases the sanggam decorating technique. A time-consuming and complex process, it involves carving a motif, filling it with white and/or red clay (which turns black after firing), and finally applying the final bluish-green glaze. This vase depicts two ovoid-framed scenes: children playing in a bamboo garden and cranes flying through clouds, symbolizing a wish for fertility and longevity.
altText: Pale green vase decorated with clouds, cranes, and children playing near bamboo trees.

title: Mastiff (Tomb Figurine)
medium: Brick-red earthenware with green lead glaze
creditLine: Gift of Russell Tyson
description: Tomb models such as this alert watchdog reflect an increasingly humanistic and mundane view of the afterlife. The dog's compact, hollow earthenware body has been molded in two halves, joined lengthwise along the head, chest, back, and rump. The lead glaze, colored green by the addition of copper oxide, has decomposed into thin layers that reflect light with silvery iridescence.
altText: A work made of brick-red earthenware with green lead glaze.

title: Storyteller
artistDisplay: Ceramist unknown (Jalisco) Ameca Valley, Jalisco, Mexico
creditLine: Bequest of Ruth Falkenau Fund in memory of her parents
description: These ceramic figures in energetic poses and with lively expressions were made in Jalisco's Ameca Valley. Like other West Mexican works of art, they were intended as tomb offerings. The range of subjects depicted by the sculptures includes gesturing individuals whose hand positions communicated well-established meanings. This sign language has yet to be described and interpreted, but such excited figures may well be recounting legends or myths.
altText: A work made of earthenware and slip.

title: Model Depicting a Ritual Center
artistDisplay: Ceramist unknown (Nayarit) Ixtlán del Río, Nayarit, Mexico
creditLine: Gift of Ethel and Julian Goldsmith
description: This distinctive West Mexican sculpture depicting an ancient ceremonial center may have been included in a tomb as an offering for the afterlife. It features houselike temples populated by flute players, a drummer, conch-shell trumpeters, dancers, women with children, and animals. In the middle of the circle, a masked figure—likely the ruler—stands atop a stepped pyramid.
altText: A work made of earthenware and pigment.

title: Still Life: Corner of a Table
creditLine: Ada Turnbull Hertle Endowment
description: This canvas, exhibited at the Salon of 1873, relates to Fantin-Latour’s largest and most famous painting of the decade, The Corner of a Table, an immense composition that includes detailed portraits of several major young Parisian poets and writers. The table around which they are posed displays many of the still-life elements that are arranged in a natural, random fashion in this work.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Coronation Stone of Moctezuma Xocoyotzin
artistDisplay: Maker unknown (Mexica, Aztec) Probably Tenochtitlan (now Mexico City), Mexico
creditLine: Major Acquisitions Fund
description: This stone, commemorating the beginning of Emperor Motecuhzoma II's reign, was originally located within the ritual center of Tenochtitlan, the capital of the empire conquered by the Aztecs between 1428 and 1519. The city's ruins lie beneath modern-day Mexico City. The sculpture legitimizes Motecuhzoma’s rule as part of the cosmic cycle and presents him as heir to the world in the present era of creation.
altText: Large plaque of stone carved with animal and geometric hieroglyphs.

title: Mount Washington
creditLine: Gift of Mrs. Richard E. Danielson and Mrs. Chauncey McCormick
description: The majestic White Mountains of New Hampshire were celebrated by artists, writers, and naturalists as a wilderness. But when Winslow Homer arrived on assignment from Harper's Weekly in 1868, the region was dominated by tourists, grand hotels, railroads, and well-groomed trails for walking and riding. Homer took a new approach in his depiction of the landscape, showing it instead as a stage for human activity, rather than as a sublime paradise.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Peacock Weather Vane
creditLine: Elizabeth R. Vaughan Fund
description: Early American weather vanes were collected in the 20th century for their sculptural qualities and celebrated as precursors to modernism. The Art Institute acquired this hand-forged vane from gallerist Edith Halpert, who distinguished herself in the New York art world by focusing on modern American art and vernacular arts from centuries prior. Weather vanes were popular among Halpert’s clients.
altText: A work made of iron.

title: Statuette of a Jackal
creditLine: Museum Purchase Fund
description: This statuette represents either the god Anubis or Wepwawet, both jackal guardians of burial sites. The figure is solid cast from copper alloy, and the details of its fur are incised. The figure may originally have decorated the top of a shrine.
altText: Metal statue of a jackal lying down with his head up and tall, thin ears alert. The work has a light green and brown patina.

title: Trial Piece with Hieroglyphs
creditLine: Museum Purchase Fund
description: Artists used stone remnants left over from larger works to practice carving hieroglyphic signs and decorative elements. Here, the profiles of a man and a feline deity may be studies for larger works. Two hieroglyphs also appear on the thin slab. The undulating horned viper at the bottom of this piece represents the sound f, while the large owl in the center has the phonetic value m.
altText: A work made of granite.

title: Stela (Commemorative Stone) Depicting the Funeral of Ramose
artistDisplay: Egyptian; Probably Armant or Thebes (now Luxor), Egypt
dateDisplay: New Kingdom, Dynasty 19, reign of Ramesses II (about 1279–1213 BCE)
creditLine: Museum Purchase Fund
description: Ancient Egyptians used mummification and ritual to transform the body and prepare the deceased for the afterlife. A pivotal step was the Opening of the Mouth ceremony, depicted here, which allowed the deceased to eat and drink in the afterlife. At the right of this scene, a jackal-headed figure holds the deceased’s human-shaped coffin. A pair of priests burn incense and pour libations, while a third recites sacred texts from a papyrus scroll.
altText: A work made of sandstone and pigment.

title: Mrs. John Nicholson (Hannah Duncan) and John Nicholson, Jr.
creditLine: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Carter H. Harrison
description: Peale was a prominent figure in the cultural and scientific life of Philadelphia in the late 18th and early 19th centuries. Mrs. John Nicholson (Hannah Duncan) and John Nicholson, Jr. is a tender portrait of mother and child. The natural backdrop and sprig of flowers in the boy’s hand signal a domestic bond. Mrs. Nicholson’s uncorseted dress and freely coiffed hair (without a wig) likewise speak to the humanistic ideals of the Enlightenment.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: View on the River Roseau, Dominica
artistDisplay: Agostino Brunias (Italian, active in England and the West Indies, 1758–96)
creditLine: Gift of Emily Crane Chadbourne
description: The Italian-born artist Agostino Brunias settled on the island of Dominica, painting scenes of Caribbean life for his planter-class patrons and white audiences abroad. By not including the brutal conditions of slavery, his compositions shaped a reassuring vision of British imperialism for those in power. Yet by centering enslaved and free people of color—and mixed-race interactions—he also foregrounded the human impact of colonialism.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: The Drinkers
creditLine: Joseph Winterbotham Collection
description: While institutionalized in Saint-Rémy, Van Gogh often copied works by artists he admired, which freed him from having to produce original compositions and allowed him to concentrate on interpretation. In his vibrant take on Honoré Daumier’s woodcarving "Physiology of Drinking," there is real pathos and a desperation in the earnest concentration with which the men drink, as if to quench a spiritual thirst.
altText: Painting of three male figures, two older men in top hats and a younger man with red hair, standing outdoors around a wooden table with a pitcher on it, drinking from glasses. A much smaller, childlike figure at left peers over the table and drinks from a white cup. The scene is rendered in winding paint strokes in shades of green and blue.

title: Dorothea and Francesca
creditLine: A. A. Munger Collection
description: Here, Cecilia Beaux explored the line between portraiture and figure painting by focusing less on the individuality of the sitters and more on their coordinated movements. Beaux was the rare woman artist competing for portrait commissions in the male-dominated art market of her time, and she fared exceedingly well. She was also an influential teacher and became the first woman to secure a faculty position at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Virgin and Child with Two Angels
dimensions: Diam.: 34.4 cm (13 1/2 in.); Framed: Diam.: 44.5 cm (17 1/2 in.)
creditLine: Max and Leola Epstein Collection
description: Botticelli’s works mark the culmination of a mystical religious tradition in the art of early Renaissance Florence. Here two angels draw back curtains to reveal the Virgin and Child, who are framed by trees in a setting suggesting a throne. The intimate presentation of the holy figures and Christ’s gesture of blessing suggest that this painting served a private devotional function.
altText: A work made of tempera on panel.

title: Virgin and Child with an Angel
creditLine: Max and Leola Epstein Collection
description: Sandro Botticelli's humanizing yet idealized depiction of the Virgin Mary embracing the baby Jesus conveys the sacred beauty of maternal love. Mary nuzzles her son’s chubby cheek as he grasps the nape of her neck. An angel looks on adoringly. Celebrated in his own time, Botticelli developed a distinctly sentimental and tactile style of painting for both religious and secular subjects.
altText: A light-skinned, blond Virgin Mary in blue holds a child, his arms reaching around her neck and face upturned toward hers. At left, an angel looks on.

title: Self-Portrait
medium: Oil on artist's board, mounted on cradled panel
creditLine: Joseph Winterbotham Collection
description: Van Gogh’s face is as well known as his art—in fact, it is inseparable from it. The artist painted more than 35 self-portraits over his lifetime. This one was created in Paris under the influence of Seurat and pointillism. The intense dabs of paint and color, anchored by his eyes, create a turbulent energy, giving the viewer a deep sense of the artist’s presence.
altText: Painting of a red-haired, bearded man with light skin, painted in short brushstrokes and multicolored dots. The background is likewise a mass of small, closely spaced colored dots, these in green, blue, and red-orange.

title: Arab Horseman Attacked by a Lion
creditLine: Potter Palmer Collection
description: Man and beast intertwine to form a single writhing body in this emotionally charged depiction of a lion attacking a horse and its rider. While many artists of the period explored the theme of man versus nature, depictions of Arab men entangled with wild animals served a specific propagandistic function, justifying the brutality of French colonial rule by depicting its subjects as violent and inhuman.
altText: A work made of oil on paperboard.

title: Lion Hunt
creditLine: Potter Palmer Collection
description: In 1832 Delacroix joined an envoy to French-colonized Algeria. In his journals he expressed admiration for Arab culture, even characterizing it as superior to that of post-revolutionary France. Nevertheless, in paintings like this he catered to violent European fantasies about the Arab world. Having never witnessed a lion hunt, he synthesized studies of landscapes, Islamic costume, and zoo animals to bring this narrative to life with intensity.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Interrupted Reading
medium: Oil on canvas, mounted on board
creditLine: Potter Palmer Collection
description: Corot rarely exhibited his late figure paintings like this compelling example, focusing instead on his idyllic landscapes. While here he chose a traditional subject—the muse-like image of a woman reading a book—Corot showed his model pausing and looking up. He also used unconventionally bold brushwork while still delighting in detail—the ribbon in the model’s hair, the delicate earrings, and the deep folds in the skirt.
altText: A pensive faced woman sits, slightly hunched, holding a book.

title: On the Stage
medium: Pastel and essence over monotype on cream laid paper, laid down on board
creditLine: Potter Palmer Collection
description: Edgar Degas depicts seven dancers performing in a ballet. The gestures of the women’s raised arms and feet capture the actions, forms, and poses of the corps de ballet (the ensemble, or chorus, of a ballet company that performs in groups). To heighten the sense of motion and spectacle, Degas smudged the edges of the forms where the dancers’ dresses meet the stage.
altText: A work made of pastel and essence over monotype on cream laid paper, laid down on board.

title: The Races at Longchamp
creditLine: Potter Palmer Collection
description: Édouard Manet composed this scene of a racetrack so that the throng of horses and jockeys thunders straight toward the viewer. In contrast to traditional sporting artists, who always showed races from the side with the horses in profile, Manet achieved a sense of expansive space with this thrilling perspective. The painting records the last moments of the race as the horses rush past the finish line, indicated by the pole with a circular top.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Sea View, Calm Weather (Vue de mer, temps calme)
creditLine: Potter Palmer Collection
description: This is one of Manet’s earliest paintings of the sea, a subject to which he returned repeatedly. It is one of three or four works that he painted in Paris from sketches made on a vacation with his family in the northern port of Boulogne-sur-Mer. Though boldly brushed and almost calligraphic in form, the vessels remain identifiable as specific types. A side-wheel packet steamer heads up the Channel, leaving the slower sailing boats in its wake.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Bordighera
creditLine: Potter Palmer Collection
description: Monet created this painting in 1884 when he traveled to Bordighera, a town on the Italian Riviera. In a letter to sculptor Auguste Rodin, he described his efforts to capture the brilliant Mediterranean light, declaring that he was “fencing, wrestling, with the sun.” In this light-drenched composition painted from a hilltop vantage point, the sea is barely visible through the interlaced trunks of pine trees.
altText: Bright landscape painting featuring spindly trees with lush leaves surrounded by light-green foliage, a small town visible between the trees at center, and a calm blue sea in the background.

title: On the Bank of the Seine, Bennecourt
creditLine: Potter Palmer Collection
description: Monet painted this work in his late 20s when he was not yet widely known but was already using radical techniques to depict scenes from modern life, such as this one, featuring his future wife, Camille Doncieux. At the time, viewers were used to paintings that aimed to mirror reality, with a smooth traditional paint surface. To them Monet's approach seemed shockingly unfinished and illegible.
altText: Painting of woman in a striped dress seated on the bank of a river, beneath a full, leafy tree, a boat at the shore and a village visible across the river.

title: The Departure of the Boats, Étretat
creditLine: Potter Palmer Collection
description: Monet painted this work and Boats on the Beach at Étretat while looking out the window of his hotel room. He centered each composition on the boats, combining blues, pinks, purples, and greens to render wet surfaces. The brightly colored hulls of beached crafts lend relative scale to the structures in Boats on the Beach, and the groups of figures at the water’s edge, composed of quick, gestural strokes, register human activity in this work.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Stacks of Wheat (Sunset, Snow Effect)
creditLine: Potter Palmer Collection
description: The Art Institute has the largest group of Monet’s "Stacks of Wheat" paintings in the world. The artist worked on the canvases in the field outside his farmhouse, painting simultaneously at several easels; he later refined them in the studio. An exhibition of these works in 1891 marked a breakthrough in Monet’s career, as well as in the history of French art.
altText: Two haystacks, dusted with snow, in a hazy, snow-covered field at sunset. The snow is highlighted in purple tones, the sky a yellow and orange gradient.

title: The Petite Creuse River
creditLine: Potter Palmer Collection
description: Claude Monet began this canvas—one of three of the Petite Creuse—in April 1889 but only returned to it later that spring, by which time the landscape had changed considerably. The oak tree, for example, was sprouting leaves, obscuring the view he had already established. Rather than rework or restart the canvas to depict the current season, Monet hired workers to defoliate the tree so that he could re-create its earlier appearance.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Acrobats at the Cirque Fernando (Francisca and Angelina Wartenberg)
creditLine: Potter Palmer Collection
description: The two girls in this painting by Pierre-Auguste Renoir are Francisca and Angelina Wartenberg, acrobats who performed in the famed Cirque Fernando in Paris. They are depicted clutching oranges tossed to them from the crowd as gifts. Although they are painted standing in the center of a circus ring, Renoir actually painted them in his studio, where he could take full advantage of natural sunlight.
altText: Two girls in acrobatic uniforms stand in an arena, one holds oranges.

title: Husking Bee, Island of Nantucket
creditLine: Gift of Honoré and Potter Palmer
description: This painting by Eastman Johnson takes its nostalgic theme from rural Nantucket. A timeless evocation of agrarian peace and cooperation, it includes a woman discovering a red ear of corn, which, according to folk tradition, would allow her to kiss the person of her choice. This use of local subject matter combined with an international style was typical of American art around the time of the centennial.
altText: Dozens of figures in a brown field filled with discarded corn silks form two rows and sit across from each other husking corn, a farm in the background.

title: Trouville (Grey and Green, the Silver Sea)
creditLine: Gift of Honoré and Potter Palmer
description: In the early 1860s, James McNeill Whistler began to develop an art-for-art’s-sake aesthetic, eschewing narrative or naturalistic details to focus more on formal concerns. In 1865 he traveled to the French town of Trouville, where he painted with Gustave Courbet and experimented with a series of simplified seascapes. The high horizon line and broad expanses of muted color in this spare composition reveal his interest in Japanese woodblock prints.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Grey and Silver: Old Battersea Reach
creditLine: Gift of Honoré and Potter Palmer
description: James McNeill Whistler painted marine subjects throughout his career. In this painting, he focused on the industrial nature of London's Thames River—boats and barges, laboring men, and smoking chimneys. Despite the realism of the subject, Whistler unified the composition with deft brushwork and a subtle palette of brown and gray that anticipates his later interest in delicate tonal harmonies.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Amphora (Storage Jar)
artistDisplay: Attributed to the Sabouroff Painter Greek; Athens
creditLine: Gift of Martin A. Ryerson
description: The vase shape is called a Nolan amphora, after Nola, Italy, where this and some of the first examples were discovered. Nolan amphorae are small, usually less than 15 inches, and have a distinctive shape: an elongated ovoid body on a thick disk foot, an offset flaring neck, an inverted lip with grooves for a lid, and handles that rise from the shoulder and curve to join the neck. Figures are drawn between the handles on the front and back.
altText: A work made of terracotta, red-figure.

title: Horse
creditLine: Gift of Robert Allerton
description: This representation of a horse, fully decorated with saddle, stirrups, and bell ornaments, is a haniwa, a terracotta figure made for ritual and funerary use. Found northeast of Tokyo, this clay figure would have likely been at a burial mound, in an area filled with figurines and animal forms, perhaps meant to represent the possessions the deceased hoped to take with them after death.
altText: A work made of earthenware.

title: Buddha
creditLine: Lucy Maud Buckingham Collection
description: Buddhism flourished in China under the Tang dynasty (618–907). This monumental Buddha exhibits the deity's distinctive features: tightly curled hair covering a cranial mound that symbolizes his enlightenment and a forehead depression that originally held a jewel representing wisdom. The pedestal base is ringed with lotus petals, white flowers that rise from muddy water and evoke Buddhist beliefs in purity and the search for enlightenment.
altText: A work made of limestone with traces of polychromy.

title: God Shiva Seated in Loving Embrace with Goddess Uma on the Bull Nandi
creditLine: Kate S. Buckingham Fund
description: Shiva Maheshvara (the Great Lord) and his divine mate, Uma (also called Parvati), sympolize the ideal Hindu couple. Shiva is most commonly worshipped in abstract linga form, but he also came to represent the perfect family man. Here, he is seated on his bull Nandi, with Uma resting on Shiva's thigh. Their sons, elephant-headed Ganesha and Skanda Karttikeya astride his peacock, appear among the figures at the base.
altText: A work made of sandstone.

title: Water Lily Pond
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Lewis Larned Coburn Memorial Collection
description: In 1893, Claude Monet began transforming the marshy ground behind his Giverny home into a pond, on the narrow end of which he built a Japanese-style wood bridge. Adding both exotic and domestic plantings, including his famous water lilies, the artist created the garden that would be one of his principal subjects for the rest of his life.
altText: Painting of a small pond dense with pink water lilies, their roots visible through the water, a railed footbridge arching over the pond and lush, dark green folliage surrounding it.

title: The Assumption of the Virgin
artistDisplay: El Greco (Doménikos Theotokópoulos; Greek, active in Spain, 1541–1614)
creditLine: Gift of Nancy Atwood Sprague in memory of Albert Arnold Sprague
description: This painting was the central element of an altarpiece that was El Greco’s first major Spanish commission and large public work. The Virgin floats upward on the crescent moon, a symbol of her purity, while the apostles express amazement and concern. El Greco’s broad brushstrokes and bold color made this painting a favorite of modern artists such as Pablo Picasso and Mary Cassatt.
altText: Painting of the Virgin Mary ascending to heaven amongst multitude of angels.

title: The Two Disciples at the Tomb
creditLine: Robert A. Waller Fund
description: Perhaps the most renowned American painter of religious works at the turn of the 20th century, Tanner moved to France in 1891 to escape the racism that limited his career. This painting depicts an event from the Gospel of Saint John in which Peter and John arrive at Christ’s empty tomb. Peter looks down somberly, while John is transfixed, bathed in a golden light.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Kylix (Drinking Cup)
creditLine: Gift of Martin A. Ryerson through The Antiquarian Society
description: This is an example of a kylix, the most popular type of wine cup in ancient Greece. Rising from a round foot and a thin stem, the cup flares out to a wide bowl with two handles on opposite sides. In the decorative band around the lip of this cup, a human figure in Grecian dress is depicted in the company of a lion.
altText: A work made of terracotta, black-figure.

title: Lekythos (Oil Jar)
artistDisplay: Attributed to the Reed Painter Greek; Athens
creditLine: Gift of Martin A. Ryerson through the Antiquarian Society
description: Athenian cemeteries housed a variety of monuments and offerings to the dead, including marble tombstones and terracotta vessels, like this vase. Called a lekythos, it held oil and was decorated in a distinctive technique known as white ground. Atop this, figures visiting tombs or bidding farewell were painted in rich colors, many of which have since faded. Most of these bottles were made for burial with the dead or to be left at their graves.
altText: A work made of terracotta, white-ground.

title: Guttus (Pouring Vessel)
creditLine: Gift of Martin A. Ryerson through The Antiquarian Society
description: During the course of the 5th and 4th centuries BCE, black vessels (commonly called black-glaze vessels) were made with increasing frequency in both Greece and southern Italy. Many of them replicate the shape of metal vessels; others have detailing that is molded or incised. While the quality of these vessels varies greatly, all would have been less expensive than vessels decorated in contemporary techniques such as red-figure.
altText: A work made of terracotta, black-glaze with stamping.

title: Madame François Buron
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by Mrs. Albert J. Beveridge in memory of her mother, Abby Louise Spencer (Mrs. Augustus Eddy).
description: After his father’s death, the young David was raised by his uncle, architect François Buron, and his wife, Marie-Josèphe Fromont. Madame Buron was supportive of David’s desire to become a painter, in opposition to her husband’s wish that he study architecture. In this intimate early portrait, David presented his aunt looking up momentarily from her reading. Her glance suggests an affectionate bond between the painter and sitter.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Head of a Luohan
dateDisplay: Northern Song, Liao, or Jin dynasty, c. 11th century
creditLine: Gift of the Orientals
description: In traditional Buddhist belief, a luohan is a disciple who has attained enlightenment through intense personal effort. Beginning in the ninth century, the worship of luohan and their depiction in art evolved primarily within the Zen sect of Buddhism. This head was created using the delicate technique of hollow dry lacquer, where layers of cloth are soaked in lacquer (a thick sap) and then painted.
altText: Sculpture of Asian man’s head, he is bald with detailed angular facial features.

title: Retable and Frontal of the Life of Christ and the Virgin
creditLine: Gift of Charles Deering
description: This ensemble comprises a retable, which was set up behind the altar table, and a frontal, which decorated the table's front. The work is a testament to the piety of Pedro López de Ayala, a major figure in the political and cultural life of late medieval Spain. For more than 500 years, it decorated his family's funerary chapel in their fortified palace in northern Spain.
altText: A work made of tempera and gold on panel.

title: Head of a Philosopher
creditLine: Gift of Mrs. Richard E. Danielson and Mrs. Chauncey McCormick
description: Giandomenico Tiepolo collaborated with his father, Giambattista, on his greatest projects, including the decoration of Madrid's Royal Palace. After his father's death, Giandomenico emerged as a highly original artist adept at depicting popular activities humorously. This is one of a group of philosophers' heads he made in response to a series by his father. The lighter, more dashing work marks a distinct departure from his father’s style.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Distant View of Niagara Falls
creditLine: Friends of American Art Collection
description: By the 19th century, Niagara Falls was already an iconic American landscape, nearly verging on mythical. Thomas Cole visited the landmark in May 1829 and composed this romanticized, autumnal scene the following year. In amplifying the natural grandeur of the American landscape, the artist wilfully ommitted the factories, scenic overlooks, and hotels that populated the area in the early 19th century.
altText: Painting of a vast autumn scene with two very small figures in Indigenous clothing standing on a cliff overlooking a massive waterfall in the distance.

title: An Alcove in the Art Students' League
creditLine: Bequest of Kate L. Brewster
description: Charles Courtney Curran documented the activities of the Art Students’ League in New York, where he studied and later taught. Here male and female students work from casts of Greek and Roman sculptures and classically inspired Renaissance objects to practice rendering the idealized human form. Once students mastered drawing sculptures, they would have advanced to a class with live models.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Portrait Vessel
artistDisplay: Ceramist unknown (Moche) Southern Moche region, north coast, Peru
creditLine: Kate S. Buckingham Endowment Fund
description: Ceramic portrait vessels produced by artists of the Moche culture are the only discernible examples of portraiture, in a Euro-American sense, from the ancient Andes. Vessels like this one were often placed in burials as funerary offerings. They may also have been sent as emblems of royal authority, or even emissaries, to other elite individuals in nearby settlements.
altText: Sculpted head of a medium-skinned man in a beige headdress with geometric pattern and distinctive stirrup-shaped top piece.

title: Two Putti Supporting a Torch
creditLine: Through prior purchase with funds provided by Mr. and Mrs. John Golitz; through prior bequest of Hans G. Cahen
description: In this terracotta sculpture, a pouting putto and his companion flank an elaborate candelabra with a lit torch. The surfaces of the baby bodies and architectural elements retain the marks of the sculptor’s tools, an indication that this work is not a finished product. Artists often used terracotta, a type of reddish-brown ceramic, for models that then served as guides for their assistants to begin carving the final version.
altText: A work made of terracotta on slate.

title: Winter Scene
artistDisplay: Francisco José de Goya y Lucientes (Spanish, 1746–1828)
creditLine: Bequest of Verde C. Graff
description: Two groups of travelers, one with a slaughtered pig in tow, converge on an icy road during a snowstorm. Goya captured the scene’s wintry atmosphere with barren trees, large swaths of cool grays and whites, and diagonal brushstrokes that convey rapid snowfall. This painting is one of a series of studies Goya created for monumental tapestries depicting the four seasons, commissioned for a dining hall at the Royal Palace of El Pardo in Spain.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Double-sided Plaque Depicting a Lion and Birds
creditLine: Museum Purchase Fund
description: This plaque was reused several times. Over the initial design of a lion, an artist drew a grid in order to copy the image to another surface. At a later date, the plaque was used as a note pad at which time the ink inscription was added. The notation is a list of names, perhaps witnesses to a transaction.
altText: A work made of limestone and pigment.

title: Portrait of a Man in Costume
creditLine: Gift of Mary and Leigh Block in honor of John Maxon
description: The 18th-century artist Jean-Honoré Fragonard is best known for his lighthearted, amorous subjects. This work, painted in lively brushstrokes, represents another important aspect of his genius—his fantasy portraits, in which he referenced earlier artworks to enliven his own characterizations of patrons and artistic friends. In this instance, Fragonard references a painting of an actor by the Italian Baroque artist Domenico Fetti.
altText: Painting of bearded, ruddy-faced man in eighteenth century style clothing.

title: The Red Room, Etretat
creditLine: Bequest of Mrs. Clive Runnells
description: Inspired by a personal photograph, this work reflects Vallotton's focus on the daily life of his household. This example employs bold blocks of solid color: the red of the bed and the pink of the child's dress, for example. The result is a graphic simplicity similar to the artist's woodblock prints of interior scenes created during this same period.
altText: Painting of a stately woman seated on a red velvet chair in a blood-red room, a blue-white fireplace to her left. She glances down at the floor with a serene expression toward a tiny blond child—a baby—who sits on the floor tearing up paper, her pink-clad back facing the viewer.

title: Young Woman at an Open Half-Door
artistDisplay: Rembrandt van Rijn (Dutch, 1606–1669) Workshop of Rembrandt van Rijn (Dutch, 1606–1669)
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection
description: This painting of a young woman, with her sidelong glance and the ambiguous lift at the corner of her mouth, exemplifies the playful nature of Rembrandt’s character studies, called tronies, as well as his clever use of doorways and windows as framing devices. However, the overall flatness of this work suggests that it might have been painted by a member of his workshop and then endorsed as a studio product with the artist’s signature and date.
altText: A young woman peers out to the right from from a Dutch door whose bottom half is closed. She wears a brown dress with a corset and a red beaded necklace.

title: The Song of the Lark
creditLine: Henry Field Memorial Collection
description: This painting by Jules Adolphe Breton was among the first to enter the Art Institute's collection when the museum opened in 1893. It quickly became one of the most popular paintings at the museum. By the 1920s, reproductions were hanging on classroom walls across the United States. In 1934, it was named “America’s Best Loved Picture” in a contest sponsored by the Chicago Daily News.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Beggar with a Duffle Coat (Philosopher)
creditLine: A. A. Munger Collection
description: This painting and Beggar with Oysters were probably conceived as companion pieces. Manet exhibited them together in 1872, along with paintings of an absinthe drinker and a ragpicker, under the collective title Philosophers. Parisian beggars held a particular fascination for Realist artists and writers. By setting his large-scale figures against empty, dark backgrounds, Manet added to their portraitlike, indeed heroic, presence.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Tomb Wall Fragment Depicting Abdu and Reputka with Offering Bearers
artistDisplay: Egyptian; Tomb of Abdu, Giza, Egypt
creditLine: Museum Purchase Fund
description: Leaning on a staff that marks his high social status, Abdu stands beside his wife, Reputka. Such portraits, showing the deceased with idealized rather than individualized faces and bodies, were commonly used in the tomb chapels of upper-class Egyptians. Some scenes—like this one of a wife embracing her husband with one arm—were standard for thousands of years. Names written in hieroglyphs personalize the image of the eternally youthful couple.
altText: A work made of limestone.

title: Old Man with a Gold Chain
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. W. W. Kimball Collection
description: In his character studies, Rembrandt explored the effect of a single figure, made dramatic through the use of rich, subtle lighting and costumes, which the artist collected to transform his models. Here, the gold chain and steel gorget suggest an honored military career, while the plumed beret evokes an earlier time. The unidentified sitter, once thought to be the artist’s father, was a favorite model.
altText: Portrait of man wearing voluminous black cloak, feathered hat, and gold medallion.

title: Solidus (Coin) Portraying Emperor Constantine I
artistDisplay: Roman; minted in Antioch (in present-day Turkey)
creditLine: Gift of Martin A. Ryerson
description: This coin featuring the emperor Constantine I (reigned 306–37 CE) was minted soon after he became sole emperor. It depicts him with a youthful, clean-shaven face and a hairstyle of thick locks arranged over his forehead. These features deliberately evoked the appearance of earlier, celebrated emperors, including Augustus (reigned 27 BCE–14 CE) and Trajan (reigned 98–117 CE), visually tying his reign to his esteemed predecessors’.
altText: A work made of gold.

title: Stater (Coin) Depicting the Goddess Kore
creditLine: Gift of Martin A. Ryerson
description: Though ancient Greece's population was largely illiterate, it could identify the place of origin of a coin by its imagery. This coin from Metapontum shows the head of the goddess Kore, crowned with grain, on the front and an ear of grain on the back. Metapontum accrued its wealth through farming, and by illustrating the ear of grain on its coins, the city-state reminded its trading partners of its agricultural abundance.
altText: A work made of silver.

title: Tetradrachm (Coin) Depicting the God Apollo Gryneios
artistDisplay: Greek; minted in Myrina, Aeolis, Asia Minor (now Turkey)
creditLine: Gift of Martin A. Ryerson
description: This coin is recognized as one of the most beautiful examples of minting from antiquity. The front depicts the head of the god Apollo. The back depicts Apollo marching right, holding a patera (shallow bowl) and garlanded laurel branch. Apollo also wears a wreath of laurel, which was his sacred plant. In his youth Apollo pursued a nymph named Daphne (another name for laurel), who chose to turn herself into a laurel tree to escape the god.
altText: A work made of silver.

title: The Advance-Guard, or The Military Sacrifice (The Ambush)
creditLine: George F. Harding Collection
description: Frederic Remington, famous for his dynamic compositions of frontier life, presented mythic, romanticized views of the American West. Here, a cavalry scout, shot by an unseen Souix warrior, slumps over his horse while the troops behind him flee the ambush. Like most of his work, it was created for a white audience who understood the West as a place of both danger and opportunity.
altText: Three cavalry scouts—light-skinned men mounted on gleaming brown horses—among light-beige, arid mountains. The figure in the foreground has begun to to slump and seems poised to fall, his rifle on the ground, his horse agitated and alarmed. The others ride off in pursuit.

title: The Bronco Buster
artistDisplay: Frederic Remington (American, 1861–1909) Cast by Henry-Bonnard Bronze Company (American, 1872–1926)
creditLine: George F. Harding Collection
description: As a painter and illustrator, Frederic Remington garnered success by crafting mythic, romanticized views of frontier life. "The Bronco Buster" was his first attempt to do so in sculpture. A technical achievement in bronze, the composition of a cowboy attempting to tame a horse portrays an idea of the Western United States in dramatic and violent terms: a white settler-colonialist in the act of subduing nature and flesh.
altText: Brown bronze statue of man with riding crop atop a rearing horse.

title: Water Lily Pond
creditLine: Gift of Mrs. Harvey Kaplan
description: During World War I, after several years of inactivity because of bad health and grief over the death of his second wife, Claude Monet embarked on a period of intense work. He began a group of monumental water lily paintings that he would later offer to the French state. Alongside the project, he painted a suite of 19 smaller canvases, including this one.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Double Pendant in the Form of a Mythical Saurian with Tusks
medium: Gold with plaster restoration of boar tusks
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by the Auxiliary Board
description: Caimans are a species of reptile closely related to the alligator. Emblems of caiman and caiman-like creatures, like this pair of pendants, were often symbolic of the land floating in the primordial sea, thus evoking the world of the original creation and the ongoing ties between the mythic past and the heroic present.
altText: A work made of gold with plaster restoration of boar tusks.

title: Bacchus Consoling Ariadne
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by Mrs. Arma Wyler
description: Aimé-Jules Dalou's first success came with images of modern life, but he later undertook allegorical subjects and historical statues for public commissions. This work depicts the mythical princess Ariadne and Bacchus, the god of wine. Having been abandoned on the Greek island of Naxos, Ariadne is tenderly awakened by the deity while a mischievous faun attempts to distract the couple with an offering of grapes.
altText: A work made of plaster.

title: Stack of Wheat (Thaw, Sunset)
creditLine: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Daniel C. Searle
description: Through 1890 and 1891, Monet created a series of paintings depicting the stacks of wheat that stood outside his farmhouse in Giverny. He painted at several easels simultaneously outside and then refined pictorial harmonies in the studio. In most of the winter views, like this one, the stacks seem wrapped by bands of hill and field, as if bedded down for the season.
altText: A lone wheat stack, in shadow, rests on a field with traces of snow, the snow taking on reflected shades of pink, yellow, orange, and blue from the unseen setting sun. A line of pale yellow illuminates the horizon above the hills beyond.

title: Saint Francis
creditLine: George F. Harding Collection
description: The Franciscans were among the reformed religious orders whose preaching and teaching activities helped revive the Roman Catholic Church in the Southern Netherlands following years of turmoil in the 1500s. Rubens here depicted the order’s founder, Saint Francis of Assisi, recognizable by the wound that imitates the pierced hands of the crucified Jesus. Rubens conveyed the saint’s spirituality through his meditative gaze and posture.
altText: A work made of oil on panel.

title: Beach at Cabasson (Baigne-Cul)
creditLine: L. L. and A. S. Coburn, and Bette and Neison Harris funds; Charles H. and Mary F. S. Worcester Collection; through prior acquisition of the Kate L. Brewster Collection
description: In 1891, as a result of his rheumatoid arthritis, Cross moved to the Côte d’Azur in southeastern France. The move deeply affected his art: after settling on the Mediterranean coast, he embraced the divided brushwork (small dashes and dots of color) and tonal gradations of “scientific Impressionism.” This methodical technique was a departure from the Impressionists’ more intuitive quick strokes of color to capture fleeting atmospheric conditions.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Magnolias on Light Blue Velvet Cloth
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by Gloria and Richard Manney; Harold L. Stuart Endowment Fund
description: This painting dates from the later part of Martin Johnson Heade’s long, varied, and peripatetic career. After traveling through the United States, to England and continental Europe, and three different times to Brazil, Heade settled in Saint Augustine, Florida, at the age of 64. There he began painting detailed arrangements of native flowers, including the Cherokee rose, orange blossom, and, as in this work, magnolia.
altText: Still life of sensuously detailed painting of four white magnolias lying on blue velvet cloth.

title: Volute Krater (Mixing Bowl)
artistDisplay: Attributed to the Painter of Copenhagen 4223 Greek; Apulia, Italy
creditLine: Katherine K. Adler Memorial Fund
description: On the front of this funerary vessel, a young warrior and a tutor or philosopher are shown standing in a naiskos, or tomb, surrounded by attendants with offerings. Above them is the head of the mythical poet and singer Orpheus. On the back, another tomb is decorated with large white figures, which may be symbolic representations of the dead or may depict marble statues of the tomb’s occupants.
altText: A work made of terracotta, red-figure.

title: Loutrophoros (Container for Bath Water)
artistDisplay: Attributed to the Varrese Painter Greek; Apulia, Italy
creditLine: Katherine K. Adler Memorial Fund
description: Though vessels like this were designed to hold water for ritual bathing before marriage, they could also be placed at the tombs of young women who did not live to a marriageable age. This example likely served such a purpose, as it depicts a woman within a naiskos, a temple-like structure marking a family gravesite, in addition to images of a bride preparing herself for her wedding day with the help of female friends and family.
altText: A work made of terracotta, red-figure.

title: Pitcher
artistDisplay: Design attributed to Edward C. Moore (American, 1827–1891) Tiffany and Company (American, founded 1837) New York
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by Mrs. Frank L. Sulzberger
description: An asymmetrical water scene wraps around the body of this pitcher. The vignette was almost certainly inspired by the work of Katsushika Hokusai, a Japanese artist known for his dynamic woodblock prints of the natural world. Tiffany and Company’s design library included three volumes of Hokusai’s work, many featuring the same graceful irises, enlivened dragonflies, and splashing carp visible on this pitcher.
altText: Shiny silver pitcher with pond design featuring reeds, dragonfly

title: Chair
artistDisplay: Cevedra B. Sheldon American, 1840–1895 Marks Adjustable Folding Chair Company American, 1877–1897 New York
creditLine: Gift of Stefan T. Edlis
description: Patent furniture reached the height of its popularity in the last quarter of the 19th century. This folding chair was patented in 1876 and touted in advertisements as “the king of all chairs.” Adjustable by the lever on the seat rail, the chair could be set into numerous positions and used variously as a lounge chair, an invalid chair, a smoking chair, or a bed.
altText: A work made of iron, walnut, cane, and upholstery.

title: Abraham Lincoln
artistDisplay: Daniel Chester French (American, 1850–1931) Cast by Roman Bronze Works (American, founded 1897)
creditLine: Gift of Elsie O. Sang in memory of Philip D. Sang
description: In 1909 the Lincoln Centennial Memorial Association of Nebraska commissioned Daniel Chester French to create a statue of Abraham Lincoln for the grounds of the state capitol. In lieu of a final payment, the association allowed French to sell bronze casts of the statue, of which at least 11 were made. French depicted Lincoln in deep thought, purposely representing Lincoln "bearing the burdens and perplexities and problems of the Great War."
altText: A work made of bronze.

title: Waterloo Bridge, Gray Weather
creditLine: Gift of Mrs. Mortimer B. Harris
description: If not for the fog, Monet once remarked, “London wouldn’t be a beautiful city. It’s the fog that gives it its magnificent breadth.” While working on his London series, he rose early every day to paint Waterloo Bridge in the morning, moving on to Charing Cross Bridge at midday and in the afternoon. He observed both motifs from his fifth-floor window at the Savoy Hotel.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Hand Mirror
creditLine: Katherine K. Adler Memorial Fund
description: Bronze mirrors were luxurious personal possessions used by women in life and then buried with the dead for use in the afterlife. One side was highly polished; the other side was usually engraved with a mythic scene, such as this one, which shows the goddess Eos carrying the body of her son, Memnon, who was killed by the hero Achilles in an episode taken from Homer’s The Iliad.
altText: A work made of bronze.

title: May: Shoki the Demon Queller Riding on a Tiger, Subjugating Goblins, from the series "Of the Twelve Months: the Fifth (Junikagetsu no uchi: gogatsu)"
creditLine: Nathalie Gookin Fund in memory of Frederick W. Gookin
