description: The tiger clutches one ferocious goblin in his jaws while Shōki’s sword subdues the others. “May” is printed in English on the right edge of the design, perhaps in an effort to make the print seem more fashionable at a moment when Western influence in Japan was growing. Images of Shōki are often hung to celebrate the Boys’ Day festival, which takes place in May.
altText: A work made of color woodblock prints; oban triptych.

title: Bureau Table
artistDisplay: Attributed to John Townsend (American, 1732–1809) Newport, Rhode Island
creditLine: Gift of Jamee J. and Marshall Field
description: This elegant piece epitomizes the Late Baroque style that flourished in Newport, Rhode Island. It is one of six bureaus attributed to John Townsend on the basis of similar construction and design features in labeled pieces by the maker. Bureau tables most likely functioned as dressing tables and were particularly popular among the Quaker citizens of Newport, who appreciated their wide array of storage possibilities.
altText: Small wooden bureau with carved half-circle designs, gilded handles.

title: A Young Lady with a Parrot
medium: Pastel on blue laid paper, mounted on laminated paper board
creditLine: The Regenstein Collection
description: Rosalba Carriera, or simply Rosalba, as she was known, was a shrewd judge of character; she enhanced but never obscured the appearance of her sitters. This pastel may depict a young Englishwoman, perhaps one of the daughters of Lord Manchester. Whoever the model, this image’s aura of grace and seduction would characterize the arts of much of the 18th century, marking Rosalba as one of the originators of the Rococo style in Italy and France.
altText: A pastel drawing of woman in blue and pink dress with blue parrot.

title: Manxman Piano
artistDisplay: Designed by Mackay Hugh Baillie Scott English, 1865-1945 Made by John Broadwood and Sons England, founded 1728 London, England
medium: Oak, ebony, ivory, mother-of-pearl, and copper
dimensions: 128.9 × 143.2 cm (50 3/4 × 56 3/8 in.); With top open: H.: 162.6 cm (64 in.); With one door open: W.: 212.4 cm (83 5/8 in.)
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by Robert Allerton, Mrs. Joseph Regenstein, Sr., Walter S. Brewster, Mrs. Emily Crane Chadbourne, Richard T. Crane, Jr., Mr. and Mrs. Leopold Blumka, Henry Manaster, Jack Linsky, Mrs. Margaret Day Blake, Mr. and Mrs. John Wilson, Mrs. Henry C. Wood, by exchange; Florene May Schoenborn and Samuel A. Marx Fund; European Decorative Arts Purchase Fund
description: Part of the English Arts and Crafts movement, architect and designer Mackay Hugh Baillie Scott created this pianoforte, an innovative solution to the awkward form of the upright piano. Scott's object is both cleverly functional and aesthetically pleasing. The opened lid and doors of the cabinet act as acoustical sounding boards. Inside is the musical instrument along with a profusion of handcrafted metalwork, including candleholders.
altText: Wooden piano with cabinets inlaid with ivory and mother-of-pearl.

title: Cabinet
medium: Rosewood with ebonized cherry, maple, walnut, satinwood, marquetry of various woods, brass, gilding, and paint
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by the Antiquarian Society through the Capital Campaign
description: Herter Brothers, one of New York’s foremost decorating firms during the 1870s and 1880s, followed the lead of English designers intent on reforming an industry that produced poorly conceived and constructed work. Advocates for beautiful and functional designs, the Herter Brothers created bold, rectilinear shapes whose exquisite surface decoration was inspired by Japanese art, an influence prevalent throughout the West at this time.
altText: Wood cabinet with lighter wood floral design and brass.

title: Teakettle and Stand
artistDisplay: Design attributed to Edward C. Moore (American, 1827–1891) Tiffany and Company (American, founded 1837) New York
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by the Antiquarian Society through the Dorothy J. Vance Fund
description: The world-renowned Tiffany and Company created this teakettle for the 1878 Exposition Universelle in Paris; it was most likely designed by Edward C. Moore. The kettle and stand, produced 12 years later, harmoniously blend the designs of the Aesthetic and Arts and Crafts movements, both of which were influenced by non-Western design. These works are quintessential representations of international taste during the late 19th century.
altText: A work made of silver with copper.

title: The Little Pond, Appledore
creditLine: Through prior acquisition of the Friends of American Art and the Walter H. Schulze Memorial collections
description: One of the Isles of Shoals located off the coast of Maine and New Hampshire, Appledore Island attracted many artists and writers to its rocky shores during the late 19th century. The Little Pond, Appledore dates from Childe Hassam's first summer sojourn there after three years in Europe and reflects his burgeoning interest in the bright palette, broken brushwork, and dramatic light effects of Impressionist painting.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: The Battle between the Gods and the Giants
creditLine: Through prior acquisition of the George F. Harding Fund
description: The victory of the Olympic gods over the ancient race of giants was a perfect subject for Wtewael to showcase exaggerated athletic poses and striking contrasts of space and light. Painted on copper, this small work almost appears gem-like. Wtewael's self-conscious display of skills was a hallmark of the international style known as Mannerism, which was fashionable in Holland around 1600.
altText: Animated scene of many mostly nude figures in close combat, on earth and aloft in low-hanging clouds, reaching toward one another with long spears.

title: Rhyton (Drinking Vessel) in Shape of Sheep's Head
artistDisplay: Attributed to the Painter of Leningrad 955 Greek; Tarentum (now Taranto), Apulia, Italy
creditLine: Bequest of Chester D. Tripp
description: Decorated tableware enlivened festive meals and could have humorous intentions. Fashioned in the shape of a sheep’s head, this vessel is a special kind of drinking cup that cannot be set down when full, encouraging the guest who held it to drink a great deal of wine.
altText: A work made of terracotta, red-figure.

title: Squat Lekythos (Oil Jar)
creditLine: Bequest of Chester D. Tripp
description: During the course of the 5th and 4th centuries BCE, black vessels (commonly called black-glaze vessels) were made with increasing frequency in both Greece and southern Italy. Many of them replicate the shape of metal vessels; others have detailing that is molded or incised. While the quality of these vessels varies greatly, all would have been less expensive than vessels decorated in contemporary techniques such as red-figure.
altText: A work made of terracotta, black-glaze with impressed decoration.

title: Portrait of a Young Woman
creditLine: Wirt D. Walker Fund
description: This painting looks like a portrait, but the costume and casual pose suggest that it could be a character study. Such works were pioneered by Rembrandt van Rijn and taken up by his pupils, including Aert de Gelder, and were sold at lower prices than commissioned portraits. Gelder continued to use his teacher’s techniques to achieve richly textured surfaces and depth into the 18th century, after Rembrandt’s popularity had faded.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Portrait of a Lady
creditLine: Max and Leola Epstein Collection
description: Frans Hals, one of the most celebrated portrait painters of the 17th century, demonstrated here his signature verve in inscribing decoration on black satin and capturing the freshness of his subject’s skin.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Portions of a Field Armor
artistDisplay: Jacob Halder (English, 1558–1608) Royal Workshops of Greenwich, England
medium: Steel, brass, gilding, leather, and silk velvet textile
dimensions: H. (mounted with arm defenses): 61 cm (30 in.) Wt. 39 lb. 10 oz. (17.7 kg)
creditLine: George F. Harding Collection
description: In 1511 King Henry VIII of England established a workshop at Greenwich Palace outside London that produced armor for the English court for over a century. It was staffed largely by German craftsmen, among them Jacob Halder, who produced this half-armor around 1588–90. Its fashionable style and lavish decoration indicates that the noble who commissioned it was looking to demonstrate his wealth and status as much as to protect life and limb.
altText: A work made of steel, brass, gilding, leather, and silk velvet textile.

title: Two-Handled Covered Cup
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by Mrs. James W. Alsdorf, Pauline Seipp Armstrong, Marshall Field, Charles C. Haffner III, Mrs. Burton W. Hales, Mrs. Harold T. Martin, Mrs. C. Phillip Miller, Mr. and Mrs. Milo M. Naeve, Mrs. Eric Oldberg, Mrs. Frank L. Sulzberger, and the Ethel T. Scarborough Fund
description: This vessel by one of New York’s foremost early silversmiths, Cornelius Kierstede, was used to serve syllabub, a whipped cream dessert flavored with wine, cider, or ale. The cover helped preserve the drink and could be inverted into a stand for the cup. A third-generation silversmith of Dutch descent, Kierstede often found patrons in wealthy Dutch colonists, like the family who commissioned this cup.
altText: Shiny silver cup with lid, two handles with leaf designs

title: Sheath with Bird and Feline or Dragon
dateDisplay: Warring States period to early Western Han dynasty, 3rd/2nd century B.C.
creditLine: Through prior gifts of Mrs. Chauncey B. Borland, Lucy Maud Buckingham Collection, Emily Crane Chadbourne, Mary Hooker Dole, Edith B. Farnsworth, Mrs. Mary A. B. MacKenzie, Mr. and Mrs. Chauncey B. McCormick, Fowler McCormick, Mrs. Gordon Palmer, Grace Brown Palmer, Chester D. Tripp, Russell Tyson, H. R. Warner, Joseph Winterbotham, Mr. and Mrs. Edward Ziff
description: This jade sheath, designed to fit a small blade, showcases the technical mastery and elegant design skills of artists of China's late Bronze Age. The sheath's fluid contours and subtle surface modeling were achieved by slowly grinding down, drilling, and polishing the stone.
altText: Jade Photography 2022

title: Fishing in Spring, the Pont de Clichy (Asnières)
creditLine: Gift of Charles Deering McCormick, Brooks McCormick, and Roger McCormick
description: This painting is set on the river Seine at the Clichy Bridge near Asnières, a suburb north of Paris where Van Gogh painted on several occasions with his friend and fellow artist Paul Signac. Van Gogh was inspired by a technique Signac innovated called divisionism, in which, using science-based color theory, he painted distinct strokes of different colors of paint next to each other to make each color more luminous.
altText: Painting in short strokes of pale blue, green, white, yellow, and pink, of a fisherman in one of two small boats on a river, a tree-lined bank and a bridge in the background.

title: Fragment of a Column Krater (Mixing Bowl)
artistDisplay: Attributed to the Cavalcade Painter Greek; Corinth
creditLine: Costa A. Pandaleon Endowment
description: This fragment comes from a large bowl that was used to mix wine and water before it was served. Unusually, it is decorated in two techniques. The bearded man holding a spear and the animals to the right and below the scene are decorated in the black-figure technique, a new technique developed in the Archaic period. The other figures are simply outlined. Also unusual is the use of yellow for the man’s garment.
altText: A work made of terracotta, black-figure.

title: Female Figure with Bowl
artistDisplay: Abogunde of Ede (active late 19th century) Yoruba Nigeria Coastal West Africa
medium: Wood, beads, and traces of pigment
creditLine: Gift of the Alsdorf Foundation, Mr. and Mrs. James W. Alsdorf, and Mr. and Mrs. Joseph P. Antonow; Samuel P. Avery Fund; gift of Herbert Baker and Gwendolyn Miller, the Britt Family Collection, and Gaston T. de Havenon; Ada Turnbull Hertle Fund; gift of Mr. and Mrs. Edwin E. Hokin, Robert Stolper, and Mr. and Mrs. Edward H. Weiss; through prior gift of Mr. and Mrs. Raymond J. Wielgus
description: This figure was made for a shrine dedicated to one of the Yoruba orisa (deities)—possibly Shango, who is associated with the power of thunderstorms, warriors, and kings. The woman’s expression, her crisp features, and the energetic pose of the child are characteristic of the acclaimed sculptor Abogunde of Ede. The figure is at once an offering, a container for offerings, and the representation of a devotee presenting an offering.
altText: A work made of wood, beads, and traces of pigment.

title: Love of Winter
creditLine: Friends of American Art Collection
description: “There has been none of my favorite snow," George Bellows wrote to a friend in January 1914. "I must always paint the snow at least once a year.” Soon after, a blizzard hit New York City, inspiring this painting. The bright colors and broad brushstrokes convey the pleasure and movement of the skaters and onlookers who are out enjoying a New York City winter.
altText: Painting of a crowd of well-dressed light-skinned people in an open, snowy field surrounded by large rolling hills. At center a woman in a bright-yellow coat and skirt holds the hand of a child in red, who pulls to turn her toward the others.

title: Lozenge Composition with Yellow, Black, Blue, Red, and Gray
creditLine: Gift of Edgar Kaufmann, Jr.
description: Piet Mondrian, a founding member of the international movement De Stijl (the Style), said “the straight line tells the truth.” Deceptively simple, his works are the result of continual tinkering to achieve absolute balance and harmony. In this work, Mondrian rotated a square canvas 90 degrees to create a dynamic relationship between the rectilinear composition and the diagonal lines of the painting's edges.
altText: A square white tile, rotated 90 degrees, crossed by black lines intersecting at 90-degree angles. A few of the shapes thus formed—some partial squares, some rectangles—are colored in a single shade of yellow, blue, black, or red.

title: Table
artistDisplay: Designed by Charles Rennie Mackintosh Scottish, 1868-1928 Glasgow, Scotland
medium: Painted and white wood and clear and opaque leaded-glass insets
creditLine: Richard T. Crane, Jr. and Edward E. Ayer endowments
description: This 10-legged table, designed by Charles Rennie Mackintosh, is only one of two produced in this style. It was made for the exhibition Architecture and Craft of the New Style, held in Moscow in 1903, where its stark-white palette shocked Mackintosh’s modern Viennese counterparts. Such international exhibitions were crucial to the promotion and dissemination of ideas among modern designers in the United Kingdom and Europe.
altText: A work made of painted and white wood and clear and opaque leaded-glass insets.

title: The Temptation of Saint Jerome
creditLine: Charles H. and Mary F. S. Worcester Collection
description: Best known for his Lives of the Artists, a monumental compendium of biographies, Vasari was a successful architect and a prolific painter for the Medici dukes of Florence. This painting is a frequently depicted episode from the life of Saint Jerome. The saint—a scholar, translator of the Bible, and advocate of monasticism—vividly described the tempting visions that assailed him when he retreated to the desert to meditate.
altText: A work made of oil on panel.

title: Chak Ak’ Paat Kuy ("Red Turkey") Playing the Ballgame
artistDisplay: Late Classic Maya Probably La Corona (Saknikte’), Usumacinta River area, Guatemala
creditLine: Ada Turnbull Hertle Fund
description: In Central America, the best-known ancient sculptors are the Maya, who decorated their sacred buildings with finely carved stone reliefs. This fragmentary ball-court panel from the late eighth century shows two men, dressed in elaborate costumes, engaged in a ritual ball game. Surrounding the figures, and clearly set off from them, are fragments of hieroglyphs by which the Maya identified the players and the date on which the game occurred.
altText: A work made of limestone.

title: In the Sea
creditLine: Joseph Winterbotham Collection
description: Böcklin’s art had little in common with Impressionism or the academic art of his time. Instead, his depictions of demigods in naturalistic settings interpret themes from Classical mythology. Böcklin also painted mysterious landscapes that made him an important contributor to the international Symbolist movement and appealed to Surrealist artists, like Giorgio de Chirico, who declared, “Each of [Böcklin’s] works is a shock.”
altText: Painting of centaur with harp, in water, surrounded by mermaids and mermen.

title: The Crystal Palace
creditLine: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. B. E. Bensinger
description: Camille Pissarro and his family left France in 1870–71 for Lower Norwood, outside London. In nearby Sydenham, he painted the glass-and-iron Crystal Palace, originally designed for London’s Hyde Park by Joseph Paxton in 1851. Here, Pissarro relegated what was considered the world’s largest building to the left side of the canvas, as if to give equal space to the scene of people parading by the town's more recently constructed middle-class homes.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Self-Portrait
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by Mr. and Mrs. Frank H. Woods in memory of Mrs. Edward Harris Brewer
description: Bazille was in his mid-20s when he executed this startlingly direct self-portrait. He created this work while sharing an apartment-studio with Claude Monet and experimenting with new painting techniques that would be central to the Impressionist movement. It was both a practice piece and, given his recent decision to abandon a medical career in favor of art, a professional manifesto.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: The Combat of the Giaour and Hassan
creditLine: Gift of Bertha Palmer Thorne, Rose Movius Palmer, Mr. and Mrs. Arthur M. Wood, and Mr. and Mrs. Gordon Palmer
description: This colorful scene was inspired by a poem from Lord Byron’s “oriental tales,” a popular series of romances. Both the poem and painting are examples of 19th-century Europeans’ interest in fantastical and often violent depictions of Middle Eastern, North African, and Asian cultures, which reinforced colonialist aims. Delacroix began painting Orientalist subjects early in his career, though he did not visit North Africa until 1832.
altText: Two men on horseback clash in battle, another man crouches with knife.

title: Venetian Glass Workers
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection
description: Trained in Paris, John Singer Sargent traveled to Spain, the Netherlands, and Italy to study how painters such as Diego Velázquez and Frans Hals captured the effects of light and rendered figures in space. This painting is one of several genre scenes featuring glass-bead workers that Sargent executed in the early 1880s. The view of the shop is dark except for the strokes of light green and silvery paint that describe the canes of glass.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Mrs. Charles Gifford Dyer (Mary Anthony)
creditLine: Friends of American Art Collection
description: The subject of this painting, Mary Anthony, and her husband, the painter Charles Gifford Dyer, were part of an expatriate community of American artists who lived and worked in Europe in the late 19th century. Sargent painted this portrait during his first extended stay in Venice as a professional artist. Rather than a formal commission, the work likely served as a souvenir of friendship and shared experiences.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Tetradrachm (Coin) Depicting the Goddess Persephone
creditLine: Gift of Martin A. Ryerson
description: The front of this coin depicts Persephone, the daughter of Demeter, the goddess of agriculture, who was abducted by Hades to be his wife in the underworld. Distraught, Demeter caused the crops to die until Persephone could return to her once a year, bringing the season of spring, symbolized here by the circle of grain in Persephone's hair. Syracuse, where this coin was made, was thought to be the site of Persephone's abduction.
altText: A work made of silver.

title: Stater (Coin) Depicting the Goddess Athena
artistDisplay: Greek, minted in Syracuse, Sicily, Italy
creditLine: Gift of Martin A. Ryerson
description: The front of this coin depicts the head of goddess Athena, helmeted, facing right. The back depicts Pegasus facing left. Athena was known for taming Pegasus and making the horse rideable.
altText: A work made of silver.

title: Architectural Relief Depicting the Gigantomachy (Battle Between Gods and Giants)
creditLine: Katherine K. Adler Memorial Fund
description: Gigantomachy was the struggle between the Giants and the Olympian gods, who were led by Zeus. Here, a god and goddess in flowing robes capture a Giant, depicted with wings and serpent-like features, to deliver the final blow in this epic battle. These three animated figures were probably once part of a series of ornamental covers called antefixes, which were placed along the lowest row of roof tiles on a small building or temple.
altText: A work made of terracotta and pigment.

title: Flowers and Fruit in a Porcelain Bowl
creditLine: Wirt D. Walker Fund
description: Long assumed to be by Francisco de Zurbarán, the leading painter in Seville, Spain, this work is now considered to be by his son, Juan de Zurbarán, who specialized in exquisitely painted still lifes during his short career. The precise, sensuous application of paint and dramatic lighting are typical of Juan, whose style can be identified through only a few signed paintings.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Te raau rahi (The Big Tree)
creditLine: Gift of Kate L. Brewster
description: “Everything in the landscape blinded and dazzled me,” wrote Paul Gauguin of his first months in Tahiti. Here, he showcased the island’s variety of bountiful fruit trees, including a thick-trunked, violet hotu at left; spindly mango and coconut trees; and three short banana plants with lush, splayed leaves. In the foreground, a man uses a stick to crack a coconut, and a family rests in the grass with a sleeping dog beside them.
altText: A work made of oil on jute canvas.

title: The Grand Canal, Venice
creditLine: Wirt D. Walker Fund
description: Although he did not begin to paint views, or vedute, until he was in his mid-40s, Francesco Guardi became an accomplished practitioner in the genre. In this work, one of his most important early cityscapes, he depicted the mouth of the Grand Canal bustling with late-afternoon activity. The emotional tenor of Guardi’s vedute—seen here in the brooding, melancholy aura of the sky—distinguishes them from the works of his predecessors.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Amédée-David, the Comte de Pastoret
creditLine: Estate of Dorothy Eckhart Williams; Robert Allerton, Bertha E. Brown, and Major Acquisitions funds
description: This portrait by French painter Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres depicts the young count Amédée-David de Pastoret at 32 years old. One of several paintings he commissioned from Ingres, the portrait highlights the nobleman’s status and swagger. Posing confidently in his finest garments and wearing a medal of the Order of the Legion of Honor, he gazes directly at the viewer with a stern expression.
altText: Portrait of white man dressed in all black with medallion and sword.

title: Stack of Wheat
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by the Searle Family Trust; Major Acquisitions Centennial Endowment; through prior acquisitions of the Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson and Potter Palmer collections; through prior bequest of Jerome Friedman
description: Through 1890 and 1891, Monet created a series of paintings depicting the stacks of wheat that stood outside his farmhouse in Giverny. These stacks were, for the artist, a symbol of sustenance and survival. He painted at several easels simultaneously in the field and then refined pictorial harmonies in the studio. The Art Institute has the world's largest group of Monet’s Stacks of Wheat.
altText: A snowy landscape in cool tones featuring a prominent, snow-dusted haystack in reddish brown in front of a row of red-brown trees and low, blue mountains, all beheath a pink-gray strip of sky.

title: Seated Bodhisattva
medium: Wood core, dry lacquer, traces of gold leaf
creditLine: Kate S. Buckingham Endowment
description: This small, finely crafted lacquer figure represents a Buddhist bodhisattva, or bosatsu, an enlightened and compassionate being who postponed Buddhahood in order to help save others. Calm, stately, and full-bodied, the bosatsu is seated in a meditative pose; his gracefully held hands, raised midair, make a gesture of assurance. This sculpture was originally gilt; traces of gold remain on the bodhisattva's face and chest.
altText: Seated wooden Buddha statue with with forefinger touching thumb.

title: The Child's Bath
creditLine: Robert A. Waller Fund
description: Known for her sensitive yet unsentimental scenes of women and children, Mary Cassatt was the only American invited to exhibit with the original French Impressionist group. In The Child’s Bath, one of her masterworks, she used cropped forms, bold patterns and outlines, and a flattened perspective, all of which she derived from her study of Japanese woodblock prints.
altText: Painting of mother in blue, purple, and green-stripped dress washing child's feet.

title: Portrait of Dr. William McNeill Whistler
creditLine: Gift of Mary T. Wentworth in memory of her husband, John
description: Born in Massachusetts, James McNeill Whistler lived all of his adult life in Europe, working in artistic centers such as Paris, London, and Venice. He painted this portrait of his brother William in London, where both of them then lived; the artist had established a studio there in 1859. William moved to the city and and became a respected physician there after the Civil War in which he served as a medical officer for the Confederate Army.
altText: A work made of oil on panel.

title: Boy on a Ram
artistDisplay: Francisco José de Goya y Lucientes (Spanish, 1746–1828)
creditLine: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Brooks McCormick
description: As painter to the king of Spain, Francisco de Goya also designed tapestries for the royal residences. To work out his designs, he first made small oil sketches and followed them with full-scale painted cartoons that served as guides for the king's weavers. This cartoon was produced for a tapestry in a series decorating the dining room in the Royal Palace of El Pardo, outside Madrid.
altText: A young, smiling boy in a ruffled collar, hat, and cumberbun rides outdoors on a brown ram, a small whip held aloft in his hand.

title: The Garden of Palazzo Contarini dal Zaffo
creditLine: Gift of Marion and Max Ascoli Fund
description: This painting by Francesco Guardi, an 18th-century landscape painter renowned for his inventive city views, depicts a luxurious Venetian green space. Elegant couples stroll, while a ballgame takes place in the distance and a single gondola slides across the lagoon. Guardi's city scenes were particularly popular with wealthy travelers making the grand tour of Europe as evidence of their extravagant trips.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Cabin in the Cotton
medium: Oil on cotton, mounted on Masonite
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by Thomas F. Pick and Mary P. Hines in memory of their mother Frances W. Pick
description: A celebrated African American artist of the mid-20th century, self-taught painter Horace Pippin began painting as therapy, hoping to regain mobility in his right arm, which was injured during WWI. While this work hung in a Philadelphia shoe repair shop, it caught the attention of artists, critics, and gallerists. It is considered an exemplar of the artist's vivid, saturated palette and feeling for intense pattern.
altText: Painting of a cabin set below a dark blue sky and fluffy white clouds. Behind it is a field of many small white dots. In front, a dark-skinned woman sits and a dark-skinned child plays among roaming chickens and dogs in a fenced-in yard.

title: Cameo Portraying Emperor Claudius as Jupiter
dateDisplay: Cameo: Roman, mid-first century Mount: Italian, late 16th century
medium: Cameo: sardonyx Mount: gold, pearls, and enamel
creditLine: Gift of Marilynn B. Alsdorf
description: This cameo showing an idealized portrait of Emperor Claudius was created for use in his imperial court. It combines Claudius's image with that of the supreme diety Jupiter. Here, the emperor holds the god’s scepter and thunderbolt, while an eagle stands at his feet, boldly equating Claudius’s power over the Roman Empire to that of Jupiter over the entire cosmos.
altText: A work made of cameo: sardonyx mount: gold, pearls, and enamel.

title: Close Helmet for the Tourney
creditLine: George F. Harding Collection
description: This helmet was used in a tourney, a sporting mock battle on horseback or on foot. To protect against dangerous strikes under the helmet, the helmet’s collar rotates on a rim that closes over the separate neck defense. The upper visor is reinforced with an additional plate to deflect strikes from a lance or sword. Evidence of repairs and sword cuts over the center ridge of the helmet suggest that this piece received some heavy use.
altText: A work made of steel, brass, and leather.

title: Portions of a Jousting Helmet
creditLine: George F. Harding Collection
description: This helmet was part of the armor worn in the joust, a sporting combat fought between pairs of mounted contestants. The visor was a movable plate attached to the helmet to protect the face, while the bevor was used to shield the chin and upper throat. Although designed primarily for protection, the pieces are decorated with etched and gilt motifs of figures and foliate strapwork.
altText: Steel helmet with brass stripe trim, leather ties.

title: Two Heads of Damned Souls from Dante's "Inferno" (recto and verso)
dimensions: Edges irregular, approx.: 40.6 × 29.8 cm (16 × 11 3/4 in.); Framed: 52.3 × 41.6 cm (20 9/16 × 16 3/8 in.)
creditLine: The Leonora Hall Gurley Memorial Collection
description: Henry Fuseli probably painted the expressive head studies on each side of this unprimed canvas while living in Italy between 1770 and 1778. Both images were engraved as illustrations for Johann Caspar Lavater’s influential book on physiognomy, a popular pseudoscience that assessed an individual’s character based on their appearance. According to that text, the heads were inspired by the damned souls in Italian poet Dante Alighieri’s epic Inferno.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Field Armor for Man
medium: Steel, iron, brass, leather, and textile
creditLine: George F. Harding Collection
description: Caught in the heat of battle with sword raised and horse rearing, this mounted figure may match many notions of a knight in shining armor but actually represents a common hired soldier. Though the armors for both man and horse were produced in Nuremberg, Germany, in the 16th century, the clothing was meticulously recreated in 2017 from period designs.
altText: A work made of steel, iron, brass, leather, and textile.

title: Merrymakers in an Inn
creditLine: George B. and Mary R. Harris Fund
description: Over the course of a long and successful career in Haarlem, Adriaen van Ostade specialized in scenes of peasant life, including tavern scenes and village fairs. The artist used clear, relatively bright colors and fine brushwork in keeping with the tastes of the later 1600s. Collectors also appreciated the range of emotions and gestures exhibited by Van Ostade’s jolly figures.
altText: A work made of oil on panel.

title: Armor for Field and Tournament
artistDisplay: Jörg T. Sorg, the Younger, after German, Augsburg, active 1502-1542
medium: Steel with gilding, iron, brass, leather, and cord
creditLine: George F. Harding Collection
description: The growing relationship between armor and costume in the 16th century is indicated in the center band of this armor. Delicately incised and etched, with scalloped edge, it mimics the embroidered front closing of a contemporary male doublet (a close-fitted bodice). The particularly fine decoration of etched floral arabesques suggests the workmanship of the Augsburg armory, perhaps of Jörg T. Sorg.
altText: A work made of steel with gilding, iron, brass, leather, and cord.

title: Head of a Guillotined Man
creditLine: Through prior gift of William Wood Prince; L. L. and A. S. Coburn Endowment; Charles H. and Mary F. S. Worcester Collection
description: This painting is one of several that Géricault produced of decapitated heads and severed limbs, and he likely painted it directly from life. The artist is known to have acquired corpses from his local morgue to study anatomy and the effects of decomposition. The head probably belonged to a convicted criminal. At that time in France, executions were carried out by the guillotine, a bladed device that sliced through the necks of its victims.
altText: A work made of oil on panel.

title: Baroque Pearl Mounted as a Cat Holding a Mouse
creditLine: Gift of Marilynn B. Alsdorf
description: This decorative personal object would have been fashionable on several levels in late 16th-century Spain. The flecked white enameling used to depict the cat's fur was used in many similar objects, and baroque pearls enjoyed great popularity for their uniqueness. This piece would have originally been on a chain or a pendant, as evidenced by the three small holes in the cat's ears and by its tail.
altText: A work made of gold, enamel, and baroque pearl.

title: Spice Box Shaped as a Skull
creditLine: Gift of Marilynn B. Alsdorf
description: This tiny pendant—under an inch tall and wide—is also a complicated spice box. The top button opens the skull to reveal two sections, the back one divided into four compartments, and a panel engraved with the names of four aromatics: Negal (cloves), Muscha (nutmeg), Canel (cinnamon), and Schlag (schlagwasser, a mixture of brandy, primrose petals, and violets, thought to be a cardiac stimulant).
altText: A work made of silver gilt.

title: Still Life—Strawberries, Nuts, &c.
creditLine: Gift of Jamee J. and Marshall Field
description: During Raphaelle Peale’s time, still lifes were relegated to the bottom of the hierarchy of painting subjects. Peale, however, ignored their low status and is now acknowledged as America’s first professional still-life painter and leading practitioner. In this particularly fine example, the rhythmic balance of fruit, nuts, and Chinese-export porcelain is enlivened by the diagonal branch of grapes becoming raisins and an orange leaf.
altText: Still life painting of strawberries, nuts, lemon, and porcelain vessels.

title: Canopic Jar of Amenhotep
artistDisplay: Egyptian; Tomb A7, Dra Abu el-Naga, Thebes (now Luxor), Egypt
dateDisplay: New Kingdom, Dynasty 18, reign of Amenhotep II (about 1427–1400 BCE)
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by Henry H. Getty and Charles L. Hutchinson
description: This now-empty jar is one of four that once held the liver, lungs, intestines, and stomach of Amenhotep, the overseer of architectural projects in the temple of Amun at Karnak (in present-day Luxor). Each jar has a hand-sculpted stopper that may represent its owner or one of the sons of Horus, gods associated with these organs. An inscription in hieroglyphs on each container promises divine protection from a different goddess over its contents.
altText: A work made of ceramic and pigment.
