title: Shabti (Funerary Figurine) of Nebseni
dateDisplay: New Kingdom, early Dynasty 18, about 1570 BCE
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by Henry H. Getty and Charles L. Hutchinson
description: To assure themselves a comfortable afterlife, Egyptians stocked their tombs with at least one figurine called an ushabti, who acted as a servant in the afterlife. The message carved on each of the figurines explained that if the deceased is called on to do any work in the afterlife, the ushabti will respond with “Here I am” and will do the job. Some tombs had as many as one ushabti for every day of the year and another 36 overseers to keep order.
altText: A work made of wood (tamarisk) and pigment.

title: Statuette of Imhotep
creditLine: Gift of Henry H. Getty, Charles L. Hutchinson, and Norman W. Harris
description: Imhotep was the architect who designed the Stepped Pyramid of King Djoser (Dynasty 3, about 2687 BCE). Fifteen hundred years later, Imhotep was deified and revered as a god of healing and wisdom. In this statue, he holds an unrolled papyrus on his lap as a sign of his learning.
altText: A work made of copper alloy.

title: Head From a Shabti (Funerary Figurine) of Queen Tiye
dateDisplay: New Kingdom, Dynasty 18, Reign of Akhenaten (about 1352–1336 BCE)
medium: Travertine (Egyptian alabaster) with traces of pigment
creditLine: Gift of Henry H. Getty, Charles L. Hutchinson, and Norman W. Harris
description: The form of the crown, full lips, down-turned edges of the mouth and almond-shaped eyes identify this fragment as Queen Tiye. She was the influential wife of pharaoh Amunhotep III. This head may originally have come from a statuette made during the reign of her son, Akhenaten.
altText: A work made of travertine (egyptian alabaster) with traces of pigment.

title: Wind-Swept Sands
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by Mrs. Eric Oldberg in honor of Milo M. Naeve; Friends of American Art and R. H. Love Galleries funds; Walter Aitken Endowment; through prior acquisitions of the Charles H. and Mary F. S. Worcester Collection
description: An influential teacher, William Merritt Chase rooted his teaching method in the Impressionist practice of painting outdoors in order to take advantage of natural light and changing weather conditions. In Wind-Swept Sands, painted in Long Island, New York, Chase used rapid brushstrokes to depict the dunes and vegetation, thin washes for the sky, and an overall gray tone to indicate an overcast day.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Statuette of Osiris-Iah
creditLine: Gift of Henry H. Getty, Charles L. Hutchinson, and Robert H. Fleming
description: According to the Egyptian religion, gods could combine with each other to form composite deities. The complex crown of this bronze statuette has characteristics of the god Osiris as well as the ibis-headed moon god Thoth. This statuette was dedicated to the dual god by a man named Pamu.
altText: A work made of copper alloy.

title: Statuette of Sobek
creditLine: Gift of Henry H. Getty, Charles L. Hutchinson, and Robert H. Fleming
description: Here the crocodile god, Sobek, associated with water and the Nile River, wears an elaborate crown adorned with horns, feathers, and a uraeus (sacred serpent). Egyptian gods were commonly depicted with human bodies and animal heads. The animal referred to the god’s personality or characteristics. For example, the crocodile head of Sobek alludes to his fierceness.
altText: A dark stone sculpture has the body of a man and the head of a crocodile. The figure wears a tall elaborate headdress, a long wig, and a garment around its pelvis.

title: Statuette of Re-Horakhty
dateDisplay: Third Intermediate Period-Late Period, Dynasty 21–26, about 1069–525 BCE
creditLine: Gift of Henry H. Getty, Charles L. Hutchinson, and Robert H. Fleming
description: Here Re-Horakhty, a combination of the solar gods Re and Horakhty, strides forward in the form of a falcon-headed male. He is identifiable by his falcon head (once crowned with a sun disk) and the golden hieroglyphs at the center of his belt, which read, “Re-Horakhty, Chief of the Gods.” Statuettes of deities like this were set up in temples and shrines to receive offerings or presented to the gods as gifts that were later ceremonially buried.
altText: A work made of copper alloy with gilding.

title: Ointment Vessel
creditLine: Gift of Henry H. Getty, Charles L. Hutchinson, Robert H. Fleming, and Norman W. Harris
description: Perfumes and fragrant ointments for soothing the skin were an important part of beauty routines in Egypt’s hot, dry climate. Like the sometimes costly cosmetics they were designed to contain, these elegant vessels were desirable luxury goods, made in varied forms from an array of materials.
altText: A work made of travertine (egyptian alabaster).

title: Relief Fragment Depicting Merettetiiyet with Offerings
artistDisplay: Egyptian; offering niche of Merettetiiyet, Teti Pyramid Cemetery, Saqqara, Egypt
dateDisplay: First Intermediate Period, Dynasty 10, about 2050 BCE
creditLine: W. Moses Willner Fund
description: This panel was part of an offering niche designed for a woman named Meret-Teti-iyet. At the top, people bring offerings to sustain her in the afterlife. Below Meret-Teti-iyet faces visitors behind piles of food. On this panel, she holds a closed lotus blossom; on the other panel in our collection, she sniffs an open lotus. The lotus, which opens with the rising sun and sinks beneath the water at night, was a symbol of rebirth in ancient Egypt.
altText: A work made of limestone and pigment.

title: Tomb Wall Fragment Depicting Offering Bearers and Butchers
creditLine: W. Moses Willner Fund
description: In the upper register of this wall fragment, priests and servants prepare food offerings, including birds and ribs of beef. The lower register portrays butchers at work. Their kilts are tucked into their waistbands to keep them clean. To the left, butchers carry away a cow’s heart and a jar of blood.
altText: A work made of limestone.

title: Mr. Potter Palmer
creditLine: Gift of Gordon and Janis Palmer
description: Chicago businessman Potter Palmer and his wife Bertha commissioned a pair of portraits in 1871 from Hiram Powers, an American sculptor living in Florence. Executed in marble with folded draperies and restrained features, the busts exemplify the classicizing style that Powers honed in Italy—and that some Americans found so appealing—in the mid-19th century.
altText: A work made of carrera marble.

title: Mrs. Potter Palmer
creditLine: Gift of Gordon and Janis Palmer
description: Chicago businessman Potter Palmer and his wife Bertha commissioned a pair of portraits in 1871 from Hiram Powers, an American sculptor living in Florence. Executed in marble with folded draperies and restrained features, the busts exemplify the classicizing style that Powers honed in Italy—and that some Americans found so appealing—in the mid-19th century.
altText: A work made of carrera marble.

title: Rehearsal of the Pasdeloup Orchestra at the Cirque d'Hiver
creditLine: Anonymous loan
description: Sargent often attended free concert rehearsals conducted by Jules-Étienne Pasdeloup, popular events in late 19th-century Paris. This composition shows his perceptive use of Impressionist techniques to depict modern, urban subjects. Sargent employed thin, abbreviated brushstrokes to capture the rich atmosphere and graphic qualities of the amphitheater’s architecture, the musicians, their sheet music and instruments, and the circus performers.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Life Study (Study of an Egyptian Girl)
creditLine: Anonymous loan
description: Sargent traveled to Egypt in 1891 in search of source material for a mural commission for the Boston Public Library. Like many 19th-century Western European artists, he was drawn to the Middle East’s perceived exoticism and its ancient histories. The identity of the woman who posed in Cairo for this full-length figure study is not known. Life Study was widely exhibited, including at the World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago in 1893.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Plaque Depicting a Quail Chick
creditLine: Museum Purchase Fund
description: This plaque depicts a fledgling quail, better known to literate ancient Egyptians as the hieroglyph for the "w" sound. Plaques that show animals, deities, and royalty were a relatively late addition to the ancient Egyptian artistic repertoire, first appearing around 664 BCE. Their function remains a mystery—they may have been used as sculptors’ models in the training of artists, dedicated in temples as gifts to the gods, or both.
altText: A work made of limestone.

title: Plaque Depicting a Queen or Goddess
creditLine: Museum Purchase Fund
description: A headdress in the form of a vulture crowns this female figure, indicating her status as a queen or goddess. Although of Greek descent, pharaohs and queens of this era used traditional Egyptian markers of royalty and divinity, including crowns, to represent themselves. Her beaded necklace is embellished with lotus blossoms and flowering papyrus umbels—plants indigenous to the Nile River valley—further indicating her close affinity with Egypt.
altText: A work made of limestone.

title: Stela of Tjenti and Nefret
artistDisplay: Egyptian; probably tomb G 3035, Giza, Egypt
creditLine: Museum Purchase Fund
description: Scenes depicting families around a table laden with food were a standard decoration in ancient Egyptian tombs. These images were eternal family portraits, ensuring an afterlife populated with loved ones and plentiful food. Here, we see a couple, their son (standing on the right), and their granddaughter, who holds her finger to her lips in a gesture symbolic of childhood. The scale of the figures' sizes denote their status within the family.
altText: A work made of limestone.

title: Ostracon with a Drawing of a King
creditLine: Museum Purchase Fund
description: Egyptian artists often made sketches on flakes of limestone, called ostraca. This example shows how the preliminary outline was done in red pigment, then corrected, and finished in black. Often these sketches were the work of two craftsmen, a draftsman and a master artist. This ostracon shows a king wearing a crown with streamers and a pleated kilt. He leans on a standard topped with the ram-headed emblem of the god Amun.
altText: A fragment of stone shows a figure drawn in black. He stands with his body facing the viewer, his head turned to the side, in elaborate attire—a headdress, necklace, arm bands, and a garment on his lower half, He holds a staff topped with a ram's head.

title: Head of an Official
creditLine: Museum Purchase Fund
description: This head of an official, with his striped wig tucked behind his ears, comes from a larger statue that was likely once displayed in a tomb chapel. Such sculptures served as receptacles for the ka (soul). To animate statues, priests performed a ceremony called the Opening of the Mouth so that the individual represented could benefit from offerings left by the living and breathe, eat, hear, and see in the afterlife.
altText: A work made of granite.

title: Plaque Depicting a Ram
creditLine: Museum Purchase Fund
description: This portrayal of a ram has two sets of horns. The elongated corkscrew horns atop its head belong to a species that was long extinct when this plaque was carved. Rather than abandoning the traditional artistic representation of this animal, artists added a second set of horns—curved—to reflect the appearance of contemporary rams.
altText: A work made of limestone.

title: Lintel Fragment Depicting Iniuia and Iuy Worshipping Deities
artistDisplay: Egyptian; Tomb of Iniuia and Iuy, Saqqara, Egypt
dateDisplay: New Kingdom, Dynasty 18, reign of Tutankhamun (about 1336–1327 BCE)
creditLine: Gift of Henry H. Getty, Charles L. Hutchinson, and Robert H. Fleming
description: This lintel fragment depicts a couple kneeling with their hands raised in an Egyptian gesture of praise, worshipping the funerary deities Osiris and Isis. It once crowned a doorway in the tomb chapel of a high-ranking official and his wife. Hieroglyphs separating the couple from the gods state that they are praising Osiris so that he will give them the “sweet breath” they need to thrive in the afterlife.
altText: A work made of limestone and pigment.

title: Les Andelys, Côte d'Aval
creditLine: Through prior gift of William Wood Prince
description: This harbor view is one of Paul Signac’s first works painted in dots and dashes of contrasting colors. The technique, called pointillism, was originated by Signac’s friend Georges Seurat. Signac would prove to be the most ardent proponent of this style, which he made his own through particular attention to geometric form.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Zenobia, Queen of Palmyra
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by the Antiquarian Society
description: Zenobia was queen of the Syrian city of Palmyra in the 3rd century and ruled it after her husband’s death. Harriet Hosmer portrayed Zenobia at the moment of her defeat by the Roman emperor. Rather than depict a scene of heightened drama, the sculptor opted for a sense of grandeur, remarking, “I have tried to make her too proud to exhibit passion or emotion of any kind; not subdued, though a prisoner; but calm, grand, and strong within herself.”
altText: White marble bust of a woman with shoulder-length wavy hair wearing a crown and robes.

title: Mother-and-Child Figure (Bwanga bwa Chibola)
artistDisplay: Luluwa Democratic Republic of the Congo Central Africa
creditLine: Wirt D. Walker Fund
description: This delicate rendering of a mother holding her newborn child celebrates human fertility. Scarification patterns, hairstyles, jewelry, and anatomical details express the Luluwa concept of bwimpe, which unites beauty with goodness. Such figures may have served as both containers for medicine and symbols of status, reflecting societal changes in the latter half of the 19th century.
altText: A work made of wood and pigment.

title: Mosaic Fragment with a Man Leading a Giraffe
creditLine: Gift of Mrs. Robert B. Mayer
description: This mosaic fragment was once part of a larger composition that paved the floor of a wealthy family home in the Eastern Mediterranean area of the Roman Empire. Composed of thousands of small tesserae, or stone cubes, it shows a giraffe and a human handler standing against a decorative backdrop of scallop-shaped semicircles.
altText: A work made of stone in mortar.

title: Water-Lily Vessel
artistDisplay: Aj Maxam (Maya) Vicinity of Naranjo, Petén region, Guatemala
creditLine: Ethel T. Scarborough Fund
description: This vessel's simple, elegant design includes images of water lilies and a hieroglyphic text. For the Maya, water lilies were symbolic of the watery surface of the underworld and the earth’s regenerative powers. The inscription below the design was the first to be deciphered on a Classic Maya vessel. It states the name of the artist, Ah Maxam (aj maxam), and declares that he is a member of the royal lineage of the kingdom of Naranjo.
altText: A work made of earthenware and pigment.

title: Gaming Set, Probably Made for the Russian Court
medium: Enameled and gilded hard-paste porcelain, gold, and diamonds
creditLine: Eloise W. Martin fund; Richard T. Crane and Mrs. J. Ward Thorne endowments; through prior gift of The Antiquarian Society
description: This richly decorated gaming box is one of the most extravagant works produced by the Du Paquier Porcelain Manufactory during its 25-year existence. Perhaps presented as a diplomatic gift, the box is painted in a complex, tightly organized pattern with colored enamels and gilding. It holds four small, similarly decorated containers that hold porcelain gambling chips mounted with gold and set with diamonds.
altText: Gilded porcelain box of betting chips for card game.

title: Stela of Amenemhat and Hemet
dateDisplay: Middle Kingdom, early Dynasty 12, about 1956–1877 BCE
creditLine: Museum Purchase Fund
description: This vibrantly painted stela commemorates the husband and wife Amenemhat and Hemet in the youthful state they intended to inhabit for eternity. The table piled with food ensures their eternal nourishment and also reflects the practice of family and community members honoring their dead. A stela like this would have been placed in a public location where visitors could come to recite the inscriptions aloud.
altText: A rectangular stone slab is painted with two large figures with medium-dark skin in profile, a man and a woman. Surrounding them are various food items, as well as a smaller male figure holding a large piece of meat. Across the top are hieroglyphics.

title: Model of a River Boat
creditLine: Gift of Henry H. Getty, Charles L. Hutchinson, Robert H. Fleming, and Norman W. Harris
description: The Nile River has been the heart of Egyptian life and culture for millennia. Ancient Egyptians traversed the Nile on boats of all shapes and sizes to conduct commerce, state business, and religious pilgrimages. Model boats like this example—equipped with oars, a mast, and a crew of 15—would have been placed in a tomb to provide the deceased with transportation in the afterlife.
altText: A painted wooden boat with 15 wooden figures, all painted with dark skin and hair, shirtless, and white cloth around their lower halves. Fourteen figures are seated as if rowing; one figures stands facing sideways at the back of the boat.

title: Canopic Jar of Amenhotep
artistDisplay: Egyptian; Tomb A7, Dra Abu el-Naga, Thebes (now Luxor), Egypt
dateDisplay: New Kingdom, Dynasty 18, reign of Amenhotep II (about 1427–1400 BCE)
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by Henry H. Getty and Charles L. Hutchinson
description: This now-empty jar is one of four that once held the liver, lungs, intestines, and stomach of Amenhotep, the overseer of architectural projects in the temple of Amun at Karnak (in present-day Luxor). Each jar has a hand-sculpted stopper that may represent its owner or one of the sons of Horus, gods associated with these organs. An inscription in hieroglyphs on each container promises divine protection from a different goddess over its contents.
altText: A work made of ceramic and pigment.

title: Stela of Amenemhat and Yatu
dateDisplay: Middle Kingdom, late Dynasty 12–early Dynasty 13, about 1870–1770 BCE
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by Henry H. Getty and Charles L. Hutchinson
description: This stela, or commemorative monument, depicts a mother, Yatu, and son, Amenemhat, surrounded by the objects they hoped to use in the afterlife. Oversized cosmetic containers sit under their seats. The flared white and red vessel beneath Yatu holds ointment, while the blue jar under Amenemhat contains eye paint called kohl. The vessel’s color suggests that it is made of anhydrite, a popular choice for cosmetic vessels during the Middle Kingdom.
altText: A work made of limestone and pigment.

title: Ointment Vessel
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by Henry H. Getty and Charles L. Hutchinson
description: Perfumes and fragrant ointments for soothing the skin were an important part of beauty routines in Egypt’s hot, dry climate. The shallow bowl here was used for scented ointments and is embellished with a pomegranate-shaped handle. Regarded as a fertility symbol because of its numerous seeds, the pomegranate became a popular decorative motif in ancient Egyptian jewelry and other objects associated with beauty.
altText: A work made of travertine (egyptian alabaster).

title: Bead Net Funerary Shroud
medium: Faience beads on bast fiber (probably linen)
creditLine: Gift of Henry H. Getty and Charles L. Hutchinson
description: Ancient Egyptians depicted Khepri, the morning form of the sun god, as a dung beetle, which can be seen in the center of this beaded shroud. Just as the sun is born anew each dawn, Egyptians planned to be reborn into a new form of existence after death. As symbols of this renewal, scarab amulets were secured to the body with linen wrappings or incorporated into nets made of beads and laid over a mummified body.
altText: A work made of faience beads on bast fiber (probably linen).

title: Saint Anthony Abbot
artistDisplay: Fra Angelico (Guido di Pietro; Italian, c. 1395/1400–1455)
creditLine: Bequest of Elizabeth Iglehart Blair
description: Fra Angelico became a Dominican friar early in his painting career. This panel was almost certainly once part of the major altarpiece he painted around 1440 for the church of the Dominican convent of San Marco, in Florence, that featured a central panel of the Virgin and Child with saints and ten additional panels depicting saints atop clouds. This panel of Saint Anthony Abbot, considered the founder of monasticism, would have been among them.
altText: A work made of tempera on panel.

title: Pair of Protomes Depicting the Forepart of a Griffin
medium: Bronze with bone or ivory inlay
creditLine: Katherine K. Adler Memorial Fund
description: Among the most impressive offerings ancient Greek believers brought to holy sites were large bronze cauldrons. Often they were embellished with cast-bronze attachments like these two mythical griffins, which would have been fastened by rivets on their collars. This hollow-cast pair is remarkable for the quality of their craftsmanship, condition, and partially preserved inlaid eyes. Griffins were revered for their protective powers and ferocity.
altText: A work made of bronze with bone or ivory inlay.

title: Fragment of a Head from a Statue of a King
creditLine: Gift of Martin A. Ryerson
description: This fragmentary sculpture portrays the head of a king. Only the right side is preserved, leaving evidence that this figure wore the customary pleated headdress with uraeus, a sacred serpent that symbolized supreme power, on his brow. His face is beardless, and softly rounded with high cheekbones.
altText: A work made of greywacke.

title: Statuette of a Sphinx from a Barque Standard
dateDisplay: Third Intermediate Period, late Dynasty 21–Dynasty 22, about 984–715 BCE
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by Norman W. Harris, Robert H. Fleming, Henry H. Getty, and Charles L. Hutchinson
description: The creature here combines a ferocious lion’s body with a king’s head to form a divine guardian, or sphinx. Small metal sphinxes like this were affixed to barques (boats) that carried the cult statues of gods and goddesses when they were brought out of their temples during religious festivals. Here, two rearing cobras flank the sphinx’s paws to help ward off threats to the deity whose statue was set in a shrine at the center of the barque.
altText: A work made of copper alloy.

title: Relief Fragment Depicting Ipi and Fowling in the Marshes
artistDisplay: Egyptian; Saqqara, Teti Pyramid Cemetery, offering niche of Ipi
dateDisplay: First Intermediate Period, Dynasty 10, about 2050 BCE
creditLine: W. Moses Willner Fund
description: This lively scene depicts two men hiding behind a reed blind and pulling closed a clap net to snare birds. Four birds, which have escaped the net, fly from the pond in which lotus flowers and lotus pads float. Below, Ipi (the tomb’s owner) surveys other activities on his estate. His name and titles are written in hieroglyphs over his head.
altText: A work made of limestone with traces of pigment.

title: Bowl
dateDisplay: Predynastic Period–Old Kingdom, Naqada II–Dynasty 6 (about 3500–2181 BCE)
creditLine: Gift of Henry H. Getty, Charles L. Hutchinson, and Norman W. Harris
description: Egyptian alabaster is a form of limestone (calcite) that is found in the Eastern Desert of Egypt. It was favored for cosmetic and ritual offering dishes because of its beautiful color and translucent quality.
altText: A work made of travertine (egyptian alabaster).

title: Amulet of a Heart
creditLine: Gift of Henry H. Getty and Charles L. Hutchinson
description: Small-scale Egyptian figurines, or amulets, were thought to promote health and good luck and were worn by both the living and dead. The human heart—the seat of the soul and memory in Egyptian belief—was represented as a jar with two small handles. Heart-shaped amulets protected the individual’s intellect and allowed the deceased to make their confession before the gods at the judgment of their soul.
altText: A work made of glass.

title: Punch Bowl
artistDisplay: Chased by Eugene J. Soligny (American, c. 1833–1901) Tiffany and Company (American, founded 1837) New York
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by the Antiquarian Society through the Mr. and Mrs. William Y. Hutchinson Fund
description: These objects created by the Tiffany Company were commissioned by the United States government and presented to Viscount d’Itajubá of Brazil in gratitude for his role in arbitrating between the United States and Great Britain after the American Civil War. Decorated with ancient Greek figures and symbols, the designs in the silver represent agriculture and commerce and were meant to symbolize prosperity of the United States after the Civil War.
altText: A work made of silver.

title: Immortals Riding Dragons: Section of a Tomb Pediment
medium: Gray earthenware with traces of slip and polychrome pigments
creditLine: Gift of Mrs. Gordon Palmer
description: These sculptures originally fit under the pitched roof of a burial chamber made of clay bricks. The carved and painted panels depict winged figures mounted on dragons striding over hills or waves. In Han mythology, such beings are described as immortals (xian), and the depiction of these beings in tombs reflects a widespread belief that the soul of the dead could leave its earth-bound existence, ascend to heaven, and become an immortal.
altText: A work made of gray earthenware with traces of slip and polychrome pigments.

title: Ointment Jar with Lid
creditLine: Gift of Henry H. Getty and Charles L. Hutchinson
description: The perfume and scented ointments worn by both men and women in ancient Egypt were also important in religious and funerary rites. This vessel typifies the classic form of ointment jar—with a flaring top and flat disk lid—that was used for over 3,000 years in Egypt.
altText: A work made of anhydrite.

title: Statuette of Wadjet or Sekhmet
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by Henry H. Getty and Charles L. Hutchinson
description: This seated, lion-headed goddess wears a large sun disk with a serpent whose body trails over the top of her head. Showing remarkable ingenuity, the artists who made this piece ensured the lioness's locks kept with Egyptian fashion. Her traditional wig's front tresses emerge from the ruff of her mane.
altText: A work made of copper alloy.

title: Amulet of Bes
creditLine: Gift of Charles L. Hutchinson, Henry H. Getty, and Norman W. Harris
description: The dwarf Bes, with his feathered headdress, lion mane and tail, and protruding tongue, was the protector of women and children in ancient Egypt. This amulet depicting him is but one example of the great many that were made in the Ptolemaic period.
altText: A work made of faience.

title: Tyet (Isis Knot) Amulet
creditLine: Gift of Charles L. Hutchinson, Henry H. Getty, and Norman W. Harris
description: Small-scale Egyptian figurines, or amulets, were thought to promote health and good luck. This type of amulet, known in Egyptian as tyet, is believed to represent a folded piece of cloth associated with Isis. It was frequently placed at the neck of the mummy.
altText: A work made of faience.

title: Kohl Jar with Lid
dateDisplay: Middle Kingdom-early New Kingdom, Dynasty 12-early Dynasty 18, about 1985-1479 BCE
creditLine: Gift of Henry H. Getty and Charles L. Hutchinson
description: This small container was designed to hold kohl, a cosmetic eye paint made of ground galena or malachite. Ancient Egyptian men and women wore kohl for its aesthetic appeal but also to dampen the harsh sunlight of North Africa and possibly even for medicinal purposes. Containers like this were buried with their owners for continued use in the afterlife.
altText: A work made of travertine (egyptian alabaster).

title: Head From an Anthropoid Sarcophagus Lid
creditLine: Gift of Henry H. Getty, Charles L. Hutchinson, Robert H. Fleming, and Norman W. Harris
description: This head is a fragment from the lid of a sarcophagus whose complete shape evoked a human form. The deeply cut eyebrows and eyes once held inlays likely made of copper alloy and glass. Ancient Egyptians crafted sarcophagi to protect mummified bodies from damage and decay and ensure a person’s existence in the afterlife. Coffins served the same purpose but were made from wood, clay, metal, or cartonnage (hardened linen and plaster), not stone.
altText: A work made of limestone.

title: Tetradrachm (Coin) Depicting Arethusa
creditLine: Gift of William F. Dunham
description: The front of this coin depicts the nymph Arethusa encircled by dolphins. On the back is a charioteer with a winged Nike flying above to crown horses with a wreath. Arethusa escaped the unwanted attentions of the river god Alpheus by swimming under the sea to the island of Sicily, where she found sanctuary. Arethusa’s path was said to explain the freshwater spring that miraculously bubbled into the nymph’s pool and that still exists in Syracuse.
altText: A work made of silver.

title: Ring Inscribed with Hieroglyphs
creditLine: Gift of Henry H. Getty, Charles L. Hutchinson, and Norman W. Harris
description: Upon death, people who were thought to have lived moral lives were reborn in the afterlife as a form of the god Osiris. This ring is inscribed with the title “Osiris,” followed by the owner’s names and titles, attesting to his faith that he would become one with the god after death.
altText: A work made of gold.

title: Ring Depicting Isis and Horus
creditLine: Gift of Henry H. Getty and Charles L. Hutchinson
description: One side of this ring bears the title of a priest of Thoeris named Horemakhbit. The other side shows the goddess Isis wearing her tall horned headdress and seated on a throne nursing Horus. They are surrounded by flowers that represent the papyrus marsh in which she sheltered her son. The name Horemakhbit means “Horus in the Marsh,” making the image of Isis and Horus a visual pun of the priest’s name.
altText: A work made of gold.

title: Double Crown Amulet
creditLine: Gift of Henry H. Getty and Charles L. Hutchinson
description: Small-scale Egyptian figurines, or amulets, were thought to promote health and good luck and were worn by both the living and dead. Here, the crowns of Northern and Southern Egypt are shown atop a half-basket which is the hieroglyph for “all” or “lord.” Therefore, this amulet may express the wish that when the deceased takes the form of Osiris, they would rule over all Egypt.
altText: A work made of gold.

title: Nehebkau Amulet
creditLine: Gift of Henry H. Getty and Charles L. Hutchinson
description: Small-scale Egyptian figurines, or amulets, were thought to promote health and good luck. Worn by the living and dead, they could be part of jewelry or incorproated into a mummy's wrappings to secure the deceased’s well-being and rebirth. This amulet takes the shape of Nehebkau, often depicted as a male with a snakehead, a deity who judged the deceased before a council of the gods.
altText: A work made of gold.

title: Djed-Pillar Amulet
creditLine: The Art Institute of Chicago
description: Amulets could be strung on cords to be worn by the living or the dead. This group of ancient amulets features a pillar with cross bars (known as the djed column) that represented the backbone of the god Osiris and conveyed stability.
altText: A work made of faience.

title: Taweret Amulet
dateDisplay: New Kingdom, Dynasty 18, reign of Akhenaten (about 1352–1336 BCE)
creditLine: The Art Institute of Chicago
description: Small-scale Egyptian figurines, or amulets, were thought to promote health and good luck and were worn by both the living and dead. This amulet takes the form of the protective Egyptian goddess Taweret, often depicted as a standing hippopotamus with a round belly referencing her ties to childbirth and fertility. Similar examples have been excavated from Tell el-Amarna, a city that had an active glass manufacturing industry.
altText: A work made of glass.

title: Tetradrachm (Coin) Depicting the God Dionysos
creditLine: Gift of William F. Dunham
description: The front of this coin depicts a young Dionysos, Greek god of wine, facing right and crowned with an ivory wreath bearing two bunches of berries at his brow. His expression is serene, and his hair is shown rolled through the diadem, with several long locks curling down his neck. On the back, Dionysos is depicted leaning lightly on a rod with a cloak over his left arm and a bunch of grapes presented in his right.
altText: A work made of silver.

title: Tetradrachm (Coin) Depicting a Cista with Snake
artistDisplay: Greek; minted in Pergamon, Asia Minor (now Turkey)
creditLine: Gift of William F. Dunham
description: The snakes used in the initiation ceremony of the cult of Dionysos were kept in a cista mystica, or sacred container. The snake represented the god himself in his role as a fertility deity and symbol of reincarnation. This very popular coin type shows the sacred snake wriggling out of a basket encircled by a wreath made of ivy leaves. As part of the rites of Dionysos, the ancient Greeks and Romans chewed ivy leaves, a mild hallucinogen.
altText: A work made of silver.

title: Stater (Coin) Depicting a Sea Turtle
creditLine: Gift of William F. Dunham
description: Coins of Aegina depicted images of sea turtles when the island of Aegina was the supreme sea power among the Greek city-states. After its defeat by Athens in 458 BCE, Aegina stopped using the sea turtle and substituted the land tortoise to symbolize its lost sea power. On the back of this coin is a geometric design comprised of a square with a windmill-like pattern.
altText: A work made of silver.

title: Pair of Wine Coolers
artistDisplay: Chased by Eugene J. Soligny (American, c. 1833–1901) Tiffany and Company (American, founded 1837) New York
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by the Antiquarian Society
description: These objects created by the Tiffany Company were commissioned by the United States government and presented to Viscount d’Itajubá of Brazil in gratitude for his role in arbitrating between the United States and Great Britain after the American Civil War. Decorated with ancient Greek figures and symbols, the designs in the silver represent agriculture and commerce and were meant to symbolize prosperity of the United States after the Civil War.
altText: A work made of silver.

title: Farm near Duivendrecht
creditLine: Gift of Dolly J. van der Hoop Schoenberg
description: Though Piet Mondrian is best known for his nonrepresentational paintings, his basic vision was rooted in landscape. He was particularly inspired by the flat topography of his native Holland, a subject he returned to even after he had begun working in an abstract style. Mondrian first sketched this farm around 1905. Nine of the 20 known related paintings and drawings of the farm, however, were created later, during World War I.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: The Interior of the Palm House on the Pfaueninsel Near Potsdam
creditLine: Through prior acquisitions of the George F. Harding Collection; L.L. and A.S. Coburn and Alexander A. McKay endowments; through prior gift of William Wood Prince; through prior acquisitions of the Charles H. and Mary F. S. Worcester Endowment
description: The work of Carl Blechen, a pivotal figure in 19th-century German painting, marks a transition from Romanticism to a more realistic view of nature. Inspired in part by his encounter with the Italian landscape and light during a trip he made around 1828 or 1829, Blechen developed a fluid technique that enabled him to capture fleeting atmospheric effects. He often used his landscapes as settings for mysterious figures, reflecting his early contact with Romantic painting and theater.
altText: Four women with musical instruments lounge in a massive garden courtyard.

title: Headrest (Isicamelo)
creditLine: Edward E. Ayer Endowment in memory of Charles L. Hutchinson
description: In Zulu culture of the 19th and early 20th centuries, neck rests signaled prestige and were used to protect the stylish and complex hairstyles of men and women during sleep. Beyond their practical use, these wooden neck rests provide connection to the spiritual realm. Though highly abstracted, this example evokes a bull, which is a source of wealth and a means of ancestral communication.
altText: A work made of wood.

title: Thistles
creditLine: Gift of Brooks McCormick
description: Beginning in 1885 and inspired by his friendship with Monet, John Singer Sargent increasingly spent time painting outside, exploring the techniques and subjects of Impressionism. Executing this work in rural England (or possibly southern France), he experimented with broken brushwork and a high-keyed palette. He continued painting outside throughout his life, a practice that provided respite from his busy schedule as an acclaimed portraitist.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: David Garrick as King Lear
creditLine: Gift of Richard L. Feigen
description: David Garrick, one of the most influential actors of 18th century Britain, appears here in the guise of the titular character from Shakespeare’s King Lear, a role he played numerous times on the stage. In this portrait, made after Garrick’s passing and based on prints created from his death mask, the actor wears a crown of wheat and flowers in reference to a famous scene in the play during which the king rages at a storm, daring it to harm him.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Mountain Brook
artistDisplay: Albert Bierstadt (American, born Solingen, Prussia, now Germany, 1830–1902)
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by Mrs. Herbert A. Vance; fund of an anonymous donor; Wesley M. Dixon Jr. Fund and Endowment; Henry Horner Straus and Mr. and Mrs. Frederick G. Wacker Jr. endowment funds; through prior acquisitions of various donors, including Samuel P. Avery Endowment, Mrs. George A. Carpenter, Frederick S. Colburn, Mr. and Mrs. Stanley Feinberg, Field Museum of Natural History, Mr. and Mrs. Frank Harding, International Minerals and Chemicals Corp., Mr. and Mrs. Ralph Loeff, Mrs. Frank C. Miller, Mahlan D. Moulds, Mrs. Clive Runnells, Mr. and Mrs. Stanley Stone, and the Charles H. and Mary F.S. Worcester Collection
description: Albert Bierstadt is best remembered for his paintings of the American West, but during his early career, the ambitious artist also created New England landscapes, particularly of the White Mountains, as seen here. When this painting was first exhibited in 1863, critics declared it Bierstadt’s “best work” and praised the artist’s skillful contrast of “light and shade,” which brings a heightened realism to the image.
altText: Painting of a small stream in the middle of the woods. In the center of the painting, there is a small waterfall over a large boulder. Radiant beams of sunlight penetrate the thick forest of birch and other trees, and a small bird sings from a broken branch over the waterfall.

title: Two Cows and a Young Bull beside a Fence in a Meadow
creditLine: In loving memory of Harold T. Martin from Eloise W. Martin, wife, and Joyce Martin Brown, daughter; Charles H. and Mary F. S. Worcester Collection; Lacy Armour Endowment; through prior gift of Frank H. and Louise B. Woods
description: During his short life, the prolific Dutch painter and etcher Paulus Potter elevated images of cows, oxen, and other domestic animals to majestic emblems of nature. His lavish attention to the physical appearances of such beasts—the varied texture and coloring of their hair, their characteristic poses, their bulky contours—borders on human portraiture and likely derived from drawings he made from life.
altText: A tired-looking brown and white cow lies down on a patch of dry earth, a dark-brown bull and cow standing behind her against an overcast sky.

title: The Knickknack Peddler
dimensions: Diam.: 7.3 cm (2 7/8 in.); Thickness: D.: 2.7 cm (1 1/16 in.)
creditLine: Through prior bequest of Arthur Rubloff
description: The knickknack peddler is a motif often featured in Chinese paintings. This object shows the peddler eagerly approaching his young customers but carelessly leaving his goods unattended among a group of mischievous little boys. While maintaining the traditional composition for this scene, the circular shape of this ivory medallion and its deeply carved surface give the image a novel sense of movement.
altText: A work made of ivory.

title: Lighthouse Clock
artistDisplay: Simon Willard and Sons American, 1753–1848 Roxbury, Massachusetts
medium: White pine, mahogany veneer, enamel, brass, and gilt and silver mounts
creditLine: Gift of the Antiquarian Society
description: In 1819 Simon Willard applied for and received a patent for the first American alarm clock. He intended for the clocks to be portable so that one could use them around the house or while traveling. Patented by Willard under the name “alarm timepiece,” clocks like this one are now referred to as lighthouse clocks for their marked similarity to the Eddystone lighthouse in the English Channel off Plymouth, England.
altText: A work made of white pine, mahogany veneer, enamel, brass, and gilt and silver mounts.

title: Portrait Figure of Metang, the 10th King of Batufam
artistDisplay: Carved by Mbeudjang (Eastern Bangwa, active early 20th century) Bamileke Kingdom of Batufam, Cameroon Coastal West Africa
medium: Wood and pigment with traces of chalk and camwood
creditLine: Major Acquisitions Centennial Endowment
description: Carved by the eastern Bangwa artist Mbeudjang, this figure represents Metang, an early 20th-century ruler of Batufam, a kingdom in the Cameroon Grassfields. Though called “portraits,” commemorative figures like this are not intended to be lifelike renderings. Rather they are idealized images of kingship and served as valued partners to rulers in protecting their realm and its people.
altText: A carved wooden figure wearing a conical hat, with an elongated neck, torso, and arms, sitting on a stool and holding a drinking vessel and a horn.

title: Four-Armed Sarasvati, Goddess of Learning, Seated in Lotus Position (Padmasana)
creditLine: Gift of Marilynn B. Alsdorf
description: Worshipped in Buddhism, Hinduism, and Jainism, Sarasvati derives her name from an ancient river in northwest India. Just as rivers sustain life, Sarasvati represents the ancient source of knowledge through the image of flowing waters. Here, she sits amid water, holding a palm leaf manuscript symbolizing knowledge in one hand and in the other a stringed instrument called a vina, symbolizing the harmonies and creative energies of the universe.
altText: A work made of chlorite phyllite.

title: God Shiva
creditLine: Gift of Marilynn B. Alsdorf
description: This bronze icon from Vietnam or Cambodia is identifiable as the Hindu god Shiva from the snake armband he wears and the presence of a third eye in the middle of his forehead. The icon's distinctive facial features suggest that the sculpture functioned as a portrait as well as an image of a deity—possibly a deified royal figure who identified himself with Shiva.
altText: A work made of bronze.

title: Elizabeth Grant Bankson Beatty (Mrs. James Beatty) and Her Daughter Susan
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by Robin and Timm R. Reynolds and Jill Burnside Zeno; Bulley and Andrews, Edna Graham, Love Galleries, Mary Swissler Oldberg, Ratcliffe Foundation, and Quinn E. Delaney funds; Walter Aitken, Dr. Julian Archie, Mr. and Mrs. Perry Herst, Jay W. McGreevy, Mr. and Mrs. John W. Puth, Stone Foundation, and Mr. and Mrs. Frederick G. Wacker, Jr. endowment funds; through prior acquisitions of the George F. Harding Collection and Ruth Helgeson
description: The first known Black painter to gain professional recognition in the United States, Joshua Johnson was celebrated for his portraits of white middle-class families. The son of a white man and an enslaved woman, Johnson was originally enslaved before becoming free when he came of age. Described as “self-taught” in a newspaper advertisement, he attracted local patrons among the city’s artisan and middle-class families.
altText: Portrait of a light-skinned woman with dark curly hair and to her right a small, blond child. Both are elegantly dressed, the woman in a dark, short-sleeved dress with gathered bodice and the child in a short-sleeved white dress. A white tassel hangs down above the child from a nearby curtain.

title: The Mill Pond
creditLine: Edward B. Butler Collection
description: A distinctive 19th-century landscape painter, George Inness excelled at capturing the poetics and mood of his environs, finding spiritual resonances in nature from its grand vistas to its quiet nooks. The Mill Pond depicts a wooded scene, in which a small figure rows a boat in the pond at middle distance. Color and atmosphere rather than line or detail communicate Inness's intensity of vision, fueled by his individual encounter with nature.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Male Figure (Nkisi Nkondi)
artistDisplay: Kongo: Vili Republic of the Congo Central Africa
medium: Wood, metal, glass, fabric, fiber, cowrie shells, bone, leather, gourd, and feathers
creditLine: Ada Turnbull Hertle Endowment
description: The term nkisi refers to spirit-invested objects empowered with medicinal and magical ingredients called bilongo. Here, the bilongo are enclosed in the cap on the head of this figure and in the mirror-sealed resin packet on the abdomen. The name nkondi refers to the figure’s ability to hunt down and punish wrongdoers when prompted by a nail or blade driven into the figure.
altText: A wooden carving of a male figure. The figure has a distinctive face, with oval-shaped eyes and mouth, and wears a cap on his head. His body is covered in various shells, bones, feathers, fabric, and metal nails, and he holds a mirror-sealed resin packet over his stomach.

title: Cow Suckling a Calf
creditLine: Gift of Marilynn B. Alsdorf
description: This panel depicts a suckling calf with his mother, whose placid eyes, floppy ears, undulating dewlap, upwardly curving horns, and hump identify her as belonging to the distinctive breed of Brahman cattle originally bred in India, where they enjoy a respected status. Cows are regarded as nourishing mothers, as depicted here, and even their waste is used both in purification rituals and for fuel.
altText: A sandstone sculpture of a cow, its head turned out toward the viewer, with a baby calf suckling underneath.

title: Goddess Hariti Seated Holding a Child
creditLine: Gift of Marilynn B. Alsdorf
description: Originally a child-devouring demoness, Hariti ultimately became a benevolent protector of children after the Buddha kidnapped one of her own to demonstrate the distress she had been inflicting upon other parents. As a Buddhist goddess, she was honored by female devotees for fertility and healthy childbirth. She was especially popular in the Gandharan region, where Greco-Roman sculptural styles had been adopted.
altText: A work made of gray schist.

title: Woman in a Garden
creditLine: A Millennium Gift of Sara Lee Corporation
description: Morisot painted figures like she was making an Impressionist landscape, using the same strokes to paint the people at the center of this piece as she used when slashing acid green and blued oranges across her canvas to capture the dappled sunlight in this garden.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Woman Bathing Her Feet in a Brook
creditLine: A Millennium Gift of Sara Lee Corporation
description: Pissarro referred to this painting in a letter of November 1894, when he wrote to his son Lucien that he wanted to send him a picture of “a little peasant girl dipping her feet in the water.” At the time, he considered the work almost finished but still lacking “that little something,” exclaiming optimistically, “I think I will get it, I feel it!” His continued ruminations on the composition may explain its heavily encrusted surface.
altText: Small dots of soft color form a woman in a red shirt and brown skirt seen up close, washing her bare feet in a lush brook while seated on a sloping bank.

title: Foot of a Cista (Storage Box)
creditLine: Katherine K. Adler Memorial Fund
description: With a bent-knee pose that connotes rapid movement, the Etruscan sun god Usil dashes across breaking waves, borne aloft by wings on his back and boots. This was one of three identical feet supporting a cista, or lidded chest, now lost, which was typically used by women to store their cosmetics and toiletries. Etruscan metalsmiths excelled in fashioning beautiful bronze objects, including incense burners, mirrors, vessels, and containers.
altText: A work made of bronze.

title: Calf's Head and Ox Tongue
creditLine: Major Acquisitions Centennial Endowment
description: Caillebotte may have been inspired by the butcher’s shop below his family home in Paris when he painted this bloody scene of animal parts ready for human consumption. The painting confronts viewers with objects that are visually unpleasant and yet rendered with highly decorative pastel colors and soft brushstrokes.
altText: A white severed calf's head is suspended from a hook in its nose at right, painted with blue undertones and pink and yellow highlights. At left is a severed ox tongue and mouth rendered in soft white, pinks, and reds, all against a blue-gray background.

title: The Girl by the Window
creditLine: Searle Family Trust and Goldabelle McComb Finn endowments; Charles H. and Mary F. S. Worcester Collection
description: Edvard Munch’s life and art have come to epitomize modern notions of anxiety. Created the same year as his renowned The Scream, this painting depicts a young girl in her nightgown gazing out at the city from her darkened room. The steep angle of the floor and the deep shadows that obliterate almost everything in the room create an unsettling and enigmatic scene.
altText: Loosely painted scene of a brown-haired girl in her nightgown standing in a dark room, gazing out a window into a brighter night, her face unseen and her hand drawing back the pale curtain. Light blues and pink whites dominate the girl and the window, while deep browns, blues, and greens color the darkened portions of her room.

title: Steer Horn Armchair
creditLine: Gift of Jamee J. and Marshall Field
description: Although furniture made from the horns of steer, elk, and deer is rooted in European tradition, it reached the height of popularity in America in the 1880s. Not only did chairs like this one evoke the romanticism and pioneering spirit of the American West, they also employed innovative, exotic materials that were prized during the Aesthetic movement. Lavishly upholstered, this diminutive example was most likely intended for a parlor.
altText: A work made of horn, silk, brass, and upholstery.

title: Machinist
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by the Antiquarian Society
description: Stebbins belonged to a community of women sculptors in Rome. Like their male colleagues, they sought to emulate the statues of antiquity. In a rare pair of marble statues, Stebbins portrays a machinist and his apprentice, an unusual theme in mid-19th-century American sculpture. Stebbins innovatively rendered a modern subject in the refined, neoclassical visual language traditionally used to depict biblical, historical, and mythological subjects.
altText: White marble statue of machinist with hammer, anvil, and cogs.

title: Machinist's Apprentice
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by the Antiquarian Society
description: Stebbins belonged to a community of women sculptors in Rome. Like their male colleagues, they sought to emulate the statues of antiquity. In a rare pair of marble statues, Stebbins portrays a machinist and his apprentice, an unusual theme in mid-19th-century American sculpture. Stebbins innovatively rendered a modern subject in the refined, neoclassical visual language traditionally used to depict biblical, historical, and mythological subjects.
altText: White marble statue of machinist assistant with sketchbook and cogs.

title: Belmead Center Table
artistDisplay: Alexander Jackson Davis (American, 1803–1892) Probably made by Alexander Roux (American, born France, c. 1813–1886) New York
creditLine: Gift of The Antiquarian Society
description: In 1845 Alexander Jackson Davis designed Belmead, a Gothic Revival villa, for the builder Philip St. George Cocke of Powhatan County, Virginia. In addition to designing Belmead’s exterior, Davis designed furniture for the interior, notably a parlor set that included side chairs. The table descended in the Cocke family along with the parlor set and, remarkably, retains its original marble top and intricately carved tracery lantern.
altText: A work made of rosewood, oak, walnut, marble.

title: Coffer
artistDisplay: Attributed to André-Charles Boulle (born France, 1642–1732) Paris
medium: Oak, tortoiseshell, brass, gilded copper, gilded bronze, pewter, ebony, and oiled paper
creditLine: Michael A. Bradshaw and Kenneth S. Harris, Eloise W. Martin, Richard T. Crane, Jr., Memorial, and European Decorative Arts Purchase funds; through prior acquisitions of Mrs. C. H. Boissevain in memory of Henry C. Dangler, Kate S. Buckingham Endowment, David Dangler, Harold T. Martin, and Katherine Field-Rodman
description: The cabinetmaker André-Charles Boulle was responsible for some of the finest examples of French furniture made during the reign of Louis XIV (1643–1715). Boulle perfected the technique of veneering furniture with a rich marquetry of tortoiseshell, pewter, and gilt copper, and further enriched his surfaces with sculptural gilt bronze mounts. Boulle's patrons included members of the royal family, aristocrats, ministers, and financiers.
altText: Ornate wooden box with golden metallic corners and embellishments, painted golden flourishes throughout. Its gold metallic clasp is embossed with a human face.

title: Moon Jar
creditLine: Gift of an anonymous donor, Louise Lutz Estate, and Russell Tyson Endowment
description: This large, milky white jar, made during Korea’s Joseon dynasty (1392–1910), is called a moon jar because of its distinctive shape and color. This example, like many moon jars, has mysterious spots—possibly from liquid it once contained or from crystal growth from the slow cooling of the kiln. Either way, these stains have become a part of the identity of Joseon moon jars.
altText: A work made of porcelain with glaze.

title: Portrait Bust of a Woman
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by The Antiquarian Society in honor of Ian Wardropper, the Classical Art Society, Mr. and Mrs. Isak V. Gerson, James and Bonnie Pritchard, and Mrs. Hugo Sonnenschein; Mr. and Mrs. Kenneth Bro Fund; Katherine K. Adler, Mr. and Mrs. Walter Alexander in honor of Ian Wardropper, David Earle III, William A. and Renda H. Lederer Family, Chester D. Tripp, and Jane B. Tripp endowments
description: Carved by an exceptionally skilled sculptor, this exquisite bust depicts a Roman woman of elegance, wealth, and distinction. The subject bears a solemn expression and wears an intricate hairstyle that emulates a type worn by Faustina the Elder (d. AD 141), wife of Emperor Antoninus Pius (r. AD 138–61), suggesting that she lived during this period. The gem-encrusted diadem alludes to her elevated social standing.
altText: White marble bust of woman wearing headband and tunic.

title: Paperweight
artistDisplay: Baccarat Glassworks (Cristalleries de Baccarat) Lorraine, France, founded 1764
creditLine: Bequest of Arthur Rubloff
description: Technological improvements to optical scientific instruments in the mid-19th century spurred a craze across Europe with identifying and classifying the natural world. Amateur botanists were eager to collect and preserve floral specimens, which they intently researched and catalogued. In response to this broad appeal, French glassmakers made paperweights that portrayed highly sought-after botanical subjects.
altText: A work made of glass.

title: Shinto Deity in the Guise of the Monk Hyeja
medium: Magnolia wood with traces of pigment
creditLine: Kate S. Buckingham Endowment
description: This figure is said to represent the seventh-century Korean monk Eji, the foremost spiritual teacher of the first great patron of Buddhism in Japan, Prince Shotoku (574–622). The sculpture is made in the ichiboku technique, using only a single block of wood. Its dramatic power is enhanced by the natabori technique, in which the sculptor's chisel marks are clearly visible on the surface.
altText: A work made of magnolia wood with traces of pigment.

title: Mrs. Charles Deering (Marion Denison Whipple)
creditLine: Anonymous loan
description: The subject of this painting, Marion Deering, was the wife of Charles Deering, a Chicago businessman, an important benefactor of the Art Institute, and Sargent's lifelong friend and patron. Here, he depicted Marion seated with her right arm resting on a chair back. He rendered her face and hand with a high degree of finish. The broader handling of paint in her dress signals his facility with the tactile and expressive possibilities of paint.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Statue of Ptah-Sokar-Osiris
medium: Wood, preparation layer, pigment, gold, and textile
creditLine: Gift of Phoenix Ancient Art, S.A.
description: This funerary statue, owned by a woman named Asetirdis (“Isis is the one who gave her”), depicts a composite of Ptah (a creator god), Sokar (the patron deity of the necropolis west of Memphis), and Osiris (the ruler of the underworld). Ptah-Sokar-Osiris’s purview encompassed all phases of life, including rebirth. A cavity in the statue’s base was meant to hold funerary texts or another sacred object to facilitate Asetirdis’s rebirth after death.
altText: A small statue consisting of a multicolored rectangular base and a painted mummified figure oriented vertically, wearing an elaborate striped headdress with a plume.

title: Fish Plate
artistDisplay: Probably by the Heligoland Painter Greek; Campania, Italy
creditLine: Gift of Yun Soo Lim Vermeule
description: Decorated tableware enlivened festive meals. This red-figure plate was used, as its decoration suggests, for serving seafood, a staple of the Mediterranean diet. Tasty juices pooled in the central concavity, which may also have contained sauces.
altText: A work made of terracotta, red-figure.

title: Two Sauceboats and Two Covered Tureens from the Washington Memorial Service
artistDisplay: Artist unknown (Chinese, made for the American market) China
medium: Hard-paste porcelain and glaze with gilding
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by Mrs. Herbert A. Vance and an anonymous donor
description: Chinese porcelain made especially for export to the United States often displays painted imagery of subjects, such as commemorative events, that appealed to wealthy American consumers. Part of a larger suite, these four pieces were commissioned around 1800 in remembrance of the nation’s first president, who died in 1799. Symbols such as the weeping willow, tomb, and eagle reflect the contemporary mourning for Washington.
altText: A work made of hard-paste porcelain and glaze with gilding.

title: Head of Medusa
creditLine: Lacy Armour Endowment
description: This plaster is a partial model for Canova's large-scale marble statue Perseus Holding the Head of Medusa. According to Greek mythology, Medusa was a serpent-haired creature whose gaze turned anyone who beheld her into stone. Perseus killed Medusa as she slept by using a mirrored shield to approach her and sever her head. Here, Canova depicted Medusa’s decapitated head, with its blank eyes, slack mouth, and cheeks caressed by snakes.
altText: A work made of plaster.

title: Footed Bowl
creditLine: European Decorative Arts General Sales Proceeds Fund; purchased with funds provided by the Antiquarian Society; Richard T. Crane, Jr. Memorial Fund; Neville and John H. Bryan, Rosenwald Glass, and Kay and Frederick Krehbiel endowment funds
description: This footed bowl was intended to make a luxurious statement in late 15th-century Italy. Brilliant blue glass, meant to replicate the color of sapphires, was a specialty of Venetian glass blowers. The finely painted enameled decoration—cherubs and fantastical sphinxes—as well as the classical shape of the vessel, reflects the Italian Renaissance admiration for art and design of ancient Rome.
altText: A work made of blue glass, enamel, and gilding.

title: Statue of Horus
creditLine: Gift of the Alsdorf Foundation
description: From about 3000 BCE, when ancient Egypt had its first kings, Egyptians considered their ruler to be the earthly manifestation of Horus, the god of divine kingship. Statues of Horus in the form of a falcon, like this one, were displayed in temples as part of the royal cult, which celebrated the king’s role as an intercessor between humans and gods.
altText: A work made of basalt.

title: Container
artistDisplay: Kongo Angola, Democratic Republic of the Congo, or Republic of the Congo Central Africa
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by Jamee and Marshall Field; Pauline S. Armstrong Endowment
description: Basketwork boxes decorated with interlocking geometric patterns were produced in the Congolese region and adjacent Angola well into the 20th century. Such containers were used for the storage of luxury wares including raffia textiles and ivory accessories. Some were exported to Europe as early as the mid-17th century and became part of the collections of royals and wealthy aristocrats.
altText: A work made of rattan, wood, and twine.

title: Concho Belt
artistDisplay: Navajo (Diné) Northern New Mexico or Arizona, United States
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by Mrs. Leonard S. Florsheim, Jr.
description: During the 1860s and 1870s, Navajos (Diné) learned silversmithing from Hispanic artisans in New Mexico. Navajo silversmiths rapidly established a distinctive style that has become one of the hallmarks of Native American art in the Southwest. Today, Navajo jewelry exhibits much greater complexity of design and the use of diverse semiprecious stones, shell, and other metals.
altText: A work made of silver and leather.

title: Cup in the Form of a Horse and Rider
artistDisplay: Hans Ludwig Kienle (born Ulm [now Germany], 1591–1653) Ulm (now Germany)
creditLine: Eloise W. Martin fund; through prior acquisition of the George F. Harding Collection; Henry Horner Strauss, Pauline S. Armstrong, Harry and Maribel G. Blum, Tillie C. Cohn, Richard T. Crane, Jr. Memorial, Stanford Marks, Michael A. Bradshaw and Kenneth S. Harris, Mrs. Edgar J. Uihlein Art Purchase, European Decorative Arts Capital Campaign funds; through prior acquisition from Albert D. Lasker; European Decorative Arts General, Mr. and Mrs. Joseph Varley funds; through prior acquisition of the Kate S. Buckingham Gothic fund; Mary Swissler Oldberg fund; through prior acquisitions of the Howard V. Shaw Memorial and Kate S. Buckingham funds
description: This 17th-century drinking cup, made for display on a buffet or sideboard, is a rare example of the work of Hans Ludwig Kienle, a German silversmith who specialized in depicting animals, including horses, lions, and stags. Here, Kienle masterfully rendered the differentiation of human and equine musculature through the contrast of silver and silver-gilt surfaces, thus animating the already dynamic subject.
altText: Small statue, silver male rider on gold horse on its hind legs.

title: A View of Vianen with a Herdsman and Cattle by a River
creditLine: Charles H. and Mary F. S. Worcester Fund
description: Aelbert Cuyp never traveled to Italy, yet he employed the golden light typical of southern Europe to dramatize his Dutch pastoral subjects. He enhanced views of the meandering rivers and flat terrain with cows and sheep, animals that abounded in the local countryside. In this relatively early painting, his use of a warm, monochrome color palette reflects the influence of his older contemporary, Jan van Goyen.
altText: A work made of oil on panel.

title: Male Face Mask (Chihongo)
artistDisplay: Chokwe Angola or Democratic Republic of the Congo Central Africa
medium: Wood, raffia, burlap, turaco feathers, guinea fowl feathers, and pigment
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by Mrs. James W. Alsdorf
description: The Chokwe use masquerades to engage with their ancestors, encouraging them to guide, protect, and educate the living. The chihongo is the male counterpart to the female mwana pwo mask. Its feathered headdress, red coloring, scarification patterns, stylized beard, and filed teeth are all markers of wisdom, leadership, and status.
altText: A work made of wood, raffia, burlap, turaco feathers, guinea fowl feathers, and pigment.

title: The Irish Question
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by Carol W. Wardlaw and Jill Burnside Zeno; Roger and J. Peter McCormick Endowment Fund
description: This highly realistic still life is an example of a trompe l’oeil painting, French for “fools the eye.” The potatoes seem to come off the canvas, but they also are symbolic, alluding to the great wave of Irish immigrants in the 1800s; while the public had cocerns about their religion and culture, industry saw them as a source of cheap labor.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Aureus (Coin) Portraying Emperor Hadrian
creditLine: Katherine K. Adler Memorial, Mr. and Mrs. Walter Alexander, and Ancient Art Purchase Funds
description: While early Roman coins depicted gods and goddesses on the front side, this changed after Caesar’s portrait appeared on a coin in 44 BCE. Thereafter, profile portraits of current rulers and imperial family members became the standard. This coin featuring Hadrian was produced similarly to how coins are produced today; the images were engraved into bronze dies and then struck, one by one, in metal.
altText: A work made of gold.

title: Chair (Kiti Cha Enzi)
artistDisplay: Swahili Lamu, Kenya Eastern and Southern Africa
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by Marshall Field V
description: This chair illustrates the complex history of trade and conquest in the region known as the Swahili Coast. The region’s natural harbors first invited exchange with partners in the Persian Gulf and Western India. Later, the Portuguese, Omani, and British imposed their authority. Each conquering state brought goods, practices, and other foreign influences, which local artisans artfully synthesized and reshaped in their own chairs.
altText: Wooden chair with woven cotton seat, back, footrest.

title: Saint Michael and the Devil
creditLine: Chester D. Tripp Endowment
description: Saint Michael, one of the seven archangels in the Old Testament, led the heavenly host against God’s enemies in the book of Revelation. This 15th-century wood sculpture represents Michael’s battle against Satan. The image would have been associated with the hope of salvation, as Saint Michael was often depicted weighing the souls of the blessed and the damned during the Last Judgment.
altText: Light wood sculpture of angel with shield looking towards devil at feet.

title: Gold Pectoral with Zoomorphic Face
creditLine: Joanne M. and Clarence E. Spanjer and Curator’s Discretionary funds
description: The Chavín de Huántar archaeological site, in the Peruvian Andes, held economic, political, and religious significance from 900 to 200 BCE. It fused previous coastal Peruvian architectural and sculptural styles with imagery of figures that were part human and part animal. This symbolism represented Chavín's priestly rulers' connection with animal forces and natural phenomena, reflecting a cosmology that once held sway throughout the Americas.
altText: A work made of gold.

title: The Nativity
creditLine: Ethel T. Scarborough Fund; John G. Searle Family Trust, L. L. and A. S. Coburn, Mr. and Mrs. Lester King, John and Josephine Louis, Samuel A. Marx, Alexander McKay, Chester D. Tripp, and Murray Vale endowment funds; purchased with funds provided by Marilynn Alsdorf, Anne Searle Bent, David and Celia Hilliard, Alexandra and John Nichols, Mrs. Harold T. Martin, Mrs. George B. Young in memory of her husband, and the Rhoades Foundation; gift of John Bross and members of the Old Masters Society in memory of Louise Smith Bross; through prior gift of the George F. Harding, Mr. and Mrs. W. W. Kimball, Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson, and Charles H. and Mary F. S. Worcester collections
description: In 1500 Fra (Friar) Bartolommeo left behind his painting career to join a monastery. Four years later he returned to painting, looking to Da Vinci, Raphael, and Michelangelo to form his new, quietly spiritual style. Here, he depicted the Nativity in a traditional, though especially intimate manner. The Virgin kneels humbly gazing at the Christ Child while Joseph assumes a post of restrained wonderment.
altText: A light-skinned man in red and woman in blue sit with an infant between them, angels beside and above them, a small town in the background.

title: Portrait of Emmanuel Rio
creditLine: Henry Tiefenbronner Endowment
description: This painting depicts Emmanuel Rio, an enslaved Brazilian man of African descent who was sent to Emperor Francis I in Vienna around 1820. Despite studying at an elite private school, where he excelled in music, Rio was assigned to work in the imperial garden. Here, Rio holds his instrument while looking at an image of Francis. The painting doesn't clearly reflect the precariousness of Rio’s situation in Vienna, which worsened after Francis died.
altText: A work made of oil on panel.

title: Sideboard
creditLine: Gift of the Antiquarian Society
description: In the mid-19th century, dining room furniture featured ornament that was intended to reinforce ideals of hospitality and gentility, like the panels depicting Aesop's Fables on this sideboard. This piece resembles the furniture designed by notable architect Frank Furness, who frequently collaborated with cabinetmaker Daniel Pabst. Although details of the carving tie it to Pabst, the design cannot be attributed conclusively to a particular hand.
altText: Large walnut sideboard with two shelves, animal designs on doors, gryphons at top.

title: Lamp with Hanging Head Dragonfly Shade and Mosaic and Turtleback Base
artistDisplay: Design attributed to Clara Pierce Wolcott Driscoll (American, 1861–1944) Tiffany Studios (American, 1902–32) Corona, New York

description: In the 1890s Louis Comfort Tiffany began using his opalescent Favrile glass to produce lamps, the form for which he would become most famous. As the artistic director of Tiffany Studios, he approved all patterns but created relatively few lamps himself. Clara Driscoll, head of the Women’s Glass Cutting Department, designed the majority of the firm’s lamps, including, likely, this one.
altText: Lamp with stained glass shade featuring dragonflies and shades of green, purple, brown.

title: Cauldron
dateDisplay: Western Zhou dynasty (1046–771 BC ), early 9th century BC
creditLine: Major Acquisitions Centennial Fund
description: Designed to contain offerings of meat in rituals, this vessel was cast with a lengthy inscription on its interior commemorating a solemn ceremony at the imperial court. Although the monsterlike masks on each leg display animal imagery common on older bronzes, the bands that encircle the bowl are more abstracted, marking a turning point in the art of early Chinese bronzes.
altText: Medium sized cauldron with green patina, two handles, and three legs.

title: Sideboard
artistDisplay: Designed by Edward William Godwin (English, 1833-1886) Made by William Watt (English, 1834-1885) London
medium: Ebonized mahogany with glass and silvered brass
creditLine: Robert Allerton, Harry and Maribel G. Blum, Mary and Leigh Block, Mary Waller Langhorne, Mrs. Siegfried G. Schmidt, Tillie C. Cohn, Richard T. Crane, Jr. Memorial, Eugene A. Davidson, Harriott A. Fox, Florence L. Notter, Kay and Frederick Krehbiel endowment funds; European Decorative Arts Purchase Fund;Irving and June Seaman Endowment Fund; through prior acquisition of the Reid Martin Estate
description: Edward William Godwin was an innovative interior decorator and designer of furniture, textiles, and theater sets. He designed his first ebonized sideboard—this is a variation—for his dining room in 1867. It represented a shift away from the weight of contemporary Gothic Revival aesthetics and toward a spare style that gained Godwin some notable contemporary clients, such as James McNeill Whistler and Oscar Wilde.
altText: Black wood sideboard with skinny poles holding cabinets, brass trim.

title: Head
creditLine: Frederick W. Renshaw Acquisition Fund; Robert Allerton and Ada Turnbull Hertle endowments; Robert Allerton Income Fund; Gladys N. Anderson Endowment
description: This Fang head was once inserted into the lid of a cylindrical bark container holding the skull and skeletal remains of an honored ancestor. Stored in the corner of a man’s sleeping room, the sculpture and box protected the ancestor’s bones and kept his power within his descendants' reach. The copper alloy inserts in the eyes would have reflected light in the dark, startling any intruder.
altText: A dark-brown painted sculpture with hints of orange showing through of a slim face with a long neck. The lips are drawn in a pout, the cheeks sunken, the hair pulled back in a swirl pattern and falling down in a slim column.

title: Jar with Horned Serpents and Interlocking, Hatched-and-Black Stepped Designs
artistDisplay: Ceramist unknown (Ancestral Puebloan), Socorro Black-on-white West-central New Mexico
creditLine: Gift of Edward and Betty Harris
description: Horned or plumed serpents were associated with the life-giving power of water in the American Southwest, Midwest, and Southeast. On this vessel, twin abstract serpents stretch out from a central point, from which arise stepped chevrons, a motif widely associated with mountains, springs, rivers, and rising thunderstorms. The overall composition suggests the symbolic representation of a sacred landscape and the ritual summoning of water.
altText: A work made of earthenware and pigment.

artistDisplay: Baccarat Glassworks (Cristalleries de Baccarat) Lorraine, France, founded 1764
creditLine: Bequest of Arthur Rubloff
description: Technological improvements to optical scientific instruments in the mid-19th century spurred a craze across Europe with identifying and classifying the natural world. Amateur botanists were eager to collect and preserve floral specimens, which they intently researched and catalogued. In response to this broad appeal, French glassmakers made paperweights that portrayed highly sought-after botanical subjects.
altText: A work made of glass.

title: Earthly Paradise
medium: Wood with paint, glass and metal
creditLine: Through prior gift of Henry Morgen, Ann G. Morgen, Meyer Wasser, and Ruth G. Wasser; purchased with funds provided by Edward M. Blair
description: This object was created collaboratively by Gauguin and his younger contemporary Émile Bernard. Their artistic experiments challenged hierarchical distinctions between fine art, grounded in aesthetics, and decorative art, associated with functionality. Bernard carved the left panel and possibly the bottom panel. Both artists incorporated animals, trees, and people from village life in Brittany, France, motifs they also used in their paintings.
altText: A work made of wood with paint, glass and metal.

title: Parrot Olla
artistDisplay: Ceramist unknown (Acoma) Pueblo of Acoma, New Mexico
creditLine: Ethel T. Scarborough and Major Acquisitions funds; Gladys N. Anderson Endowment Fund
description: There is a long tradition of Indian ceramic making in the American Southwest that began in the early centuries AD and continues to today. This large, rounded, and beautifully proportioned vessel is covered by exuberant, colorful figures representing macaws and other birds, double rainbows, flowers, and plants—imagery that reflects the ancient and ongoing theme of communal participation in nature's eternal renewal.
altText: A work made of earthenware and slip.

title: Equestrian and Four Figures
artistDisplay: Bankoni Bougouni region, Mali Northern Africa and the Sahel
creditLine: Ada Turnbull Hertle Endowment
description: Terracotta figures like this set might have served a ritual purpose. The adornment on the figures, including the hairstyles and possible scarification marks, suggest status and wealth. The horse and rider with a knife strapped to his left arm may evoke the significant role that cavalry played in the expansion of empires and the control of trade routes in West Africa during past centuries.
altText: A work made of terracotta.
