description: Produced beginning in 1710, Meissen porcelain was an exclusive luxury good of its time. Around 1728, Augustus, the king of Poland, conceived of replicating the animal kingdom in porcelain for a Baroque palace. By the year of his death, more than 30 birds and almost 40 animals had been made, many by the sculptor Johann Joachim Kändler, who drew this vulture from life.
altText: Porcelain vulture with red, black, feathers on white tree stump.

title: Madame Paul Escudier (Louise Lefevre)
creditLine: Bequest of Brooks McCormick
description: In this depiction of Louise Escudier, Sargent undercut traditional portrait conventions by prioritizing the dramatic effects of light and dark in a Parisian apartment. It's based on a series of atmospheric views of working-class women in darkened interiors that the artist produced on two trips to Venice between 1880 and 1882. These compositions helped to establish Sargent’s reputation in Paris as a daring and original painter.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Standing Bather, Seen from the Back
creditLine: Bequest of Brooks McCormick
description: When making an artwork, Cezanne often significantly altered his original design. This canvas was cut from a larger painting, retaining remnants of the other composition. In the lower-left corner, a series of blue lines might be legs of a seated figure; the body may have continued on another part of the canvas. These lines on top of the background foliage, indicate that he added a second figure after completing the first, before changing his mind.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Lilies (Corey Memorial Window)
artistDisplay: Tiffany Glass and Decorating Company (American, 1894–1902) Corona, New York
creditLine: Gift of St. Andrew Reformed Episcopal Church
description: This memorial window, dedicated to Francis Edwin Corey and his wife, Vernera Leonard Corey, is one of several that Tiffany Glass and Decorating Company designed for Christ Reformed Episcopal Church in Chicago. When this church was demolished in 1962, the windows were moved to St. Andrew Reformed Episcopal Church in Tinley Park, Illinois. A frequent subject for Tiffany, lilies were fitting for commemorative works as a symbol of resurrection.
altText: A work made of leaded favrile glass.

title: Oil Bottle with Peony Motif
creditLine: Gift of Dorothy Braude Edinburg to the Harry B. and Bessie K. Braude Memorial Collection
description: Cosmetic containers in celadon, also known as greenware, were widely used during Korea's Goryeo dynasty (918–1392) by ladies of the court and aristocratic households. Often beautifully adorned with floral motifs, these containers held face powder, blush, hair oil, or fragrance and became prized possessions among elite women. This particular example, features a bulbous shape and intricately carved peonies, a symbol of wealth and beauty.
altText: A work made of stoneware with celadon glaze.

title: The Captive Slave (Ira Aldridge)
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by Mary Winton Green, Dan and Sara Green Cohan, Howard and Lisa Green and Jonathan and Brenda Green, in memory of David Green
description: This painting by John Philip Simpson is both a powerful abolitionist statement and a striking portrait of the celebrated Shakespearean actor Ira Aldridge. A freeborn American, Aldridge became the first Black man to play Othello on the London stage in 1833. Simpson’s painting highlights Aldridge’s gifts of expression as a tragic actor.
altText: Painting of a dark-skinned man seated and wearing a red open-necked tunic. He looks up to the right. His wrists are shackled and a large chain rests at his right, running down the bench he sits upon.

title: View of Saleve, near Geneva
medium: Oil on paper, mounted to canvas
creditLine: Through prior gift of Henry Morgen, Ann G. Morgen, Meyer Wasser, and Ruth G. Wasser
description: An ardent explorer of the remotest corners of France, Théodore Rousseau painted View of Salève, near Geneva during a three-month stay in the mountainous Jura region. With a few deft strokes, Rousseau conveyed steep, rocky outcroppings; plains dotted with shrubs; and the luminosity of moisture-laden clouds and sky. Although his larger canvases were excluded from the official Salon, his smaller panoramic oil sketches found mainstream admirers.
altText: A work made of oil on paper, mounted to canvas.

title: Tetradrachm (Coin) Portraying Queen Cleopatra VII
artistDisplay: Roman; minted in Eastern Mediterranean (possibly Antioch, Syria)
creditLine: Katherine K. Adler Memorial Fund
description: Cleopatra was queen of Egypt when the Roman Empire was expanding into the eastern Mediterranean. By allying herself with the Roman generals Julius Caesar and Mark Antony, she hoped to maintain her country’s independence and her own authority. This coin was minted during this alliance, pairing Cleopatra's and Mark Antony's faces on each side. Cleopatra’s image appears on the front, identifying her as the more important of the two rulers.
altText: A work made of silver.

title: The Prairie on Fire
creditLine: Through prior acquisition of the George F. Harding Fund; purchased with funds provided by Jamee J. and Marshall Field; Americana Endowment Fund
description: Alvan Fisher was a pioneering American landscapist whose work offered a precedent for the Hudson River School. As a Romantic-era artist, Fisher preferred dramatic episodes, which involved striking contrasts between light and dark. In this version the prairie grasses are exquisitely rendered, and the figures are dwarfed by nature, underscoring both the landscape’s beauty as well as its dangers.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Plate 50 A from Plan of Chicago 1909: Chicago. View of the Proposed Park on the South Shore Looking Northwest Towards the City.
artistDisplay: Daniel Hudson Burnham, American, 1846-1912 Edward Herbert Bennett, American, born England, 1874-1954 Paul C. Lautrup, American, born Denmark, 1844-1913
creditLine: On permanent loan to The Art Institute of Chicago from the City of Chicago
description: One of the most significant results of the Plan of Chicago is the system of lakefront parks, which runs over 18 miles along Lake Michigan. Building on the landscape developed for the World’s Columbian Exposition, Burnham imagined these green spaces as providing a “continuous playground for the people,” with playing fields, lagoons for boating, and paths for promenades. In this drawing, the parks appear completely removed from the city streets.
altText: A work made of pastel on paper.

creditLine: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Walter Alexander
description: This precious bronze object is a votive, or devotional gift, made as an offering to the gods. They come in many forms, including animals, beads, and brooches. Once a shrine was full, the votives were ceremonially buried to make room for more offerings.

title: Amphora (Storage Jar)
artistDisplay: Attributed to the Ivy Leaf Group Etruscan
creditLine: Katherine K. Adler Memorial Fund
description: During the sixth and fifth centuries BCE, the Etruscans, who lived north of Rome, imported Athenian ceramics decorated with scenes of Greek mythology, religion, and daily life. Etruscan artists, no doubt eager to capitalize on the demand, set up a workshop to produce facsimiles. Though the poor quality of the local clay did not allow for the refined finishes of Athenian vases, the painter of this vase created a highly skilled composition.
altText: A work made of terracotta, black-figure.

title: Fragment of a Funerary Lekythos (Monument in the Shape of an Oil Jar)
artistDisplay: Attributed to the Demagora Master Greek; Halai Aixonides, Athens
creditLine: Katherine K. Adler Memorial Fund, Mr. and Mrs. Walter Alexander Classical Endowment Fund, Costa A. Pandaleon Greek Art Memorial Fund, and David P. Earle III Fund
description: This stone fragment takes the shape of a lekythos, a small terracotta jar of oil often left at a grave just as we might leave flowers today. Inscriptions identify the three figures. The bearded man at left is named Leon. He clasps hands with Demagora, who sits before him and is presumably his wife. Their daughter, Helike, stands behind her mother and watches the couple bid an eternal farewell, although it is unclear which of the three has died.
altText: A work made of marble.

title: Tetradrachm (Coin) Depicting the Goddess Athena
creditLine: Gift of Martin A. Ryerson
description: The emblems chosen to represent an ancient city often related to its patron god or goddess.The most famous of civic badges was the profile of Athena, the goddess of Athens, and it was stamped on the city’s coins. While other cities modernized their coins, Athens kept this design to emphasize the dependability of its currency. The purity and stability of Athens’s coinage made it the standard throughout the Mediterranean for centuries.
altText: A work made of silver.

title: Aquamanile in the Form of a Lion
artistDisplay: Follower of Johannes Apengeter (German, active about 1325-50)
creditLine: Through prior bequest of the George F. Harding Collection; Chester D. Tripp, Jane Gidwitz Memorial; and European Painting and Sculpture Purchase funds
description: Aquamaniles like this sculptural form were used for hand washing in both sacred and secular rituals during the Middle Ages and usually featured animal forms. This vessel takes the shape of a lion but incorporates three other creatures: a dog that is locked in the lion’s fierce jaws, a basilisk or winged dragon on the lion’s back forming the pitcher’s handle, and a serpentine creature at the end of the lion’s tail.
altText: A work made of copper alloy.

title: Mars, Venus and Cupid
medium: Engraving in black on cream laid paper
creditLine: The Amanda S. Johnson and Marion J. Livingston Fund
description: This engraving was one of Raimondi’s most sought-after works. Here, we see Mars, the Roman god of war, sitting with his elbow on his knee as he twists his muscular body to grab Venus, the goddess of love, by the shoulder. Venus looks down and away, toward Cupid, who pushes a flaming torch, a symbol of passionate love, at her. Mars and Venus had an affair while she was married to Vulcan, the god of fire.
altText: A work made of engraving in black on cream laid paper.

title: At the Circus: The Bareback Rider (Au Cirque: Écuyère)
creditLine: Patterson/Taylor Acquisition Fund; Mr. and Mrs. Donald W. Patterson Endowment Fund
description: One of Toulouse-Lautrec’s favorite haunts was the Cirque Fernando, also the subject of his large painting, Equestrienne (At the Cirque Fernando). Like many of the artists in his circle, Toulouse-Lautrec experimented with styles and materials beyond easel painting. His decision to paint on a tambourine with little castanets was perhaps inspired by the instrument’s association with bohemian life and creative freedom.
altText: A work made of oil on vellum.

title: Statuette of a Striding Figure
creditLine: Anonymous loan
description: Cast in solid copper, this statuette is thought to represent a supernatural being that served as an intermediary between the physical world and the spiritual realm. The muscular, bearded figure wears a headdress of goat horns and ears, a raptor skin over his shoulders, a cylindrical belt around his waist, and boots with curved toes. His eyes are inlaid with shell or stone; the now-missing pupils were probably made from a contrasting material.
altText: A work made of copper.

title: Portrait Statue of a Man, Possibly Emperor Trajan
creditLine: Anonymous loan
description: This ancient Roman sculpture is a portrait statue that is now unfortunately missing its head. The figure wears full military regalia; his body armor is decorated with symbols intended to ward off evil, and his heavy cloak, draped over his shoulder, is a type often worn by Roman military commanders. This elaborate ensemble suggests that he was important—possibly a general or even the emperor.
altText: A work made of marble.

title: Kylix (Drinking Cup)
artistDisplay: Attributed to the Workshop of Nikosthenes Greek; Athens
creditLine: Anonymous loan
description: This vase honors Dionysos as the god of both wine and the theater. When used, raised to a drinker's mouth, it doubled as a mask, with the handles serving as ears and the circular hollow a mouth. The round, wide eyes might have symbolized the intoxicating effects of the drink, the wine god’s gaze, or both. Drinking vessels decorated in this manner are called eye cups.
altText: A work made of terracotta, black-figure.

title: Kylix (Drinking Cup)
creditLine: Promised gift of Mrs. J. William Holland
description: In the center of this scene, a young man dons armor for battle. The woman standing before him holds his shield as attendants look on. Riders approaching on horses and a running youth give the impression of urgency. Because the soldier is not bearded, which indicates youth, and is so much taller than the other figures, which often indicates special status, the young man might represent the Greek hero Achilles.
altText: A work made of terracotta, black-figure.

title: Fireplace Surround
artistDisplay: Designed by George Washington Maher American, 1864–1926 Made by Louis J. Millet American, 1855–1923
creditLine: Gift of Alan Wanzenberg in memory of Jed Johnson
description: Prairie School architect Maher developed a system of design that he called the “motif rhythm theory,” in which he created a signature motif based on local natural forms and used it in various decorative details to harmonize the interior and exterior of a house. Maher frequently collaborated with Louis J. Millet on his commissions, including the Patrick J. King House (1901), from which this fireplace surround came.
altText: A work made of oak and glazed earthenware.

title: The Fountain at Grottaferrata
creditLine: Through prior gift of Mrs. Henry C. Woods; through prior gift of Dellora A. Norris; Lacy Armour Fund; through prior gift of Henry Morgen, Ann G. Morgen, Meyer Wasser and Ruth G. Wasser; Louise and Frank Woods Purchase Fund in honor of Mrs. Edward Harris Brewer
description: Full of golden light, this painting depicts an idealized view of the Italian countryside. Like many young artists of the time, Richter traveled to Rome from Germany to study Classical ruins and the Mediterranean landscape. This work, finished years after he returned to Germany, is based on his detailed drawings of the countryside just outside Rome, including elements that made the site famous, like the fortified monastery in the background.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Mosaic Floor Panel Depicting a Bound Rooster
creditLine: Gift of Lynn Hauser and Neil Ross
description: Roman houses were frequently adorned with wall paintings and floor mosaics, the imagery of which was intended to signify the owner’s wealth and hospitality as well as the quantity and variety of goods available in the house. The bound rooster in this panel might have represented the abundance of livestock available on the host’s estate.
altText: A work made of stone and mortar.

title: Biconical Bead Necklace
creditLine: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Walter Alexander
description: These precious bronze objects are votives, or devotional gifts, which were offered to the gods. They come in many forms: miniature animals, primarily horses, or items of personal adornment, including beads and brooches. This assemblage is characteristic of the thousands of votives that were hung from sacred trees or placed in sanctuaries around Greece. Once a shrine was full, the votives were ceremonially buried to make room for more offerings.
altText: A work made of bronze.

title: Panel from a Sarcophagus Depicting the Abduction of Persephone
creditLine: Anonymous loan
description: This panel—once the long side of a sarcophagus, or coffin––depicts the abduction of Persephone by Hades, the Greek god of the underworld. On the left, Persephone's mother, Demeter, the Greek goddess of the harvest, drives a chariot in search of her daughter. Persephone kneels in the center of the panel, looking upward in the moment before her abduction. On the right, Hades flees with the girl thrown over his shoulder.
altText: A work made of marble.

title: Vase in the Form of a Tropical Plant with Bird and Deity
medium: Stoneware painted with slip and gold
creditLine: Through prior purchase of the Estate of Suzette Morton Davidson, Major Acquisitions Centennial Endowment, Dellora A. Norris Funds
description: In 1886 Paul Gauguin was invited to design pottery with the well-known ceramist Ernest Chaplet. Rather than simply decorating premade vessels, Gauguin chose to model his own unconventional forms by hand, jokingly calling them his “monstrosities.” Here, the wide lip and distinctive shoulder of the vase echo the shape of the tall plant on its surface, while the protruding leaves on its sides suggest handles yet have no utilitarian function.
altText: A work made of stoneware painted with slip and gold.

artistDisplay: Artist unknown (Teotihuacan) Teotihuacan, Vallery of Mexico, Mexico
creditLine: Through prior gifts of Mr. and Mrs. Arthur M. Wood and Mr. and Mrs. William E. Hartmann; Robert Allerton Trust Fund; through prior gifts of Ethel and Julian R. description: Teotihuacan was one of the largest cities in the world during the first millennium CE. Masks like this were displayed in residential compounds and temples, where they were the focus of rituals commemorating ancestors. Although this mask shares features common to others from the city—a broad forehead, prominent nose, receding chin, and widely spaced cheekbones—it is subtly unique, indicating that it may be a stylized portrait.
altText: A work made of stone, spondylus shell, and stucco.

title: Illinois Plate
medium: Porcelain, enamel, and glaze with gilding
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by Harry Root
description: When Potter was a diplomat and United States Consul in Germany, he began the hobby of china painting after he saw women in the consulate taking lessons. This Illinois plate—part of a series of “states” plates—is decorated in polychromatic minerals, gold, and silver. Inside the gold, filigree-patterned cartouche, “Illinois” is depicted as a bald eagle against rays of sunshine, with the state motto, “State Sovereignty, National Union.”
altText: A work made of porcelain, enamel, and glaze with gilding.

title: Mirror with a Handle in the Form of a Female Figure
creditLine: Anonymous loan
description: In Etruria, bronze mirrors were luxury objects designed primarily for women. The front of the bronze disk would have been highly polished in order to reflect the viewer’s image. This example has a handle in the form of a winged Lasa, a minor deity associated with Turan, the Etruscan goddess of love. Because Lasa is thought to have been associated with funerary rites, the vessel she holds might evoke the ceremonial anointing of the dead.
altText: A work made of bronze.

title: Saint John the Baptist in the Wilderness
creditLine: Lacy Armour Fund, Chester D. Tripp Estate Fund, European Painting General Sales Proceeds, Mrs. Albert Beveridge Fund, Rhoades Foundation
description: Adam Elsheimer created imaginary, highly composed landscapes in small paintings on copper. Traveling to Rome in 1600, he was inspired by the city's monuments and artistic environment. In this work, the youthful saint echoes ancient Greek and Roman sculpture while the wooded landscape is indebted to Northern European painting. Though Elsheimer died in Rome at a young age, his painting influenced his fellow artists, including Peter Paul Rubens.
altText: A work made of oil on copper.

title: Openwork Hexagonal Ko-Kiyomizu Ware Bowl
creditLine: Japanese Art Shinkokai Acquisition Fund and Asian Art Acquisition Fund
description: Ko-kiyomizu ware (which translates as “Old Kiyomizu” ware) was named after a temple in Kyoto. It was made in the 18th century and is characterized by brightly colored overglaze enamel. All sides of this bowl feature a complex pattern of medallions covered in blue and green glaze, with peonies along the bottom interior and outside walls. The veins of the leaves, arabesques, and other areas were painted gold after the piece was fired.
altText: A work made of stoneware with overglaze enamels.

title: Hydria (Water Jar)
artistDisplay: Attributed to the Chicago Painter Greek; Athens
creditLine: Gift of Fred Eychaner in honor of Karen B. Alexander
description: This hydria, or water jar, depicts three women engaged in feminine activities. The subject on the left examines her face in a mirror; the central figure holds a chest of jewelry and cosmetics; and the woman on the right holds a large fruit. The artist today known as the Chicago Painter decorated this vase. He takes his name from a larger vessel acquired by the Art Institute in 1889, which was the first example of his work to be identified.
altText: A work made of terracotta, red-figure.

title: Statue of Young Dionysos
creditLine: Anonymous loan
description: This statue depicting Dionysos, god of wine and theater, is one of very few bronze statues to have survived from antiquity. It is thought that the figure once held a kantharos, or wine cup, in his raised right arm and may have held a thyrsos, a staff topped by a pine cone, in his left, since the deity is shown holding them in other ancient sculptures and paintings.
altText: A work made of bronze, copper, and silver (modern).

title: Bowl with Calligraphic Design
medium: Earthenware, white slip with black slip decoration under a transparent glaze
creditLine: Gift of Harvey and Beth Plotnick
description: In the 10th and 11th centuries, a tradition of painting ceramics in thick, colored slips (watered-down clay) became common practice in central and eastern Iran. These vessels were typically decorated with simple calligraphic lines, often containing blessings or pious insights, not unlike fortune cookie messages. Here the text reads, "[Generosity] is a disposition of the dwellers of Paradise . . . regret."
altText: A work made of earthenware, white slip with black slip decoration under a transparent glaze.

title: Solidus (Coin) of Empress Irene
artistDisplay: Byzantine; minted in Constantinople (now Istanbul, Turkey)
creditLine: Gift of the Classical Art Society
description: Throughout history, coins have served as important tools to convey leaders' power. This rare example depicts Empress Irene, one of only three female rulers to hold sole power during the Byzantine Empire. She wears a crown with pearl adornments and a jewel-encrusted scarf and holds an orb and cross-topped staff—all traditional accessories that signaled male imperial power and dominion over the Christian world.
altText: Gold coin featuring a frontal image of a figure wearing a crown, with strands of pearls hanging to her shoulders, holding crosses in each hand. Text around the border reads, "EIRINH BASILISSA," or "Empress Irene."

title: Statue of a Young Satyr Wearing a Theater Mask of Silenus
artistDisplay: Roman, with restorations by Alessandro Algardi (Italian, 1598-1654)
creditLine: Anonymous loan
description: This playful marble sculpture depicts a young satyr—a creature that is part human and part horse or goat and often represents the untamed elements of human nature. The satyr thrusts his hand through the mouth of a theater mask in a gesture both mischievous and menacing. The ancient Roman work is the only free-standing depiction of a masked child satyr known to exist today.
altText: A stone sculpture of a very young, infant-like child standing and wearing a mask in the shape of an older, bearded man. The child pushes its tiny hand through the mask's mouth hole.

title: A Woman at the Élysée Montmartre (Femme à l’Élysée Montmartre)
creditLine: Lacy Armour Fund, Dellora A. Norris Fund, through prior gift of Mr. and Mrs. Chauncey B. Borland, Josephine and John Louis Fund, purchased with funds provided by of John and Alexandra Nichols
description: Like Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec, Anquetin's work focused on modern life, particularly Parisian nightlife. This painting depicts an unescorted woman—unusual at that time—walking through the garden of the Élysée Montmartre, a dance hall in Montmartre. Who she is remains a mystery, but her unusual printed dress and extravagant hat, more theatrical than fashionable, suggest that she might be an off-duty performer.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Woman Strolling
medium: Tropical laurel (Terminalia), stained red and black
creditLine: Through prior bequest of Joseph Winterbotham
description: Gauguin sought to expand the Impressionists’ definition of fine art to include objects—like this sculpture—that might be dismissed as decoration or craft. When he first exhibited this figurine at the Sixth Impressionist Exhibition in 1881, critics disparaged the work and considered it simplistic and crudely whittled. The avant-garde set, however, celebrated its stylized form.
altText: A work made of tropical laurel (terminalia), stained red and black.

title: Decorated Wooden Box
medium: Stained wood with iron, leather, and inlaid with two netsuke masks
creditLine: Through prior bequest of Joseph Winterbotham
description: The box showcases Gauguin’s curiosity about global art forms, which he appropriated and combined in the service of his own creative vision. Across the front of this box, Gauguin fashioned dancers reminiscent of those seen in the work of his contemporary Edgar Degas. On the back, he inlaid Japanese fasteners, called netsuke, shaped as miniature masks. Inside, he hewed a rough, macabre human figure inspired by oak coffins of the Danish Bronze Age.
altText: A work made of stained wood with iron, leather, and inlaid with two netsuke masks.

title: Tureen
creditLine: Mary Swissler Oldberg Fund
description: This exuberant tureen exemplifies the highly imaginative and technically advanced hollowware that made Gorham one of the leading silver manufacturers in the 19th century. The firm was the first major American silver company to introduce Japanese-inspired designs into their product line, ahead of competitors like Tiffany and Company.
altText: A work made of silver.

Williams, Capital Campaign General Acquisitions, Wentworth Greene Field Memorial, Samuel P. Avery, Morris L. Parker, Irving and June Seaman Endowment, and Betty Bell Spooner funds
description: In the 1510s, Sebastiano del Piombo traveled to Rome, where he was drawn into the lively competition between the period's two great luminaries, Michelangelo and Raphael. Michelangelo took Sebastiano under his wing, teaching him his monumental style and providing drawings for commissions. This painting represents a popular composition by Piombo, who became one of the most distinguished painters working during the High Renaissance.
altText: A work made of oil on panel.

title: Statuette of a Horse
creditLine: Katherine K. Adler, Costa A. Pandaleon Greek Memorial, and Mr. and Mrs. Walter Alexander Classical Endowment, James H. Allan and Christopher D. Allan funds
description: This small statuette was created in Greece around the time of the first Olympic games (776 BCE). It was made as a gift for a god and was probably deposited at a religious site. Devotional gifts took many forms, but statuettes of horses were especially popular because the creatures were symbols of affluence. Following the stylistic preference of the time, the sculptor used a few simple shapes to capture the animal’s essence.
altText: A work made of bronze.

title: Saracenic Coffee Pot and Sugar Bowl
artistDisplay: Design attributed to Edward C. Moore (American, 1827–1891) Tiffany and Company (American, founded 1837) New York
creditLine: Mary Swissler Oldberg Fund
description: This coffee pot, with its spherical base, narrow neck, and elongated spout, is based on Islamic vessels. Tiffany and Company first incorporated Islamic elements into their wares at the Paris Universal Exposition in 1867. Edward C. Moore, the chief silver designer, drew inspiration from his own collection of Middle Eastern art objects and design books, appropriating such elements as thin, sinuous forms and intricate, repeating patterns.
altText: A work made of silver and silver gilt.

title: Crucifixion
creditLine: C. Harker and Mae Svoboda Rhodes Acquisition Fund
description: This small cross was made and signed by a woman artist, María Josefa Sánchez. Sánchez was active from 1639 to 1649, probably in Castile, but little else is known about her. Women rarely worked as professional artists in 17th-century Spain; those few who did usually trained in the workshops of their fathers. Some women artists of the period, Sánchez included, may have been nuns who produced devotional works for monastic communities.
altText: A work made of oil on panel.

title: Table
artistDisplay: Attributed to A. & H. Lejambre (American, active 1865–1907) Philadelphia
medium: Rosewood, rosewood veneer, and walnut paint-grained rosewood (secondary woods: ash, bird's eye maple, and walnut), with brass, copper, shell, ebony, and mother-of-pearl inlay, and gilt-brass feet
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by the Antiquarian Society
description: Lightweight and portable, this table could be moved as needed to hold and display household goods. Its luxurious materials, including rosewood, ebony, and mother-of-pearl, enhance the dynamic hexagonal design with its asymmetrical inlay of iridescent insects crawling across the surface. The table is a great example of the late 19th-century Aesthetic Movement, which advocated that functional items should be elevated to art objects.
altText: A work made of rosewood, rosewood veneer, and walnut paint-grained rosewood (secondary woods: ash, bird's eye maple, and walnut), with brass, copper, shell, ebony, and mother-of-pearl inlay, and gilt-brass feet.

title: Coffin of Nespahertahat
artistDisplay: Egyptian; possibly Deir el-Bahri, Thebes (now Luxor), Egypt
creditLine: Gift of Henry H. Getty, Charles L. Hutchinson, Robert H. Fleming, and Norman W. Harris
description: The lid of this human-shaped coffin represents its owner with his arms crossed over his chest. At the time, instead of being entombed in elaborately decorated chapels, elite Egyptians were encased in nesting sets of wooden coffins painted with scenes designed to guide them in the afterlife. This is the inner coffin of what was likely a set of two. The intricate painted decoration presents the deceased in the company of the gods and goddesses.
altText: A work made of wood and pigment.

title: Bust of a Young Man
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by an anonymous donor honoring teachers and their students.
description: This portrait of a model was made in 90 minutes during a demonstration at a London art school. Artist Aimé-Jules Dalou did not speak English, so his classes were visual performances. The sculptor Édouard Lantéri recalled that Dalou “completely carried his students away with him. He knew how to inspire them with the desire to work as well as the love of work, and succeeded in awakening an extraordinary enthusiasm where all before seemed dormant.”
altText: A work made of patinated plaster.

title: Venus, Cupid and Ceres
creditLine: Old Masters Society Fund
description: A newly discovered work by Cornelisz van Haarlem, this colorful painting interprets the ancient witticism, “Without food and drink, love grows cold.” The supple, translucent flesh demonstrates the interest in naturalism that blossomed in Northern Europe in the late 16th and early 17th centuries, which led artists to work increasingly “from life,” that is, from observation of models.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Pair of Candelabra
artistDisplay: Chased by Eugene J. Soligny (American, c. 1833–1901) Tiffany and Company (American, founded 1837) New York
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by the Antiquarian Society through the Mr. and Mrs. William Y. Hutchinson Fund
description: These objects created by the Tiffany Company were commissioned by the United States government and presented to Viscount d’Itajubá of Brazil in gratitude for his role in arbitrating between the United States and Great Britain after the American Civil War. Decorated with ancient Greek figures and symbols, the designs in the silver represent agriculture and commerce and were meant to symbolize prosperity of the United States after the Civil War.
altText: A work made of silver.

title: Storage Jar
artistDisplay: David Drake (American, c. 1801–1870s) Lewis Miles Stoney Bluff Manufactory [plantation] (American, c. 1840–70s) Edgefield, South Carolina
creditLine: Through prior bequest of Arthur Rubloff; Wesley M. Dixon Jr. Endowment Fund
description: This boldly inscribed storage jar was made by David Drake, who was born enslaved around 1800 and learned the art of hand-coiling, throwing, and glazing pottery in Edgefield, South Carolina. Drake was not the only artisan active in Edgefield, and his audacious works represent the artistry, skill, and resilience at a time when enslaved people faced criminalization and violence for reading, writing, or even signing one’s name.
altText: A work made of stoneware and glaze.

title: A Vanitas Still Life with a Flag, Candlestick, Musical Instruments, Books, Writing Paraphernalia, Globes, and Hourglass
creditLine: Through prior bequest of Joseph Winterbotham; Rhoades Foundation and Julius Lewis Acquisition Endowment Fund; European Painting Discretionary Fund
description: Collier was well known in his own time for his still lifes, which replicated in intricate detail actual maps and globes. Here, he reproduced a portion of Frederik de Wit’s 1660 map of the Americas and Jodocus Hondius’s terrestrial globe with a view of Mexico, both of which allude to the Dutch Republic’s international trade networks and the ambition to possess the world through cartographic knowledge.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Self-Portrait as a Chimera
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by Constance T. and Donald W. Patterson and Pamela Kelley Hull
description: This sculpture, which doubles as an inkwell, was created by Sarah Bernhardt, a French actor and artist and perhaps the first global superstar. Here, Bernhardt portrayed herself as a chimera, a mythological creature composed of disparate animals. Bernhardt joined her torso and head to clawed haunches, bat wings, and a dragon-like tail, fashioning a distinct public image for herself through her artwork.
altText: A work made of brass.

title: Close Helmet from an Armor of Tsar Dmitry I
medium: Steel, brass, and traces of gilding
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by John Edwardson; through prior acquisition of the George F. Harding Collection; purchased with funds provided by Paul Carbone; Laird Landmann Arms and Armor Fund; purchased with funds provided by Daniel Manoogian, purchased with funds provided by Michael Haney.
description: This helmet belonged to Tsar Dmitry I, also known as Pseudo-Demetrius I for his false claim of being the son of Ivan the Terrible. Dmitry was highly influenced by Western tastes, and this Italian-made helmet was the height of Western fashion at the time. The upper visor, etched with the Moscow coat of arms and an imperial double-headed eagle, announced the sovereignty of its wearer.
altText: A work made of steel, brass, and traces of gilding.

title: Looking upon the River
creditLine: Purchased with funds provided by the bequest of Muriel J. Kogan
description: In the 1860s, Julie Hart Beers launched a successful career as an artist, supporting herself and her family through her artwork, teaching, and leading sketching excursions for groups of women throughout New England and the Adirondack Mountains. Her detailed, atmospheric landscapes, captured with swift brushwork, both earned her critical acclaim and contributed to the 19th-century landscape painting movement known as the Hudson River School.
altText: Highly detailed painting in mostly earth tones of a forested area that opens up at a small path to frame on all sides a light-blue body of water an a small sailboat, rolling mountains in the distance.

title: Statuette of Venus
creditLine: Katherine K. Adler Memorial Endowment Fund; Cynthia and Terry E. Perucca Fund
description: This statuette depicts Venus, Roman goddess of love, sexuality, and maternity, wearing nothing but the diadem (crown) atop her head. Earlier images often represented her modestly clothed, reinforcing her role as mother of the Roman people. By the first century, Venus was regularly shown fully nude, reflecting body types associated with her Greek counterpart, Aphrodite, whose domain leaned more toward the pleasures of erotic love and seduction.
altText: Profile view of a bronze sculpture with green patina of a nude woman with her right hand raised to eye level. She wears a tiara, her hair in a bun.

title: Young Roman
creditLine: Through prior bequest of Joseph Winterbotham; purchased with funds provided by an anonymous donor, Anne Searle Bent, and Celia and David Hilliard
description: In this plaster bust of her teenage brother, Paul, Claudel portrayed the future writer and diplomat as a proud Roman patrician. His solemn expression and direct gaze contrast the thin drapery that swirls around his shoulders and ripples across his chest. Painted by the artist with transparent layers of yellow, red, green, and brown, the plaster sculpture imitates the time-worn surfaces of ancient Greek and Roman bronzes.

title: Still Life with Grapes and Flowers
creditLine: Through prior purchase with funds provided by Eugene and Helen Huang in memory of Ada and Wilfred Polkinghorne, Justin K. Thannhauser, A. A. Munger Collection, bequest of Celia Schmidt Estate
description: In this exquisite still life, Mélanie de Comoléra skillfully depicted a variety of flowers, fruits, and other luxury objects. On a marble ledge sits a wide bowl, overflowing with grapes and plums. Behind it, a glass pitcher holds a mix of colorful flowers. In the foreground, key limes and jalapeño peppers, botanical species that are not indigenous to Europe, evoke themes of colonialism and global trade.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Fruit Basket
medium: Soft-paste porcelain, underglaze blue decoration, and glaze
creditLine: Vance American Art Fund; Americana, Jane and Morris Weeden, and Roger and J. Peter McCormick endowment funds
description: This delicate fruit basket is a rare example of early American porcelain, one of only 20 known surviving works by American China Manufactory. American manufacturers were slow to develop porcelain wares because of the hazards of the materials and equipment, a lack of skilled craftspeople, and foreign price competition. Even though the American China Manufactory was short-lived, this basket represents the early advancements of the industry.
altText: A work made of soft-paste porcelain, underglaze blue decoration, and glaze.

title: Interior. The Music Room, Strandgade 30
creditLine: Joseph Winterbotham Collection
description: This painting is part of a series by Vilhelm Hammershøi capturing his sparsely decorated apartment at Strandgade 30 in Copenhagen, Denmark. Hammershøi often moved furniture and objects around his home like studio props: here, he placed a chair, piano, cello, and violin in a corner of the drawing room. Despite the inclusion of musical instruments, the scene evokes only eerie silence, with no sense of a human presence to play them.
altText: A work made of oil on canvas.

title: Mount Fuji and the Miho Pine Forest
artistDisplay: Soga Shōhaku 曾我 蕭白 Japanese, 1730-1781
medium: Pair of six panel screens; ink and light colors on paper
creditLine: Through prior gift of Mr. and Mrs. Samuel M. Nickerson
description: This 18th-century folding screen, part of a pair, is by one of the best-known painters in Japan, Soga Shōhaku, revered for his unusual subjects and eccentric style. This screen depicts a rising dragon encased in clouds who is kicking up the wind and rain, affecting the boats on the water. In his wake, the dragon leaves behind a turbulent atmosphere, with dark clouds surrounding Fuji.
altText: A work made of pair of six panel screens; ink and light colors on paper.

title: Mount Fuji and the Miho Pine Forest
artistDisplay: Soga Shōhaku 曾我 蕭白 Japanese, 1730-1781
medium: Pair of six panel screens; ink and light colors on paper
creditLine: Through prior gift of Mr. and Mrs. Samuel M. Nickerson
description: This 18th-century folding screen, part of a pair, is by one of the best known painters in Japan, Soga Shōhaku, revered for his unusual subjects and eccentric style. This screen focuses on the iconic Mount Fuji, a sacred site since ancient times. Shо̄haku depicted the mountain completely covered in snow, painting it in negative. The white of the mountain is the color of the bare paper, and the outlines of the peak are done with ink wash.
altText: A work made of pair of six panel screens; ink and light colors on paper.
